nonexample.explanation: For R90°F, calling the fixed line 90° would point to the y-axis. Direct multiplication fixes (1,1), so the line is 45°, half the rotation angle.

proofSteps: Multiply Rθ by F on the right to obtain [[cosθ,sinθ],[sinθ,−cosθ]]. Multiplying on the left gives FRθ=[[cosθ,−sinθ],[−sinθ,−cosθ]].
The unit vector at angle θ/2 is fixed by RθF, using cos(θ−θ/2)=cos(θ/2) and sin(θ−θ/2)=sin(θ/2). FRθ fixes the line at −θ/2.
Direct multiplication gives FRθF=R−θ, so a reflection conjugates a rotation to its inverse.
Every orthogonal 2×2 matrix has an orthonormal first column (cosθ,sinθ); its second column is either (−sinθ,cosθ) or its negative. Thus the two families Rθ and RθF exhaust O(2).

boundaryCheck.question: At θ=0, which line is fixed by both RθF and FRθ?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Both products equal the fixed F=diag(1,−1); changing the reflection convention here would contradict the matrix.

application.question: At θ=90°, which line does RθF fix?
application.explanation: The fixed line makes half the angle of θ with the x-axis: +45°.

transfer.question: When do FRθ and RθF agree modulo a full turn?
transfer.explanation: Equality requires Rθ=R−θ, hence 2θ=0 modulo 360°. The two classes are 0° and 180°.

orthogonal-plane.connection: The same matrix discipline carries into R³, where an arbitrary axis and continuous angle describe spatial rotations but only special ones preserve a cube.

orthogonal-axis-angle.hook: A 60° turn around a cube diagonal is a genuine rotation. Why is it not a cube symmetry?
orthogonal-axis-angle.objects: Real column vectors in R³. Enter any nonzero axis a, normalize n=a/‖a‖, and rotate by θ using the right-hand rule. The cube vertex set is {(±1,±1,±1)}; it is extra structure beyond Euclidean space.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What unit axis has the direction of (1,1,1)?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Its norm is √3, so divide every component by √3.

examples.title: A body-diagonal third-turn
steps: Let n=(1,1,1)/√3 and θ=120°. Rodrigues’ formula yields R(x,y,z)=(z,x,y).
The axis is fixed, every cube vertex is permuted, and three applications give the identity.
Within turns about this oriented body diagonal, 0°, 120°, 240° and 360° preserve the cube.

examples.title: A general axis remains valid
steps: Take a=(1,2,0) and θ=60°. Normalization gives n=(1,2,0)/√5.
Rodrigues’ formula still gives an orthogonal determinant-one matrix fixing n.
It does not carry the cube vertex set to itself, so no cube-vertex permutation or cube-group word exists.

nonexample.title: Confusing SO(3) with the cube group
nonexample.explanation: At 60° about (1,1,1), the cube moves rigidly in space but its final vertices do not coincide with the original eight. A continuous rotation is not automatically one of the 24 cube rotations.

proofSteps: Decompose v into its component (n·v)n along the unit axis and its component perpendicular to n. Fix the first component.
On the perpendicular plane, turn through θ: Rv=cosθ v+(1−cosθ)(n·v)n+sinθ(n×v). This is Rodrigues’ formula and preserves inner products and orientation.
Substituting v=n gives Rn=n. The axial eigenvalue is 1, and the perpendicular plane has trace 2cosθ, so tr R=1+2cosθ.
At θ=0, every axis gives I. At θ=180°, n and −n give the same map. For the body diagonal, cube preservation requires a 120° multiple, because the three incident edges at an axis endpoint must cycle.

boundaryCheck.question: At θ=180°, what ambiguity remains in an axis-angle description?
choices: n and −n give the same rotation
the rotation ceases to be orthogonal
boundaryCheck.explanation: A half-turn has one axis line, but its two orientations coincide. At θ=0 every axis is possible.

application.question: About (1,1,1), which choice is a cube symmetry?
application.explanation: A 120° turn cycles the three coordinate directions and permutes all eight cube vertices.

transfer.question: For axis (1,2,0) and θ=60°, what may the lab report?
choices: An SO(3) matrix and no cube permutation
A cube word even when vertices leave the cube
transfer.explanation: The nonzero axis gives a valid spatial rotation. A cube permutation and word require preservation of the selected vertex set.

orthogonal-axis-angle.connection: The finite cube group sits inside SO(3). Its action on vertices and conjugacy classes becomes meaningful only after the cube-preservation test succeeds.

mh2220-cayley-embedding.hook: Can every element of a finite group be represented by a distinct permutation without guessing a geometric action?
mh2220-cayley-embedding.objects: For a group G, λg:G→G sends x to gx. It is a left action. Permutations compose right factor first: λg∘λh applies λh before λg. For finite |G|=n, label G to regard each λg as an element of Sₙ.

prerequisiteCheck.question: In S₃, what is λg(e) for any g?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Left multiplication sends the identity to g. This single image will detect whether two regular permutations are equal.

examples.title: C₃ becomes a 3-cycle
steps: Label C₃ additively as 0,1,2. Translation by 1 sends 0→1, 1→2, 2→0, the cycle (0 1 2).
Translation by 2 gives its square, and translation by 0 is the identity permutation.
The three distinct images of 0 certify three distinct permutations.

examples.title: S₃ embeds in S₆
steps: Label the six permutations of three letters by e,(12),(23),(13),(123),(132). For g=(123), the first image in its regular row is λg(e)=g.
For any g,h,x, the two-step image λg(λh(x))=g(hx) equals (gh)x=λgh(x). The live table checks all six x for the selected pair.
Each row of the regular table is a permutation: multiplying on the left by g⁻¹ reverses it. Six distinct first images give six distinct rows.

nonexample.title: Cayley degree need not be minimal
nonexample.explanation: The regular action of S₃ uses six points, giving S₃↪S₆. Its natural action on three letters already gives S₃≅S₃, so Cayley’s construction does not prove minimal permutation degree.

proofSteps: For any g∈G, λg has inverse λg⁻¹ because g⁻¹(gx)=x and g(g⁻¹x)=x. Hence λg belongs to Sym(G).
Associativity gives (λg∘λh)(x)=g(hx)=(gh)x=λgh(x) for every x; λ is a homomorphism.
If λg=λh, evaluate both at e: g=λg(e)=λh(e)=h. Thus λ is injective.
For finite |G|=n, a labeling of the elements identifies Sym(G) with Sₙ. Infinite groups still embed in Sym(G), but the finite-degree statement no longer applies.

boundaryCheck.question: What does Cayley’s construction guarantee for a finite group of order n?
choices: An embedding into Sₙ, not necessarily minimal
A faithful action on every n-point set
boundaryCheck.explanation: The regular action always uses the group’s n elements. A smaller faithful action may exist, but needs separate analysis.

application.question: For C₃ under addition, what permutation is λ₁ on 0,1,2?
application.explanation: Translation by one cyclically permutes all three residues.

transfer.question: Why is the left-regular map for S₃ injective even before computing the full table?
transfer.explanation: An equal pair of permutations would agree at e, forcing the corresponding group elements equal. Group order alone would not prove faithfulness.

mh2220-cayley-embedding.connection: Regular left multiplication is one action among many. The action on three letters can have smaller degree; orbit and stabilizer tools compare such actions.

mh2220-dihedral.hook: Reflect a triangle, then rotate it. Which written product records that chronology?
mh2220-dihedral.objects: Dₙ acts on labelled vertices 0,…,n−1 of a regular n-gon, n≥3. Let r send i→i+1 and s send i→−i modulo n. Composition ab applies b first. Thus doing s then r is rs.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For n=4, where does r send vertex 3?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Add one modulo four: 3+1≡0.

examples.title: Triangle motions have six forms
steps: For n=3, rotations e,r,r² move vertex 0 to 0,1,2 and preserve cyclic order.
The reflections s,rs,r²s also send 0 to 0,1,2, but reverse cyclic order.
Their images of labels plus orientation distinguish all six motions; a mere endpoint would not.

examples.title: Square chronology and reduction
steps: On a square, do s first and r second: the product is rs, which sends i to 1−i.
Do r first and s second: sr sends i to −i−1, and direct calculation gives sr=r⁻¹s.
Reduce srrs by moving s right: sr²s=r⁻². This is a quarter-turn inverse squared, the half-turn.

nonexample.title: Unlabelled shape hides the action
nonexample.explanation: A symmetric square looks unchanged after every symmetry. Without labelled vertices, seeing the same outline cannot determine whether the motion is e, r or s, nor the order of two moves.

proofSteps: The maps r(i)=i+1 and s(i)=−i satisfy rⁿ=e and s²=e by residue arithmetic.
For every vertex i, sr(i)=−i−1=r⁻¹s(i), proving sr=r⁻¹s as transformations.
Use sr=r⁻¹s to move all s letters right; cancel s² and reduce powers of r modulo n. Every word becomes rᵏ or rᵏs for 0≤k<n.

The n rotations preserve cyclic orientation; the n reflections reverse it. Within each family, the image of vertex 0 distinguishes k. Therefore all 2n forms are distinct for n≥3, and their multiplication law is (rᵃsᵇ)(rᶜsᵈ)=rᵃ⁺⁽⁻¹⁾ᵇᶜsᵇ⁺ᵈ, exponents modulo n and 2.

boundaryCheck.question: Which convention makes “reflect, then rotate” equal rs?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Composition rs applies s first, then r. Reversing the convention would change every word calculation.

application.question: In D₄, what is sr²s?
application.explanation: Conjugation inverts r, so sr²s=r⁻²=r² modulo four.

transfer.question: A word in r,s reduces to rᵏs. What evidence distinguishes it from rᵏ?
choices: It reverses cyclic orientation on labelled vertices
transfer.explanation: Both may send vertex 0 to k. Orientation of the labelled cycle distinguishes the two families.

mh2220-dihedral.connection: A dihedral action is a homomorphism into permutations of the vertex labels. The next action unit formalizes that representation and its orbits.

mh2220-actions.hook: The same S₃ element can move a letter but fix a group element. What changed?
mh2220-actions.objects: A left action is G×X→X with e·x=x and (gh)·x=g·(h·x). The group G and acted-on set X are different types. For S₃, compare the three-letter action, left multiplication on S₃ and conjugation on S₃.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For (12) acting on the letters {1,2,3}, where does 2 go?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The transposition swaps 1 and 2 and fixes 3.

examples.title: A labelled triangle before the abstraction
steps: Let r=(123) rotate labels 1→2→3→1 and s=(12) reflect by swapping labels 1 and 2; multiplication applies the right factor first.
On the full labelled set X={1,2,3}, the six motions send the ordered label triple (1,2,3) to e:(1,2,3), r:(2,3,1), r²:(3,1,2), s:(2,1,3), rs:(3,2,1), r²s:(1,3,2).
These six different maps form the action G=D₃≅S₃ on X. The physical triangle alone is insufficient to distinguish them without its labels.

examples.title: One group, three actions
steps: For the natural action, (12) sends letters 1↔2 and fixes 3.
For the regular action on the six group elements, (12) sends e to (12) and has no fixed point.
For conjugation on the six group elements, (12) sends e to e. These orbit questions differ because X and the action formula differ.

examples.title: Verify a nongeometric action
steps: Let S₃ act on itself by g·x=gxg⁻¹. The identity acts trivially.
The composite g·(h·x)=ghx h⁻¹g⁻¹=(gh)x(gh)⁻¹, so the action law holds.
Conjugacy classes, not physical trajectories, are its orbits.

nonexample.title: A tempting failed action
nonexample.explanation: Define g⋆x=g⁻¹x on G itself. For noncommuting g,h, g⋆(h⋆x)=g⁻¹h⁻¹x=(hg)⁻¹x, while (gh)⋆x=(gh)⁻¹x=h⁻¹g⁻¹x. This is not a left action of a nonabelian G.

proofSteps: For any left action, define ρ(g):X→X by ρ(g)(x)=g·x.
The law gives ρ(g)ρ(h)(x)=g·(h·x)=(gh)·x, so ρ is a homomorphism into Sym(X).
The map ρ(g⁻¹) is inverse to ρ(g), since both composites act as e. Thus each group element acts bijectively.
Conversely any homomorphism G→Sym(X) gives a left action by evaluation.

boundaryCheck.question: Which pair names the acted-on set and the group for regular left multiplication of S₃?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The set can happen to equal the underlying group, but its role as X remains separate from the acting group.

application.question: Where does (12) send e under regular left multiplication and conjugation?
application.explanation: Regular multiplication gives (12)e=(12); conjugation gives (12)e(12)⁻¹=e.

transfer.question: Why does g⋆x=g⁻¹x fail as a left action for nonabelian G?
transfer.explanation: Each map is bijective and e works, but g⋆(h⋆x)=(hg)⁻¹x rather than (gh)⁻¹x.

mh2220-actions.connection: Once an action is fixed, a point has an orbit and stabilizer. The next lesson proves their size relation by a coset bijection.

mh2220-orbit-stabilizer.hook: Why can six group elements give only three images of a point?
mh2220-orbit-stabilizer.objects: For a left G-action on X, Gₓ={g:g·x=x} is a subgroup, while G·x={g·x:g∈G} is a subset of X. Left cosets gGₓ correspond to orbit points; they are not quotient-group elements unless Gₓ is normal.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For S₃ on {1,2,3}, which object is a point stabilizer of 1?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The identity and (23) fix 1. A stabilizer is a subset of the acting group, not of the point set.

examples.title: S₃ on three letters
steps: The orbit of 1 is {1,2,3}; the stabilizer G₁={e,(23)} has two elements.
The three left cosets of G₁ map to 1,2,3 under gG₁↦g·1.
The count 3·2=6 is orbit–stabilizer. G₁ is not normal, so these cosets form a G-set, not a quotient group.

examples.title: A cube vertex
steps: The 24 proper cube rotations act on eight vertices. Every vertex is reachable from any other, so its orbit has size eight.
Rotations fixing one chosen vertex cycle the three incident edges, giving a stabilizer of order three.
The product 8·3=24 checks the same theorem on a different geometric set.

nonexample.title: A stabilizer is not the orbit
nonexample.explanation: For S₃ on three letters, the stabilizer of 1 has two group elements; the orbit has three letters. Treating the two as subgroups of the same object is a type error.

proofSteps: Map the left coset gGₓ to g·x. If gh and g represent the same coset with h∈Gₓ, then (gh)·x=g·(h·x)=g·x, so the map is well-defined.
If g·x=k·x, then k⁻¹g fixes x; hence gGₓ=kGₓ, proving injectivity.
Every orbit point is g·x by definition, proving surjectivity.
For finite G, coset counting gives |G·x|=[G:Gₓ]=|G|/|Gₓ|. This is a bijection of G-sets, with no normality claim.

boundaryCheck.question: What extra condition would make G/Gₓ a quotient group rather than only a coset G-set?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Orbit–stabilizer needs only a subgroup. Quotient multiplication additionally needs normality.

application.question: S₃ acts on three letters. If |G₁|=2, what is |G·1|?
application.explanation: The orbit has 6/2=3 points.

transfer.question: A 24-element rotation group acts transitively on eight cube vertices. What is a vertex stabilizer size?
transfer.explanation: Orbit–stabilizer gives 24/8=3. A stabilizer counts rotations, not vertices.

mh2220-orbit-stabilizer.connection: Stabilizers at different points may be nontrivial even when the action kernel is trivial. The next two lessons separate these global and local properties.

actions-faithful-transitive.hook: Can a group action move every point into one orbit while some nonidentity element fixes a point?
actions-faithful-transitive.objects: For a G-set X: faithful means only e fixes every x; transitive means one orbit equals X; free means every point stabilizer is {e}; regular means both free and transitive. Compare S₃ acting on three letters, on itself by left multiplication, and on itself by conjugation.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which test defines a faithful action?
choices: Every orbit is all of X
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Faithfulness is global: only the identity may act trivially on every point. A faithful action may have nontrivial point stabilizers.

examples.title: Faithful and transitive, but not free
steps: S₃ on {1,2,3} is transitive because a permutation can send 1 to any letter.
It is faithful because a permutation fixing all three letters is identity.
The point stabilizer of 1 contains (23), so the action is not free or regular.

examples.title: Regular versus nontransitive
steps: S₃ acting on itself by left multiplication is free: gx=x implies g=e. It is transitive: choose g=yx⁻¹ to send x to y.
Conjugation of S₃ on itself is faithful because its kernel is the center {e}.
Conjugation is not transitive: e is fixed by everyone and forms a singleton orbit.

nonexample.title: Confusing one fixed point with a kernel
nonexample.explanation: Every g fixes e under conjugation, but many g move transpositions. A single fixed point does not put those elements in the whole-action kernel.

proofSteps: For any action, the kernel is ⋂ₓGₓ. Hence free implies faithful whenever X is nonempty, but faithful need not imply free.
Transitive means for every x,y some g sends x to y; it says nothing about the size of Gₓ.
If an action is free and transitive, each ordered pair x,y has exactly one mover: existence by transitivity and uniqueness since stabilizers are trivial. This is regularity.
In the natural S₃ action, a nonidentity transposition fixes one letter but cannot fix all three, proving faithful and transitive does not imply free.

boundaryCheck.question: Which implication holds for a nonempty G-set?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A trivial stabilizer at every point makes the intersection trivial. The natural S₃ action disproves both tempting reverses.

application.question: S₃ on three letters has orbit size 3 and point stabilizer size 2. Which properties hold?
application.explanation: The action is faithful and transitive, while (23) fixes 1.

transfer.question: Conjugation on S₃ fixes e but has kernel {e}. Which conclusion follows?
choices: It is faithful but not transitive
transfer.explanation: The whole kernel is the center, which is trivial, while e is a singleton orbit.

actions-faithful-transitive.connection: The kernel is an intersection of all stabilizers. For one orbit, that intersection is the core of its point stabilizer; the next lesson checks when this differs from the whole-action kernel.

actions-stabilizer-kernel-core.hook: A point stabilizer can be large while the action kernel is trivial. Where did the stabilizer elements go?
actions-stabilizer-kernel-core.objects: For a left G-set X, Gₓ fixes one point; kerρ=⋂ₓGₓ fixes all points. Core_G(H)=⋂g∈G gHg⁻¹. On the single orbit G·x, its action kernel is Core_G(Gₓ).

prerequisiteCheck.question: For S₃ on {1,2,3}, which transposition fixes 1?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: (23) swaps the other two labels and fixes 1.

examples.title: Three conjugate stabilizers
steps: For S₃ on three letters, G₁={e,(23)}, G₂={e,(13)}, and G₃={e,(12)}.
These are conjugate: a permutation sending i to j carries Gᵢ to Gⱼ.
Their intersection is {e}, so a nontrivial point stabilizer coexists with a trivial whole-action kernel.

examples.title: One conjugation orbit is not the whole action
steps: Under conjugation on S₃, the orbit of e is {e} and Gₑ=S₃. Its core is S₃ because all conjugates of the whole group are itself.
The whole-action kernel is Z(S₃)={e}; a transposition moves some other points.
Thus the core of a stabilizer computes the kernel on the selected orbit, not necessarily on all of X.

nonexample.title: A core is not always the whole kernel
nonexample.explanation: At e under conjugation, Core_G(Gₑ)=S₃ while kerρ={e}. Replacing an intersection over every point by the stabilizer of a single orbit is valid only when that orbit is all of X.

proofSteps: Set H=Gₓ. The rule gH↦g·x is well-defined: replacing g by gh with h∈H does not change g·x. It is onto the orbit by definition, and g·x=k·x iff k⁻¹g∈H iff gH=kH, so it is injective. Left multiplication on cosets makes the bijection equivariant.
For any g∈G, the stabilizer of g·x is gGₓg⁻¹: h fixes g·x iff g⁻¹hg fixes x.
Intersecting these stabilizers over all points of G·x gives ⋂g∈G gGₓg⁻¹=Core_G(Gₓ).
The whole-action kernel is the intersection over all X, equivalently the intersection of the orbit kernels.
If the action is transitive, one orbit is X and core equals whole kernel. Without transitivity, the selected core can be strictly larger.

boundaryCheck.question: When does Core_G(Gₓ) necessarily equal the whole-action kernel?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The core is the kernel on that orbit. They coincide if the selected orbit is the entire acted-on set.

application.question: For S₃ on {1,2,3}, what is G₁∩G₂∩G₃?
application.explanation: Each nonidentity transposition fixes just one different letter, so none belongs to all three stabilizers.

transfer.question: Under conjugation on S₃ at x=e, what are Core_G(Gₑ) and kerρ?
transfer.explanation: The singleton orbit has all of S₃ as kernel, but the full conjugation action has kernel the trivial center.

actions-stabilizer-kernel-core.connection: Orbit kernels and normal cores are useful in Sylow conjugacy and subgroup actions: a fixed coset can encode containment of one p-subgroup in a conjugate of another.

groups-cauchy.hook: A prime divides the group order. Where must an element of that prime order hide?
groups-cauchy.objects: Let G be finite and p a prime divisor of |G|. The set T of p-tuples (g₁,…,gₚ) with product e has |G|^(p−1) elements. Cyclic rotation of the entries acts on T.

prerequisiteCheck.question: How many choices are free in a tuple of length p whose product must be e?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Choose the first p−1 entries; the last is their inverse product.

examples.title: A group of order six
steps: For S₃, p=3 divides six, so Cauchy predicts an element of order three.
The two three-cycles (123) and (132) have order three. Counting alone predicts existence, not their exact names.

examples.title: A cyclic group of order ten
steps: For C₁₀, p=5 divides ten. The element 2 modulo ten has additive order five.
The same group has an element of order two, namely 5 modulo ten, because 2 also divides ten.

nonexample.title: A composite divisor needs more
nonexample.explanation: A₄ has order 12 but no element of order six. Cauchy applies to a prime divisor p, not an arbitrary divisor; Lagrange has no converse for element orders.

proofSteps: Choose T={(g₁,…,gₚ)∈Gᵖ:g₁⋯gₚ=e}. The first p−1 choices determine the last, so |T|=|G|^(p−1) is divisible by p.
Rotate a tuple cyclically. If its product is e, the rotated product g₂⋯gₚg₁=g₁⁻¹(g₁⋯gₚ)g₁=e; rotation preserves T and gives an action of Cₚ.
Every rotation orbit has size one or p. Fixed tuples are precisely (g,…,g) with gᵖ=e. Thus the number of such g is congruent to |T|≡0 modulo p.
The identity is one solution, so there are at least p solutions. Choose a nonidentity one; its order divides prime p and therefore equals p.

boundaryCheck.question: What must p be for the orbit argument to force a nonidentity element of order p?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Prime orbit sizes and divisibility of |T| use p prime and p∣|G|.

application.question: Which element of additive C₁₀ has order five?
application.explanation: The least positive k with 2k≡0 mod 10 is five.

transfer.question: Why does one identity tuple imply another fixed tuple?
choices: The fixed tuple count is a positive multiple of p
transfer.explanation: Orbit counting makes the fixed count divisible by p; one cannot be the whole count.

groups-cauchy.connection: Cauchy supplies the prime-order base case. Sylow existence upgrades it to the full p-power dividing |G|.

mh2220-sylow-existence.hook: Does every prime power dividing a finite group order occur as a subgroup order?
mh2220-sylow-existence.objects: Write |G|=pᵃm with p prime and p∤m. A Sylow p-subgroup has order pᵃ. We prove existence by induction on |G| using either a central subgroup of order p or a proper centralizer retaining pᵃ.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For |G|=24, what is the largest power of 2 dividing |G|?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: 24=2³·3, so a Sylow 2-subgroup has order eight.

examples.title: S₃ has two prime cases
steps: For p=2, each subgroup generated by a transposition has order two; these are Sylow 2-subgroups.
For p=3, ⟨(123)⟩={e,(123),(132)} has order three and is Sylow.

examples.title: Cyclic group of order twelve
steps: For p=2, the subgroup ⟨3⟩ in additive C₁₂ has order four.
For p=3, ⟨4⟩ has order three. Prime-power orders occur although an arbitrary divisor need not correspond to a subgroup in a general group.

nonexample.title: A divisor is not a Sylow order
nonexample.explanation: In a group of order 12, a subgroup of order two is a 2-subgroup but is not Sylow: the largest 2-power dividing 12 is four. The theorem cannot be applied with an arbitrary divisor such as six.

proofSteps: Induct on |G|. If p divides |Z(G)|, Cauchy in the finite abelian center gives a central subgroup C of order p. Induction gives a subgroup of G/C of order p^(a−1); its preimage in G has order pᵃ.
Otherwise p does not divide |Z(G)|. The class equation |G|=|Z(G)|+Σ[G:C_G(x)] over noncentral classes implies at least one noncentral class size is not divisible by p.
For that x, C_G(x) is proper, and |C_G(x)|=|G|/[G:C_G(x)] still contains the full factor pᵃ. Induction inside C_G(x) gives a subgroup of order pᵃ.
The base case |G|=1 is vacuous for p dividing |G|. A subgroup of order pᵃ is maximal among p-subgroups because its order already contains the full p-part of |G|.

boundaryCheck.question: Why does the chosen centralizer retain the full p-power pᵃ?
choices: Its index is coprime to p
boundaryCheck.explanation: A noncentral class with size not divisible by p has p-coprime index.

application.question: What orders must Sylow 2- and 3-subgroups of a group of order 24 have?

transfer.question: If a central subgroup C has order p, what order must the subgroup in G/C have to lift to a Sylow subgroup of G?
transfer.explanation: The preimage order multiplies by |C|=p.

mh2220-sylow-existence.connection: Existence provides the subgroups. The coset action next proves that every p-subgroup lies inside a conjugate of any chosen Sylow subgroup.

mh2220-sylow-conjugacy.hook: Why can two maximal p-subgroups differ yet always have the same shape?
mh2220-sylow-conjugacy.objects: Let G be finite with |G|=pᵃm, p∤m. Choose Sylow Q of order pᵃ, and let a p-subgroup H act by left multiplication on the left cosets G/Q.

prerequisiteCheck.question: If |G|=6 and |Q|=2, how many left cosets does G/Q have?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The index is 6/2=3.

examples.title: Three Sylow 2-subgroups of S₃
steps: The subgroups ⟨(12)⟩, ⟨(23)⟩ and ⟨(13)⟩ all have order two.
Conjugation by a three-cycle permutes them. They are distinct but conjugate, so each is isomorphic to C₂.

examples.title: The unique Sylow 3-subgroup of S₃
steps: Q=⟨(123)⟩ has order three and index two.
It is normal, so every conjugate is Q; there is exactly one Sylow 3-subgroup.

nonexample.title: Equal order alone is too weak
nonexample.explanation: In D₄, the central half-turn subgroup ⟨r²⟩ and a reflection subgroup ⟨s⟩ both have order two; the first is central and cannot be conjugate to the second. Neither is a Sylow 2-subgroup of the order-eight group.

proofSteps: The coset set G/Q has m points, a number coprime to p. H acts on it by h·(gQ)=hgQ; each nontrivial H-orbit has size divisible by p.
Because the total number m is not divisible by p, at least one coset gQ is fixed by all of H.
Fixedness means hgQ=gQ for all h∈H, equivalently g⁻¹Hg≤Q. Thus every p-subgroup sits in a conjugate gQg⁻¹.
If H=P is itself Sylow, inclusion between two groups of order pᵃ is equality. Therefore P=gQg⁻¹. A Sylow subgroup is normal exactly when it is the unique Sylow subgroup.

boundaryCheck.question: What makes the fixed-coset argument work?
choices: H has the same order as Q
boundaryCheck.explanation: The fixed point exists for any p-subgroup H because [G:Q] is p-coprime.

application.question: How many Sylow 2-subgroups does S₃ have?
application.explanation: Each transposition generates a different subgroup of order two.

transfer.question: Why does a fixed coset gQ prove conjugacy when H is Sylow?
choices: The inclusion g⁻¹Hg≤Q is between equal finite orders
transfer.explanation: Containment plus equal order turns inclusion into equality.

mh2220-sylow-conjugacy.connection: Conjugation on the Sylow set is transitive. Its stabilizer is a normalizer, giving the divisibility and congruence restrictions on the count.

mh2220-sylow-counts.hook: Arithmetic says several Sylow counts are possible. Which ones can the group realize?
mh2220-sylow-counts.objects: For |G|=pᵃm with p∤m, let nₚ be the number of Sylow p-subgroups. Fix one P. Conjugation on the Sylow set has stabilizer N_G(P), so nₚ=[G:N_G(P)].

prerequisiteCheck.question: For |G|=6 and p=2, what is m?

examples.title: S₃ separates candidates from reality
steps: For |S₃|=6 and p=2, n₂ divides 3 and is 1 modulo 2: arithmetic allows 1 or 3.
The three transpositions generate three distinct order-two subgroups, so S₃ realizes n₂=3. Arithmetic alone did not decide.

examples.title: A forced normal Sylow subgroup
steps: For |S₃|=6 and p=3, n₃ divides 2 and is 1 modulo 3.
Only n₃=1 survives; ⟨(123)⟩ is normal.

nonexample.title: A permitted number need not occur
nonexample.explanation: For p=2 in S₃, the arithmetic candidate n₂=1 passes both congruence and divisibility, but S₃ has three Sylow 2-subgroups. The restrictions are necessary, not sufficient.

proofSteps: Sylow conjugacy makes the G-action on Sylow p-subgroups transitive. The stabilizer of P is N_G(P), so nₚ=[G:N_G(P)]. Since P≤N_G(P), this index divides [G:P]=m.
Let P itself act by conjugation on the Sylow set. P fixes itself. Suppose it fixes another Q; then P≤N_G(Q), making PQ a subgroup because Q is normal in PQ.
The order |PQ|=|P||Q|/|P∩Q| is a p-power. By maximality of a Sylow subgroup, PQ=P=Q. Hence P is the only fixed Sylow subgroup.
Every other P-orbit has size divisible by p. Counting the one fixed point modulo p gives nₚ≡1 mod p. These conditions restrict possibilities but do not ensure each candidate occurs.

For |G|=30, the conditions give n₅∈{1,6} and n₃∈{1,10}. If neither is 1, the six order-five subgroups contribute 6·4=24 distinct nonidentity elements; different prime-order subgroups intersect only in the identity.

The ten order-three subgroups likewise contribute 10·2=20 distinct nonidentity elements. None has order 5, so this would require 44 nonidentity elements in a group with only 29. This contradiction proves n₅=1 or n₃=1.

boundaryCheck.question: Why does nₚ divide m=[G:P]?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The normalizer contains P, so [G:N_G(P)] divides [G:P].

application.question: For |G|=6 and p=2, which n₂ values survive arithmetic alone?
application.explanation: Divisors of m=3 are 1 and 3; both are 1 mod 2.

transfer.question: If nₚ=1, what follows?
choices: The unique Sylow p-subgroup is normal
transfer.explanation: Conjugation preserves the Sylow set; its unique member is fixed by all g∈G.

mh2220-sylow-counts.connection: Small-group classification uses these restrictions together with Cauchy and conjugation action, rather than treating candidate counts as a classification.

mh2220-small-groups.hook: Why do groups of order six have exactly two isomorphism types?
mh2220-small-groups.objects: Let |G|=6. Cauchy supplies r of order three and s of order two. H=⟨r⟩ has index two, hence is normal. Conjugation by s is an automorphism of H, with only two possible images of r: r or r⁻¹.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the index of an order-three subgroup in a group of order six?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The index is 6/3=2.

examples.title: Commuting generators give C₆
steps: If srs⁻¹=r, then r and s commute. H∩⟨s⟩={e}, so the six products rⁱsʲ are distinct.
The element rs has order six, yielding G≅C₆.

examples.title: Inverting conjugation gives S₃
steps: If srs⁻¹=r⁻¹, the relations r³=s²=e and srs=r⁻¹ describe triangle symmetries.
The six normal forms rⁱsʲ map distinctly to S₃ using r=(123), s=(12), so G≅D₃≅S₃.

nonexample.title: Equal cardinality is not enough
nonexample.explanation: C₆ and S₃ both have six elements, but C₆ is abelian and S₃ is not. Drawing six vertices or checking size alone does not identify the group.

proofSteps: Cauchy gives elements r,s of orders 3,2. H=⟨r⟩ has index two and is normal; s lies outside H, H∩⟨s⟩={e}, and the products rⁱsʲ exhaust G.
Conjugation by s restricts to an automorphism of C₃. Such an automorphism sends generator r to r or r⁻¹. These are the only cases.
If srs⁻¹=r, generators commute. The product rs has order six, so G≅C₆.

If srs⁻¹=r⁻¹, the six distinct normal forms obey the dihedral relations. Sending r to (123) and s to (12) gives an isomorphism with S₃. This classification needs the conjugation action, not a premature name for an extension.

boundaryCheck.question: Why is H=⟨r⟩ normal in G?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Every index-two subgroup is normal because the two left and right cosets are H and its complement.

application.question: If srs⁻¹=r⁻¹, which familiar order-six group results?
application.explanation: These are the triangle symmetry relations.

transfer.question: What property distinguishes the two order-six types?
choices: Whether s conjugates r to r or r⁻¹
transfer.explanation: The two automorphisms of C₃ produce commuting or inverting multiplication.

mh2220-small-groups.connection: The same normal-subgroup and conjugation tools later organize groups of larger order and semidirect products.

m3220-rings.hook: Two operations share one set. Which axioms belong to which operation?
m3220-rings.objects: Course convention: a ring R is an abelian group under +, has associative multiplication and both distributive laws; a multiplicative 1 and commutativity are optional unless stated. A unital ring has 1. In the zero ring, 0=1 if one allows the trivial unital ring.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What structure must (R,+) have in every ring?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Addition has 0 and additive inverses and is commutative; multiplication need not have inverses.

examples.title: ℤ and its even subring
steps: ℤ has its usual addition and multiplication, is commutative, and has identity 1. It is an integral domain.
2ℤ is closed under both operations and additive inverses, and inherits distributivity; under the course convention it is a ring. It has no multiplicative identity of its own.

examples.title: Matrices and the zero ring
steps: For any field F, M₂(F) has matrix addition as an abelian group, associative multiplication and identity I₂. Multiplication is not commutative: E₁₂E₂₁=E₁₁, while E₂₁E₁₂=E₂₂.
The one-element zero ring has 0·0=0 and satisfies ring axioms. If it is called unital, its 1 equals 0; a theorem requiring 1≠0 excludes it.

nonexample.title: Multiplicative inverses are not an axiom
nonexample.explanation: ℤ is a ring even though 2 has no multiplicative inverse. Requiring inverses for every nonzero element would ask for a division ring, a stronger structure.

proofSteps: From additive group axioms, 0 and additive negatives exist. Associativity of multiplication and both distributive laws are separate requirements; neither follows from the addition table.
For any a, a0=a(0+0)=a0+a0. Add the additive inverse of a0 to obtain a0=0; similarly 0a=0.
Then 0=(a+(-a))b=ab+(-a)b, so (-a)b=-(ab), and likewise a(-b)=-(ab). These sign laws need distributivity and cancellation, not commutativity or 1.
For 2ℤ, inherited associativity/distributivity and closure prove the ring axioms. If 2k were its identity, (2k)·2=2 would give 2k=1 in ℤ, impossible.

boundaryCheck.question: Which property is optional in this course’s ring convention?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The notes allow rings without 1, such as 2ℤ. State a unital hypothesis when a theorem needs it.

application.question: What are E₁₂E₂₁ and E₂₁E₁₂ in M₂(F)?
application.explanation: Matrix-unit multiplication gives EᵢⱼEₖₗ=δⱼₖEᵢₗ.

transfer.question: A theorem assumes a nonzero unital commutative ring. Can it be applied automatically to 2ℤ or M₂(F)?
choices: No: 2ℤ lacks 1 and M₂(F) is noncommutative
transfer.explanation: The extra hypotheses must be checked for each example, not inferred from the word ring.

m3220-rings.connection: The next lesson adds a unital hypothesis to discuss units and separates invertibility from zero divisors.

m3220-units.hook: Is every nonunit a zero divisor?
m3220-units.objects: In a unital ring, a unit u has a two-sided inverse v with uv=vu=1. In a commutative ring, a nonzero zero divisor a kills a nonzero b. In a noncommutative ring, left and right zero divisors can differ.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Is 2 a unit in ℤ?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Only ±1 are units of ℤ; 1/2 is not an integer.

examples.title: ℤ versus ℤ/8ℤ
steps: In ℤ, 2 is a nonzero nonunit but not a zero divisor because ℤ is a domain.
In ℤ/8ℤ, [3] is a unit since 3·3≡1; [2] is a nonzero zero divisor since 2·4≡0. The units are [1],[3],[5],[7].

examples.title: Finite matrices and one-sided inverses
steps: Over a field F, A∈M₂(F) is a unit exactly when det A≠0. A nonzero singular matrix kills a nonzero vector, so it is a zero divisor in M₂(F).
For square matrices over F, AB=I₂ implies det A·det B=1 and hence BA=I₂. Thus a one-sided inverse becomes two-sided in this finite matrix example, though not in every unital ring.

nonexample.title: Infinite shifts separate one side from two
nonexample.explanation: On the vector space with basis e₀,e₁,…, define S(eᵢ)=eᵢ₊₁ and L(e₀)=0, L(eᵢ₊₁)=eᵢ. Then LS=I but SL≠I. These endomorphisms are one-sided inverses, not units; the finite-square-matrix implication cannot be used without its hypothesis.

proofSteps: In ℤ/nℤ, [a] has an inverse exactly when integers u,k solve au+kn=1. Bézout says this is equivalent to gcd(a,n)=1.
For n=8, the residues coprime to 8 are 1,3,5,7. A residue 2 has 2·4=0 mod 8 with both factors nonzero, so it is a zero divisor.
In an integral domain, if nonzero a killed nonzero b, ab=0 would contradict the domain axiom. Thus a domain may have nonunits but has no nonzero zero divisors.
For square matrices over a field, AB=I forces det A≠0, so A is invertible and B=A⁻¹. The shift example shows why this argument needs finite dimension.

boundaryCheck.question: When does AB=I force BA=I in the stated matrix argument?
choices: For finite square matrices over a field
boundaryCheck.explanation: The determinant argument uses finite square matrices over a field; infinite shifts disprove the general claim.

application.question: Which residues are units in ℤ/8ℤ?
application.explanation: Exactly the residues coprime to eight are units.

transfer.question: What does 2∈ℤ show about the proposed rule “every nonunit is a zero divisor”?
choices: It is false even in an integral domain
transfer.explanation: A zero divisor must kill a nonzero element; 2 cannot do that in ℤ.

m3220-units.connection: Ideals absorb multiplication, whether or not their elements are units. They are the right subobjects for quotient rings.

m3220-ideals.hook: Why can an additive subgroup fail to support quotient multiplication?
m3220-ideals.objects: A two-sided ideal I of a ring R is an additive subgroup with rI⊆I and Ir⊆I for every r∈R. In a commutative ring the two absorptions coincide. A left ideal needs only rI⊆I.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which condition is extra for a two-sided ideal beyond additive subgroup closure?
choices: Absorption under multiplication by every ring element on both sides
Closure only under its own multiplication
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The quotient product needs changes in either representative to remain inside I.

examples.title: Principal ideals in commutative rings
steps: In ℤ, nℤ is an ideal: sums and additive negatives remain multiples of n, and r(nk)=n(rk).
For a field F, (X²+1)⊂F[X] is an ideal. The coefficient field matters for later factor and quotient claims: over ℝ it yields a copy of ℂ, while over F₂ the polynomial is (X+1)².

examples.title: A matrix left ideal is not two-sided
steps: In M₂(F), let L={[[a,0],[b,0]]:a,b∈F}, the matrices supported in the first column. Left multiplication preserves the zero second column, so L is a left ideal.
E₁₁∈L but E₁₁E₁₂=E₁₂∉L; right absorption fails, so L cannot define ordinary quotient-ring multiplication.

nonexample.title: A subring need not be an ideal
nonexample.explanation: The diagonal matrices in M₂(F) form a unital subring. Yet E₁₂·E₂₂=E₁₂ is not diagonal, so the subring is not a two-sided ideal.

proofSteps: An ideal is an additive subgroup, so cosets a+I can be added. To multiply cosets independently of representatives, changes a→a+i and b→b+j must leave (a+i)(b+j)−ab=aj+ib+ij in I.
For the first-column matrix set L, any A times a member of L still has zero second column; E₁₁E₁₂ leaves L, proving it is only a left ideal.
Let J be a nonzero two-sided ideal of M₂(F), with F a field. Choose A∈J with an entry aᵢⱼ≠0. Then Eₖᵢ A Eⱼₗ=aᵢⱼEₖₗ∈J for all k,l.
Multiplying by aᵢⱼ⁻¹I₂ gives every matrix unit Eₖₗ∈J; their F-linear combinations span M₂(F), so J=M₂(F). Thus only 0 and the whole ring are two-sided ideals.

boundaryCheck.question: Which assumption lets a nonzero matrix entry produce every matrix unit in the proof?
choices: The coefficient ring is a field
boundaryCheck.explanation: We divide by the nonzero entry aᵢⱼ, which requires a field.

application.question: What happens to E₁₁E₁₂ for the first-column left ideal L?
application.explanation: Matrix-unit multiplication gives E₁₂; its nonzero second column violates membership.

transfer.question: Why is an arbitrary subring insufficient for R/I multiplication?
choices: Every subring is already an ideal
transfer.explanation: A subring may fail absorption by elements of R outside itself, so products of cosets can depend on representatives.

m3220-ideals.connection: Selecting a two-sided ideal makes quotient multiplication meaningful. The V10 lattice tracks which ideals of R survive in R/I.

m3220-ring-hom.hook: Does a ring map have to send 1 to 1?
m3220-ring-hom.objects: Course convention: a ring homomorphism φ:R→S preserves addition and multiplication; preserving 1 is an additional unital-map condition when R,S have identities. Kernel is φ⁻¹(0), and image is φ(R).

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which equality is required of every ring homomorphism here?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Multiplication is preserved; the course treats 1-preservation as an extra condition.

examples.title: Unital evaluation and reduction
steps: Evaluation evᵢ:ℝ[X]→ℂ sends f to f(i). It preserves +,·,1, has kernel (X²+1), and is surjective because a+bi is evᵢ(a+bX).
Reduction ρ:ℤ→ℤ/8ℤ sends n to [n]; it preserves 1, has kernel 8ℤ and image the whole quotient.

examples.title: A multiplicative map that does not preserve 1
steps: Define j:ℤ→ℤ×ℤ by j(n)=(n,0). It preserves + and multiplication componentwise.
Its target identity is (1,1), while j(1)=(1,0). Under the course convention it is a ring map but not a unital map.

nonexample.title: Image need not be an ideal
nonexample.explanation: The image of j is ℤ×{0}, a subring of ℤ×ℤ; this happens to be an ideal, but in general the image of a ring map need not be an ideal. For the inclusion ℤ→ℚ, the image ℤ is a subring and is not an ideal of ℚ because (1/2)·1∉ℤ.

proofSteps: Additive preservation gives φ(0)=0 and φ(−a)=−φ(a), so ker φ is an additive subgroup.
If a∈ker φ and r∈R, then φ(ra)=φ(r)φ(a)=0 and φ(ar)=φ(a)φ(r)=0. Thus ker φ is a two-sided ideal even when R is noncommutative.
For x=φ(a), y=φ(b), the sum/difference and product are images of a±b and ab. Therefore im φ is a subring; it contains 1_S only if φ is unital or another preimage of 1_S exists.
A map is injective exactly when its kernel is {0}, because φ(a)=φ(b) iff φ(a−b)=0. This uses the additive group structure.

boundaryCheck.question: For f:ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ, f(n)=[2n], which homomorphism axioms hold? Check addition, multiplication and preservation of 1 separately.
choices: Addition and multiplication hold; only 1 fails
boundaryCheck.explanation: f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b). But f(1·1)=[2] while f(1)f(1)=[4], and f(1)=[2]≠[1]. Thus it is not a ring homomorphism under either unital convention.

application.question: What is ker(ℤ→ℤ/8ℤ)?
application.explanation: Exactly multiples of eight reduce to zero.

transfer.question: Why is the image of a ring homomorphism not automatically an ideal of its codomain?
choices: It need not absorb multiplication by codomain elements outside the image
transfer.explanation: The inclusion ℤ⊂ℚ is a counterexample: (1/2)·1 is outside ℤ.

m3220-ring-hom.connection: Kernel ideals make quotient maps possible. The next lesson checks multiplication of cosets before the isomorphism theorem.

m3220-quotient-ring.hook: What makes the product (a+I)(b+I) independent of the chosen representatives?
m3220-quotient-ring.objects: Let I be a two-sided ideal of a ring R. The quotient R/I has classes a+I; addition and multiplication are (a+I)+(b+I)=(a+b)+I and (a+I)(b+I)=ab+I. Fix the coefficient ring in each polynomial example.

prerequisiteCheck.question: In ℤ/8ℤ, what class is 10?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: 10−2=8 belongs to 8ℤ, so the classes agree.

examples.title: Integer quotient with visible zero divisors
steps: For R=ℤ and I=8ℤ, the quotient classes are [0],…,[7], with [2][4]=[0] although neither factor is zero.
Changing 2 to 10 changes its representative but not the product class: 10·4−2·4=32∈8ℤ.

examples.title: One coefficient ring, one quadratic quotient
steps: Take R=ℝ[X], I=(X²+1), and evaluation evᵢ:R→ℂ. Division by monic X²+1 writes every f=q(X)(X²+1)+a+bX with a,b∈ℝ.
evᵢ(f)=a+bi, so evᵢ(f)=0 exactly when a=b=0. Thus ker evᵢ=I, and [X]²=[−1] in R/I. The coefficient ring remains ℝ throughout.

nonexample.title: An additive subgroup without absorption
nonexample.explanation: Constants H={0,1}⊂F₂[X] are an additive subgroup but not an ideal: X·1=X∉H. Although X and X+1 differ by 1∈H, multiplying by X changes their products by X∉H, so quotient multiplication would depend on representatives.

proofSteps: If a′=a+i and b′=b+j with i,j∈I, then a′b′−ab=aj+ib+ij. Two-sided absorption and additive closure put all three terms in I.
Likewise a′+b′−(a+b)=i+j∈I. Thus both quotient operations are well-defined; associativity/distributivity descend from R.
In ℝ[X], divide f by X²+1 to obtain unique a+bX remainder. Evaluation at i vanishes iff a+bi=0, hence iff a=b=0, proving ker evᵢ=(X²+1).
The induced map [f]↦f(i) is well-defined and bijective onto ℂ. The relation [X]²=[−1] holds in the quotient, not as an equality X²=−1 in ℝ[X].
For the displayed integer-coefficient theorem, evaluate φ:Z[X]→Z[i] at i. It is a ring map, onto because a+bi=φ(a+bX), and (X²+1) lies in its kernel.

Division by the monic polynomial X²+1 works within Z[X]: repeatedly subtract the integral leading coefficient times a power of X times X²+1, until the remainder is a+bX. If φ(f)=0, the remainder evaluates to a+bi=0, forcing a=b=0. Hence kerφ=(X²+1).

The induced map Z[X]/(X²+1)→Z[i] is therefore well-defined, onto and injective by the kernel calculation. The earlier real-coefficient example has the same argument with R and C, but a different coefficient ring.

boundaryCheck.question: Why must I be two-sided in a possibly noncommutative ring?
choices: Both aj and ib must lie in I
boundaryCheck.explanation: Changing either representative creates products on both sides of elements of I.

application.question: In ℝ[X]/(X²+1), what is [X]²?
application.explanation: X²+1 belongs to I, so the classes of X² and −1 agree.

transfer.question: Why does the constants subgroup H⊂F₂[X] fail as a quotient-ring ideal?
choices: H is not closed under addition
transfer.explanation: Absorption fails, producing representative-dependent products.

m3220-quotient-ring.connection: The first ring isomorphism theorem packages this descent and identifies exactly when the induced map is injective or surjective.

m3220-first-ring-isomorphism.hook: A map kills an ideal. Does it become a map from the quotient, and is that map an isomorphism?
m3220-first-ring-isomorphism.objects: Let φ:R→S be a ring homomorphism and I a two-sided ideal with I⊆ker φ. The induced map φ̄:R/I→S sends [r] to φ(r). Its image is im φ and kernel is (ker φ)/I.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What must hold for [r]↦φ(r) to be independent of representatives modulo I?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: If r−r′∈I, their images agree exactly when φ kills I.

examples.title: Reduction modulo 12 followed by modulo 6
steps: Let φ:ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ be reduction and I=12ℤ⊂ker φ=6ℤ. The induced map ℤ/12ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ sends [n]₁₂ to [n]₆.
It is surjective but not injective: [0]₁₂ and [6]₁₂ differ yet have the same image. Its kernel is 6ℤ/12ℤ.

examples.title: Evaluation at i gives an isomorphism
steps: For φ=evᵢ:ℝ[X]→ℂ, polynomial division shows ker φ=(X²+1).
Taking I=ker φ gives a bijective induced map ℝ[X]/(X²+1)→ℂ; its inverse sends a+bi to [a+bX].

nonexample.title: The codomain can be larger than the image
nonexample.explanation: The inclusion ℤ→ℚ has kernel {0}; the first isomorphism theorem gives ℤ/{0}≅ℤ as the image, not an isomorphism with all of ℚ.

proofSteps: Well-definedness: if r+I=r′+I, then r−r′∈I⊆ker φ, so φ(r)=φ(r′). The formula therefore defines a unique map because every coset has a representative.
The induced map preserves addition and multiplication by the corresponding laws for φ. Its image is im φ, since every φ(r) is reached by [r].
Its kernel consists of classes [r] with r∈ker φ, namely (ker φ)/I. It is injective exactly when ker φ=I.
It is surjective onto S exactly when φ is surjective. Regardless, choosing I=ker φ gives the first isomorphism R/ker φ≅im φ.

boundaryCheck.question: Which condition makes the induced map R/I→S injective?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The induced kernel is (ker φ)/I, which is zero exactly when the two ideals coincide.

application.question: Let φ:ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ send n to [n]₆ and I=12ℤ. Construct the induced map ℤ/12ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ and identify its kernel.
application.explanation: Because 12ℤ⊆ker φ=6ℤ, representatives differing by 12 have the same image modulo 6. The unique descended map sends [n]₁₂ to φ(n)=[n]₆. Its kernel is {[0]₁₂,[6]₁₂}.

transfer.question: If φ:R→S is not surjective, what does R/ker φ identify with?
transfer.explanation: The induced map reaches exactly the image; a larger codomain remains larger.

m3220-first-ring-isomorphism.connection: The quotient lattice workbench links ideals containing I to ideals of R/I. The next unit studies polynomial divisibility and factorisation in such rings.

m3220-euclidean.hook: Why does repeated division produce both a gcd and its Bézout coefficients?
m3220-euclidean.objects: In a Euclidean domain R, a nonzero b divides a with a=qb+r and either r=0 or δ(r)<δ(b). δ is a Euclidean function; it need not be a discrete valuation.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which remainder permits another strict descent?
choices: Any r with larger δ than b
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The integer Euclidean function is |·| and each nonzero remainder has smaller value.

examples.title: 252 and 198: every division
steps: 36=2·18+0. The last nonzero remainder is gcd(252,198)=18.

nonexample.title: A Euclidean function is not automatically a valuation
nonexample.explanation: The integer size |n| gives division descent, but |ab|=|a||b| is not the nonarchimedean sum law of a discrete valuation; no valuation claim follows.

proofSteps: At each step a=qb+r implies (a,b)=(b,r): r=a−qb and a=qb+r give both inclusions of generated ideals.
The strictly decreasing nonnegative integer values δ(b),δ(r),… cannot continue forever, so a zero remainder occurs.
The final nonzero remainder generates the original two-generated ideal. Back-substitution expresses it as a linear combination of the initial inputs.
In ℤ the positive generator is the gcd; in an arbitrary Euclidean domain the generator is determined only up to a unit.

boundaryCheck.question: Why must the Euclidean algorithm stop?
choices: The nonzero remainder values strictly decrease in ℕ
boundaryCheck.explanation: Well-ordering of ℕ forbids an infinite strict descent.

application.question: What Bézout identity follows for 252 and 198?
application.explanation: Back-substitution through 54 and 36 gives 18=4·252−5·198.

transfer.question: What invariant survives 252=198+54?
transfer.explanation: Each pair generates the same ideal; the remaining remainders retain this invariant.

m3220-euclidean.connection: The minimum-remainder argument upgrades Euclidean descent to every ideal being principal.

m3220-pid.hook: Why is every ideal of a Euclidean domain generated by one element?
m3220-pid.objects: A PID is an integral domain in which every ideal is principal. A principal ideal is one ideal of the form (a); that does not by itself make the whole ring a PID.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which ideal needs a separate case in the minimum-remainder proof?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The zero ideal is already generated by 0, and choosing a nonzero element of it is impossible.

examples.title: The zero ideal
steps: If I={0}, then I=(0). No positive Euclidean value is needed.
Every element of I is 0=0·0, so the reverse inclusion I⊆(0) is immediate. The nonzero minimum argument starts only after this case.

examples.title: A nonzero ideal
steps: Choose nonzero a∈I with minimal δ(a) among nonzero elements of I.
For b∈I divide b=qa+r; then r=b−qa∈I. If r≠0, δ(r)<δ(a), contradicting minimality.
Thus r=0 for every b∈I, so I⊆(a); a∈I gives (a)⊆I. Hence I=(a).

nonexample.title: Reversing the arrow
nonexample.explanation: Euclidean⇒PID is proved. A reverse implication needs an independent theorem or counterexample; the minimum-remainder proof does not provide Euclidean division from principality.

proofSteps: A Euclidean domain is an integral domain with division descent. Its zero ideal is principal as (0).
For a nonzero ideal use well-ordering of δ(I\{0}) to choose a minimal nonzero a.
Every b∈I has b=qa+r; ideal closure puts r in I, and Euclidean minimality forces r=0.
Therefore every ideal is principal. In a PID, ascending chains of ideals stabilize because the union is itself a principal ideal whose generator appears in one member of the chain.

boundaryCheck.question: Why does the proof not choose a minimum from I={0}?
choices: The zero ideal is not principal
boundaryCheck.explanation: Handle I=(0) separately; the minimum argument applies only to nonzero ideals.

application.question: Let I=(18,30)⊂ℤ. Which generator does the Euclidean proof produce?

transfer.question: Which statement follows from proving (6) is principal?
choices: That one ideal is principal, not that its entire ring is a PID
Every commutative ring is a PID
transfer.explanation: PID is a property of all ideals of an integral domain.

m3220-pid.connection: Next distinguish factorisation existence from uniqueness, using principal ideals and prime irreducibles.

m3220-ufd.hook: What can fail when two products of irreducibles represent the same element?
m3220-ufd.objects: A UFD is an integral domain where every nonzero nonunit factors into irreducibles, and those factors are unique up to order and associates. Existence and uniqueness are separate claims.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which change does not violate uniqueness in ℤ?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Signs are units in ℤ, so the two displayed integer factorizations differ only by associates.

examples.title: PID route: existence and uniqueness
steps: If a nonunit is reducible, write a=bc with both nonunits. In a PID, strict containment (a)⊊(b) follows, since equality would force c to be a unit.
An infinite extraction would give a strictly ascending chain of ideals, impossible in a PID. Thus a finite irreducible factorisation exists.
For irreducible p in a PID, (p) is maximal among proper principal ideals and hence prime. Thus p|ab implies p|a or p|b. Repeated cancellation matches irreducibles up to associates.

examples.title: 6 in ℤ[√−5]
steps: 6=2·3=(1+√−5)(1−√−5). Norm a²+5b² is multiplicative and units have norm 1.
N(2)=4 and N(3)=9. Neither can split into nonunits: a norm-2 or norm-3 factor would be needed, and a²+5b²=2 or 3 has no solution.
N(1±√−5)=6. A nontrivial split would require norm 2 and 3 factors, which do not exist. The four factors are irreducible; their norms 4,9,6,6 show the two multisets are not associates.

nonexample.title: A different ordering is not a counterexample
nonexample.explanation: 3·2 and 2·3 are the same factorization up to order; multiplying factors by units also does not break UFD uniqueness.

proofSteps: PID implies ACC on ideals: the union of an ascending chain is an ideal (a), and a belongs to some stage, forcing stabilization.
Repeatedly splitting a reducible nonunit strictly enlarges its generated principal ideal, so ACC gives finite existence.
If irreducible p has (p)⊆(a)⊆R, then p=ab. Irreducibility makes a a unit or an associate of p, so (p) is maximal and therefore prime.
Prime divisibility and cancellation match factors one by one; only units and permutations remain. ℤ[√−5] shows uniqueness can fail outside this hypothesis.

boundaryCheck.question: Which two obligations define a UFD?
choices: Existence and uniqueness up to associates/order
boundaryCheck.explanation: A terminating factorization alone says nothing about whether two irreducible lists agree.

application.question: Why do 2·3 and (1+√−5)(1−√−5) witness nonuniqueness?
choices: All four factors are irreducible and the two pairs are not associates
The factors differ only by units
application.explanation: The norm rules out norm 2 or 3 factors and distinguishes associate classes.

transfer.question: If two factorizations differ only by units and order, what failed?
choices: Nothing; uniqueness permits associates and permutation
transfer.explanation: Normalize by associates before diagnosing uniqueness.

m3220-ufd.connection: Polynomial UFD arguments use primitive content and Gauss’s lemma; first perform legal polynomial division.

m3220-polynomial-division.hook: Which leading coefficients make cancellation possible?
m3220-polynomial-division.objects: For f,g∈A[X], division by g≠0 with f=qg+r and deg r<deg g works when A is a field, or when g is monic over any commutative ring A. Uniqueness follows from degree of a product with monic g.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Over ℤ[X], which divisor always admits long division with integral quotient?
choices: Any polynomial with nonzero leading coefficient
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A monic leading coefficient needs no inverse.

examples.title: Cancel every leading term
steps: Over ℚ[X], divide X³+2X²+X+1 by X+1. Subtract X²(X+1), leaving X²+X+1.
Subtract X(X+1), leaving 1. Thus quotient X²+X and remainder 1; direct multiplication recovers the dividend.

examples.title: A nonunit blocks integral cancellation
steps: Trying to divide X by 2X+1 in ℤ[X] requires leading quotient coefficient 1/2, outside ℤ.
Over ℚ[X], X=(1/2)(2X+1)−1/2. This is a legal field division, not a ℤ[X] quotient/remainder.

nonexample.title: An illegal quotient over ℤ
nonexample.explanation: Writing X=(1/2)(2X+1)−1/2 does not prove division in ℤ[X]; both proposed quotient and remainder leave the coefficient ring.

proofSteps: At each step cancel the leading term with a scalar inverse in a field, or with the leading coefficient 1 when g is monic.
The new remainder has strictly smaller degree, so repeated cancellation terminates.
If f=qg+r=q′g+r′ with deg r,deg r′<deg g, then (q−q′)g=r′−r. For a field or monic g, any nonzero left side has degree at least deg g, a contradiction.
Over a general ring with a nonunit leading coefficient, the cancellation coefficient may not exist; the same uniqueness claim is not being asserted without hypotheses.

boundaryCheck.question: Why does division by 2X+1 fail for f=X over ℤ[X]?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The leading quotient term would be 1/2, which is unavailable in ℤ.

application.question: Divide X³+2X²+X+1 by X+1 over ℚ. What is (q,r)?
application.explanation: Two cancellation steps leave remainder 1.

transfer.question: Why is division by monic X²+1 valid over ℤ[X]?
choices: Leading cancellation uses coefficient 1 without inversion
transfer.explanation: Monicity is enough over a commutative coefficient ring.

m3220-polynomial-division.connection: Content and primitive factors connect polynomial division to factorisation over ℚ and ℤ.

m3220-gauss.hook: When does a factorisation over ℚ descend to one over ℤ?
m3220-gauss.objects: For nonzero f∈ℤ[X], content c(f) is the positive gcd of its coefficients; primitive part f/c(f) has content 1. Gauss’s lemma says a product of primitive integer polynomials is primitive.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the content of 6X²+9X+3?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The positive gcd of 6,9,3 is 3; the primitive part is 2X²+3X+1.

examples.title: Primitive product
steps: If primitive f and g had a product whose coefficients all share a prime p, reduce both modulo p.
Their reductions are nonzero in the integral domain Fₚ[X], so their product cannot be zero; contradiction.

examples.title: Clear rational factors
steps: Suppose primitive F∈ℤ[X] factors as nonconstant A B in ℚ[X]. Write A=(a/b)A₀ and B=(c/d)B₀ with primitive A₀,B₀∈ℤ[X] and rational scalars.
Gauss makes A₀B₀ primitive. Since F=(ac/bd)A₀B₀ is primitive too, the scalar is ±1 (compare integer content after lowest terms).
Thus F=±A₀B₀ is a factorization in ℤ[X] with the same positive factor degrees. Conversely an integer factorization is already rational.

nonexample.title: Content 6 does not imply primitive
nonexample.explanation: 6X²+9X+3 has content 3. Apply Gauss to 2X²+3X+1 and track the scalar content separately.

proofSteps: Every nonzero integer polynomial splits as content times primitive part, unique up to sign.
If a prime divides all coefficients of a primitive product, reduction modulo p makes a product of two nonzero polynomials zero in Fₚ[X], impossible.
Any rational factors can be written as rational scalar multiples of primitive integer polynomials by clearing denominators and dividing their contents.

The primitive product has content 1, so comparison with the primitive target forces the scalar to be ±1. Nonconstant degrees survive, giving equivalence of reducibility over ℚ and ℤ for primitive positive-degree polynomials.

boundaryCheck.question: Why is Fₚ[X] suitable for the primitive-product proof?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Nonzero reductions cannot multiply to zero.

application.question: What is the primitive part of 6X²+9X+3?
application.explanation: Divide every coefficient by content 3.

transfer.question: A primitive F∈ℤ[X] factors into nonconstant polynomials over ℚ. What follows?
choices: It factors into nonconstant integer polynomials up to a unit
transfer.explanation: Clear denominators, take primitive parts, and use Gauss to force the remaining scalar to ±1.

m3220-gauss.connection: Eisenstein supplies a sufficient irreducibility certificate after Gauss passes from ℤ[X] to ℚ[X].

m3220-eisenstein.hook: Can a change of variable reveal an irreducibility certificate?
m3220-eisenstein.objects: For f=aₙXⁿ+⋯+a₀∈ℤ[X], a prime p is Eisenstein if p∤aₙ, p divides every aᵢ for i<n, and p²∤a₀. Then primitive f is irreducible over ℚ; failure of this sufficient test is inconclusive.

prerequisiteCheck.question: If p divides the leading coefficient, can that p certify Eisenstein?
choices: Yes if it divides the constant
Yes if p² divides the constant
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The leading coefficient must remain nonzero modulo p.

examples.title: Shift X⁴+1
steps: Substitute X+1: (X+1)⁴+1=X⁴+4X³+6X²+4X+2.
For p=2, the leading coefficient 1 is odd; all lower coefficients 4,6,4,2 are even; the constant 2 is not divisible by 4.
Eisenstein proves the shifted polynomial irreducible in ℚ[X]. The substitution X↦X+1 is an automorphism of ℚ[X] with inverse X↦X−1, so X⁴+1 is irreducible too.

examples.title: A failed direct test
steps: X⁴+1 has coefficients 0,0,0,1; p=2 fails because its constant 1 is not divisible by 2.
This direct failure is inconclusive; the shift produces a successful certificate.

nonexample.title: Failure does not mean reducible
nonexample.explanation: No suitable prime for the displayed coefficients is not a factorization. X⁴+1 itself demonstrates the gap between a failed direct test and irreducibility.

proofSteps: Suppose f=gh with positive degrees over ℤ after taking primitive parts via Gauss.
Modulo p, all lower terms vanish, so f̄=āₙXⁿ. Thus both reduced factors have only monomial terms up to units and in particular both integer constant terms are divisible by p.
Their product constant is then divisible by p², contradicting p²∤a₀.
Translation X↦X+1 preserves factors in both directions through its inverse, so an Eisenstein certificate for the shifted polynomial certifies the original.

boundaryCheck.question: For (X+1)⁴+1 and p=2, which condition checks the constant term?
boundaryCheck.explanation: All lower coefficients are even, and the constant has exactly one factor of 2.

application.question: What is (X+1)⁴+1?
application.explanation: Binomial expansion adds 1 to the constant of (X+1)⁴.

transfer.question: A direct Eisenstein search fails for X⁴+1. What can you conclude?
choices: Nothing about reducibility; try another criterion or translation
transfer.explanation: Eisenstein is sufficient, not necessary. Translation gives a successful p=2 certificate.

m3220-eisenstein.connection: The next lesson compares root tests, rational roots and reduction modulo p without treating failed tests as proofs.

m3220-irreducibility-tests.hook: Why does a polynomial without roots sometimes still factor?
m3220-irreducibility-tests.objects: Over a field, a degree-2 or degree-3 polynomial is reducible exactly when it has a root. In degree 4, two quadratics can multiply without a linear factor. Rational roots of primitive integer polynomials obey the numerator/denominator divisor test.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which degrees admit the simple root criterion over a field?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A nontrivial factorization of degree 2 or 3 includes a degree-1 factor; degree 4 may split 2+2.

examples.title: A rootless reducible quartic
steps: Over ℚ, (X²+1)(X²+2)=X⁴+3X²+2. Each quadratic lacks a rational root, so their product has none.
Yet the displayed quadratic factors prove reducibility. No-root is not an irreducibility proof in degree 4.

examples.title: Two valid certificates
steps: X³+2X+1 over F₂ has values 1 at 0 and 0 at 1, so it has a root and is reducible; X³+X+1 evaluates to 1 at both 0 and 1, so is irreducible over F₂.

For primitive monic X⁴+X+1∈ℤ[X], its reduction modulo 2 has no roots and is not divisible by the sole monic irreducible quadratic X²+X+1 (remainder 1); hence it is irreducible over F₂ and therefore over ℚ.

nonexample.title: No rational root is not enough in degree four
nonexample.explanation: X⁴+3X²+2 has no rational root but factors into two nonconstant quadratics over ℚ.

proofSteps: For degree 2 or 3, a nontrivial factorization has a degree-1 factor, equivalent to a root over the field.

For primitive f∈ℤ[X], a rational root a/b in lowest terms forces a|constant and b|leading coefficient by clearing denominators. Exhausting these candidates proves no rational roots, not general high-degree irreducibility.
For primitive f with leading coefficient nonzero modulo p, irreducibility of f̄∈Fₚ[X] implies irreducibility over ℚ by Gauss and degree preservation of reductions.
The converse is false and a reducible reduction is inconclusive for the original polynomial. For quartics, also exclude irreducible quadratic divisors before certifying reduction irreducibility.

boundaryCheck.question: Why does no-root imply irreducible for a cubic but not a quartic?
choices: A cubic factorization needs a linear factor; a quartic can split 2+2
boundaryCheck.explanation: Degree counting supplies the exact boundary of the root criterion.

application.question: Which polynomial is reducible over ℚ despite having no rational root?
application.explanation: It equals (X²+1)(X²+2).

transfer.question: Primitive f∈ℤ[X] has leading coefficient nonzero mod p and irreducible reduction mod p. What follows?
choices: f must have a rational root
transfer.explanation: Gauss and degree preservation carry any rational factorization to a nontrivial factorization modulo p, contradicting the certificate.

m3220-irreducibility-tests.connection: V12 compares factorization across coefficient fields and labels each conclusion by its actual proof certificate.

m3220-fractions.hook: When do two numerator-denominator pairs name the same fraction?
m3220-fractions.objects: Let R be a commutative ring and S a multiplicative subset of regular elements (non-zero-divisors). Write (a,s)~(b,t) iff at=bs. The fraction field uses all nonzero elements of a domain; a selected S inverts only its members.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Why is a zero divisor dangerous as a denominator?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Regularity supplies the cancellation used in transitivity of simple cross multiplication.

examples.title: Transitivity with regular denominators
steps: Assume at=bs and bu=ct for pairs (a,s),(b,t),(c,u). Multiply the first equality by u and substitute bu=ct to get atu=cts.
Cancel the regular t to obtain au=cs. Thus (a,s)~(c,u).

examples.title: Arithmetic respects classes
steps: For sums, (a/s)+(b/t)=(at+bs)/(st); for products, (a/s)(b/t)=ab/(st).
Replacing a/s by a′/s′ with as′=a′s gives equal products after multiplying by the same b/t; expanding the two sum numerators similarly gives equality after cross multiplication.

nonexample.title: Cross multiplication with zero divisors can be too strict
nonexample.explanation: In R=ℤ/6ℤ and S={1,2,4}, the localization relation allows (1,1)~(4,1) because 2(1−4)=0 modulo 6. But direct cross multiplication gives 1≠4; the general relation needs an annihilating u∈S.

proofSteps: Reflexivity follows as=as and symmetry reverses equality. Transitivity uses the regular middle denominator to cancel t in atu=cts.
For addition, if as′=a′s and bt′=b′t, expand and regroup to show (at+bs)s′t′=(a′t′+b′s′)st.
For multiplication, ab s′t′=a′b′ st follows by multiplying the two representative equalities. Therefore both operations are independent of representatives.
If S includes zero divisors, use (a,s)~(b,t) iff some u∈S satisfies u(at−bs)=0. This also explains why R→S⁻¹R may fail to be injective.

boundaryCheck.question: Which hypothesis justifies cancelling t in the transitivity proof?
choices: t is nonzero but possibly a zero divisor
boundaryCheck.explanation: Atu=cts implies t(au−cs)=0; regularity forces au−cs=0.

application.question: In ℤ, are 1/2 and 2/4 equivalent under cross multiplication?
choices: Only if 2 is a unit in ℤ
application.explanation: Both cross products equal 4, so the pairs represent the same fraction.

transfer.question: Why is ℤ[1/3] smaller than ℚ?
choices: It only permits denominators that become powers of 3 after reduction
Its numerators must be multiples of 3
transfer.explanation: Only the selected multiplicative set is inverted; 1/2 is absent from ℤ[1/3].

m3220-fractions.connection: Localisation packages this construction by its universal property, even when denominators are zero divisors.

m3220-localization.hook: What map must exist after a chosen set becomes invertible?
m3220-localization.objects: For commutative R and multiplicative S containing 1 and excluding 0 when a nonzero localization is wanted, S⁻¹R consists of fraction classes under u(at−bs)=0 for some u∈S. The canonical map sends r to r/1.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What must a map ψ:R→T do to factor through S⁻¹R?
choices: Send every s∈S to a unit in T
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The forced value ψ(a)/ψ(s) needs ψ(s) invertible; ψ itself may have a kernel.

examples.title: Universal map for ℤ[1/3]
steps: Let S={3ⁿ:n≥0} and ψ:ℤ→ℚ be inclusion. Since ψ(3) is invertible, define ψ̄(a/3ⁿ)=a/3ⁿ in ℚ.
If fractions agree in the localization, multiplying their difference by a power of 3 gives zero; the same relation holds in ℚ, so ψ̄ is well-defined and unique.

examples.title: A noninjective canonical map
steps: Take R=ℤ/6ℤ and S={1,2,4}. Since 2·3=0 in R, the class 3/1 is zero in S⁻¹R although 3≠0 in R.
The universal property still holds. It does not imply injectivity of R→S⁻¹R.

nonexample.title: Universal does not mean injective
nonexample.explanation: The unique factor map exists when S maps to units; it can collapse elements annihilated by S. In the zero-divisor example, 3/1=0/1.

proofSteps: Define (a,s)~(b,t) when u(at−bs)=0 for some u∈S; multiplication of witnesses proves transitivity and compatibility with arithmetic.
The canonical map j:R→S⁻¹R sends r↦r/1 and sends every s∈S to a unit, with inverse 1/s.
For ψ:R→T sending S to units, define ψ̄(a/s)=ψ(a)ψ(s)⁻¹. If u(at−bs)=0, applying ψ and cancelling the units ψ(u),ψ(s),ψ(t) proves well-definedness.
Any factor map must send a/s=(a/1)(s/1)⁻¹ to that value, proving uniqueness. The kernel of j is {r:sr=0 for some s∈S}; regular S makes j injective.

boundaryCheck.question: Does the universal property require R→S⁻¹R to be injective?
choices: No; injectivity additionally follows when S consists of regular elements
boundaryCheck.explanation: A zero divisor in S can annihilate a nonzero element while the universal map remains valid.

application.question: What is the forced image of 5/9 under the factor map ℤ[1/3]→ℚ extending inclusion?
application.explanation: Every denominator becomes a unit in ℚ, so the value is ψ(5)ψ(9)⁻¹.

transfer.question: For R=ℤ/6ℤ and S={1,2,4}, why does 3/1=0/1?
transfer.explanation: The localization relation admits an S-annihilator; this is precisely why the canonical map can lose injectivity.

m3220-localization.connection: At a prime ideal, the inverted set is its complement and units can be classified by the numerator.

m3220-prime-localization.hook: Which fractions are units near the prime 3?
m3220-prime-localization.objects: In ℤ₍₃₎=S⁻¹ℤ with S={n∈ℤ:3∤n}, a reduced rational a/b belongs exactly when 3∤b. It is a unit exactly when 3∤a, and a nonunit exactly when 3|a. Compare ℤ[1/3], which inverts powers of 3 instead.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Is 1/2 in ℤ₍₃₎?
choices: No, 2 is not a power of 3
Only if 2 is a unit of ℤ
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Prime localization inverts all integers outside (3), including 2.

examples.title: Classify reduced fractions
steps: 1/2 is present and a unit in ℤ₍₃₎; its inverse 2 is present. It is absent from ℤ[1/3].
3/2 is present but a nonunit in ℤ₍₃₎ because its numerator is divisible by 3.
1/3 is absent from ℤ₍₃₎ but is a unit of ℤ[1/3]; it is also present in ℚ.

examples.title: The unique maximal ideal
steps: The nonunits are precisely fractions a/b with 3|a and 3∤b. They form 3ℤ₍₃₎.
Any fraction outside this ideal has numerator prime to 3 and reciprocal b/a inside the ring, so every proper ideal lies in 3ℤ₍₃₎. The residue field is F₃.

nonexample.title: Reduce before classifying
nonexample.explanation: 3/6 equals 1/2. The unreduced denominator 6 is divisible by 3, but the rational number belongs to ℤ₍₃₎ and is a unit; classify reduced fractions.

proofSteps: For a reduced a/b, membership in ℤ₍₃₎ is equivalent to 3∤b; cancel common factors before inspecting b.
If 3∤a, b/a is allowed, so a/b is a unit. If 3|a, any inverse would force a numerator divisible by 3 to equal 1 after cross multiplication, impossible.
The nonunits form 3ℤ₍₃₎, an ideal. Every element outside it is invertible, so it is the unique maximal ideal.
ℤ[1/3] has reduced denominators ±3ⁿ; ℚ permits every nonzero denominator. These rings invert different sets even though all embed in ℚ.

boundaryCheck.question: Why must 3/6 be reduced before testing membership in ℤ₍₃₎?
choices: It equals 1/2, whose denominator is prime to 3
boundaryCheck.explanation: Membership is a property of the rational class, not a chosen presentation.

application.question: Classify 3/2 in ℤ₍₃₎.
application.explanation: The reduced denominator 2 is allowed, but the numerator 3 lies in the unique maximal ideal.

transfer.question: Where is 1/3 present?
choices: ℤ[1/3] and ℚ, but not ℤ₍₃₎
transfer.explanation: The prime localization does not invert 3; the other two do.

m3220-prime-localization.connection: Noetherian conditions concern stabilizing ideals rather than whether a ring has finitely many elements.

m3220-noetherian.hook: Why can an infinite ring satisfy an ascending-chain condition?
m3220-noetherian.objects: A commutative ring R is Noetherian when every ideal is finitely generated, equivalently every ascending chain of ideals stabilizes. For modules, replace ideals with submodules. This is unrelated to finite cardinality.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Does the infinite ring ℤ have to be non-Noetherian?
choices: Yes; it has infinitely many integers
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Ideal generation and ascending chains, not the number of elements, decide Noetherianity.

examples.title: Finite generation forces stabilization
steps: For I₁⊆I₂⊆⋯, the union I is an ideal. If I=(a₁,…,aₖ), all its generators appear by some stage N.
Then I⊆I_N, hence I_n=I_N for n≥N.

examples.title: Infinite-variable counterexample
steps: In F[X₁,X₂,…], let I_n=(X₁,…,X_n). Then X_{n+1}∉I_n, witnessed by setting X₁,…,X_n=0 while retaining X_{n+1}.
The union I=(X₁,X₂,…) is not finitely generated: finitely many proposed generators involve only finitely many variables, so a fresh X_j lies outside their generated ideal.

nonexample.title: Infinite does not imply non-Noetherian
nonexample.explanation: ℤ has infinitely many elements but every ideal is (n), hence finitely generated and ACC. The infinite-variable polynomial ring fails because of a specific strict chain, not its cardinality.

proofSteps: If every ideal is finitely generated, the union of an ascending chain is an ideal whose finite generators all occur in one stage; the chain stabilizes.
Conversely, if an ideal I is not finitely generated, choose a₁∈I, then a₂∈I\(a₁), and inductively a_{n+1} outside (a₁,…,a_n). This gives a nonstabilizing ascending chain.
The same proof applies to submodules of a fixed module. A Noetherian ring means R is Noetherian as an R-module; it does not assert every module is Noetherian.
In F[X₁,X₂,…], fresh variables certify strictness of I_n. Hilbert’s basis theorem concerns finitely many polynomial variables over a Noetherian base and does not cover this infinite-variable ring.

boundaryCheck.question: What does Noetherian mean for a module M?
choices: Every submodule is finitely generated, equivalently ACC on submodules
Every element of M is a unit
boundaryCheck.explanation: The chain condition is applied to submodules of that fixed module.

application.question: Why is (X₁)⊊(X₁,X₂) in F[X₁,X₂,…]?
application.explanation: Set X₁=0; every multiple of X₁ vanishes while X₂ need not.

transfer.question: An ideal I is not finitely generated. What chain can you build?
choices: Choose a new element outside each previously generated ideal
A finite chain containing all elements
transfer.explanation: The successive finitely generated ideals strictly increase, contradicting ACC.

m3220-noetherian.connection: The chain explorer keeps the ring/module context and theorem prerequisites visible.

m3220-modules.hook: Can a nonunit of the ring act as an invertible operator?
m3220-modules.objects: A left R-module M is an abelian group with (rs)m=r(sm), (r+s)m=rm+sm, r(m+n)=rm+rn and 1m=m when R is unital. The action is a ring map (unital when R has 1 and the module satisfies 1m=m) R→End_Z(M). A right action instead gives Rᵒᵖ→End_Z(M).
