prerequisiteCheck.question: For a left action, which order expresses (rs)m?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The product rs acts by first s, then r. A right action has different typing.

examples.title: Unit versus nonunit on a cyclic module
steps: Take R=ℤ and M=ℤ/3ℤ. Scalar 2 is not a unit of ℤ, but multiplication by 2 sends [0],[1],[2] to [0],[2],[1] and is its own inverse.
On the regular module ℤ, multiplication by 2 misses odd integers and is not invertible. A unit ±1 acts invertibly on every unital ℤ-module by its ring inverse.

examples.title: Action as a homomorphism
steps: For M=ℤ/6ℤ, send r∈ℤ to the additive endomorphism [x]↦[rx].
Composition satisfies φ(rs)=φ(r)∘φ(s), and φ(1)=id. The kernel 6ℤ is the annihilator of the whole module.

nonexample.title: Nonunit does not mean noninvertible action
nonexample.explanation: The assertion “only units act invertibly on every particular module” is false: 2 acts invertibly on ℤ/3ℤ. The correct universal statement is that units always act invertibly.

proofSteps: Module associativity and distributivity say precisely that r↦(m↦rm) is a ring homomorphism into additive endomorphisms, with multiplication given by composition.
If u∈R has inverse v, then u(vm)=(uv)m=m and v(um)=m, so u acts invertibly on every unital left module.
The converse for a fixed M fails because the action map need not detect nonunits: 2 acts bijectively on ℤ/3ℤ but not on ℤ.
For a right action m·r, the operator r acts by m↦mr and composition reverses products; this is a left action of the opposite ring Rᵒᵖ.

boundaryCheck.question: What is the correct statement about units and module actions?
choices: Units always act invertibly; nonunits may do so on a particular module
boundaryCheck.explanation: Ring inverses give operator inverses on all modules; a nonunit can still induce an invertible operator on a quotient.

application.question: How does scalar 2 act on ℤ/3ℤ?
application.explanation: 2·[1]=[2] and 2·[2]=[1], so the induced endomorphism is its own inverse.

transfer.question: For a right R-action, what ring maps into End_Z(M) by r↦(m↦mr)?
choices: R with the same multiplication order in every case
transfer.explanation: Right-action composition reverses product order, so the homomorphism is typed from the opposite ring.

m3220-modules.connection: Stable additive subgroups give submodules and well-defined quotient actions.

m3220-submodules.hook: When does an additive subgroup support quotient scalar multiplication?
m3220-submodules.objects: For a left R-module M, N≤M is a submodule when it is an additive subgroup and rN⊆N for every r∈R. Then r(m+N)=rm+N is a well-defined left action on M/N.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What extra condition turns an additive subgroup N into a submodule?
choices: Closure under every scalar in R
Closure under one chosen scalar only
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A full R-submodule must be stable under the entire ring action.

examples.title: An operator module
steps: Let F=ℚ, M=F² and T=diag(2,1). Give M the F[X]-action p(X)·v=p(T)v.
The line Fe₁ is stable under T and therefore every polynomial p(T), so it is an F[X]-submodule. The line F(e₁+e₂) is not T-stable because T(e₁+e₂)=2e₁+e₂ is not a scalar multiple.

examples.title: A quotient and its image
steps: For f:ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ, f(n)=[n], the submodule ker f=6ℤ.
The map ℤ/6ℤ→im f sending n+6ℤ to [n] is well-defined, linear and bijective. This is the first module isomorphism theorem.

nonexample.title: One operator is not a whole algebra
nonexample.explanation: A subspace stable under a single operator T is a submodule for F[T]≅F[X]/ann(M), but need not be stable under an additional independently acting operator; check every generator of the acting algebra.

proofSteps: For N a submodule, if m′=m+n with n∈N then rm′−rm=rn∈N. Hence the quotient action is independent of representatives.
Distributive and associative module laws descend from M. The quotient map q:M→M/N is linear with kernel N.
For any linear f:M→P, ker f is a submodule, im f is a submodule, and [m]↦f(m) induces a well-defined bijection M/ker f→im f.
For an operator T, stability under T implies stability under all polynomials p(T) by addition and composition, but says nothing about unrelated operators.

boundaryCheck.question: Why is r(m+N) independent of a representative?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Changing m by n∈N changes rm by rn, which remains in N.

application.question: For T=diag(2,1) over ℚ, which line is an F[X]-submodule?
application.explanation: e₁ is an eigenvector, so all p(T) preserve its line. The diagonal line is not T-stable.

transfer.question: A subspace is stable under T but not U. Is it automatically a module over the algebra generated by T and U?
choices: No, U must preserve it too
Only if the subspace is finite
transfer.explanation: Stability under one operator yields an F[T]-submodule, not a submodule for a larger acting algebra.

m3220-submodules.connection: Presentations encode generators and relations; exactness then records kernels and images.

modules-generators.hook: When does a short exact sequence become a direct sum?
modules-generators.objects: A presentation F₁→F₀→M→0 gives generators from F₀ and relations from im(F₁→F₀). Exactness at an object means incoming image equals outgoing kernel. A short exact 0→A→B→C→0 splits when there is a section C→B (equivalently a retraction B→A).

prerequisiteCheck.question: Does one generator make ℤ/6ℤ a free ℤ-module?
choices: Yes; every cyclic module is free
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Finite generation counts generators; freeness requires no nontrivial linear relations.

examples.title: Cyclic presentation and nonsplitting
steps: The presentation ℤ --×6→ ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ→0 has generator e=[1] and relation 6e=0.
The full sequence 0→ℤ --×6→ ℤ --q→ ℤ/6ℤ→0 is exact: ×6 is injective; im ×6=6ℤ=ker q; q is surjective.
It does not split as ℤ-modules: a section ℤ/6ℤ→ℤ sends [1] to a torsion element killed by 6, hence to 0; it cannot satisfy q∘s=id.

examples.title: A split model
steps: For 0→ℤ --i→ ℤ⊕ℤ --p→ ℤ→0, let i(a)=(a,0) and p(a,b)=b.
The section s(b)=(0,b) satisfies p∘s=id. Every (a,b)=i(a)+s(b), and i(A)∩s(C)=0, so B≅A⊕C.

nonexample.title: Exact does not mean split
nonexample.explanation: The sequence 0→ℤ --×6→ ℤ→ℤ/6ℤ→0 is exact but has no ℤ-linear section. Exactness alone does not identify its middle term with a direct sum.

proofSteps: In 0→A --i→ B --p→ C→0, exactness means i injective, ker p=im i and p surjective. Check each object, not just the middle one.
If a section s:C→B has p∘s=id, then for b∈B the difference b−s(p(b)) lies in ker p=im i. Write it uniquely as i(a), giving b=i(a)+s(c).
If i(a)=s(c), applying p gives c=0, then injectivity of i gives a=0. Thus the sum is direct and B≅A⊕C.
For the cyclic presentation, the relation 6e=0 proves nonfreeness; torsion-freeness of ℤ rules out a section of q.

boundaryCheck.question: Which extra map proves a short exact sequence splits?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A right inverse to p gives complementary copies of A and C.

application.question: At the middle ℤ of 0→ℤ --×6→ ℤ --q→ ℤ/6ℤ→0, what is im(×6)=ker q?
application.explanation: Both sides are the multiples of 6; that is exactness at the middle object.

transfer.question: Why does the cyclic exact sequence fail to split over ℤ?
choices: Any map ℤ/6ℤ→ℤ kills [1] because ℤ has no nonzero 6-torsion
transfer.explanation: A section would send [1] to a nonzero integer killed by 6, impossible.

modules-generators.connection: Annihilators distinguish relations for one vector from relations killing the whole module.

m3220-annihilator.hook: Which scalars kill one vector, and which kill every vector?
m3220-annihilator.objects: For a left R-module M, Ann_R(m)={r∈R:rm=0} is a left ideal. Ann_R(M)=⋂_{m∈M}Ann_R(m) is a two-sided ideal. In a commutative ring both are ideals; in a noncommutative ring keep the side explicit.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For a left R-module, what kind of ideal is Ann_R(m) in general?
choices: A left ideal, not necessarily two-sided
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: If rm=0 then (sr)m=s(rm)=0; (rs)m need not vanish for a fixed m.

examples.title: Two annihilators of ℤ/6ℤ
steps: For M=ℤ/6ℤ, Ann_Z([2])=3ℤ because r[2]=0 iff 6|2r iff 3|r.
Ann_Z(M)=6ℤ because a scalar kills every class exactly when it kills [1]. Thus vector and module annihilators differ.

examples.title: Kernel, image and first isomorphism
steps: Multiplication by 2 on M=ℤ/6ℤ has kernel {[0],[3]} and image {[0],[2],[4]}.
The induced map M/ker(×2)→im(×2) sends [x]+ker to [2x] and is a bijective ℤ-module map. Both quotient and image have three elements.

examples.title: An operator module
steps: For M=ℚ² and T=diag(2,1), the F[X]-action is p(T). Ann(e₁)=(X−2), while Ann(M)=((X−2)(X−1)).
The second polynomial vanishes on both eigenspaces; X−2 alone does not kill e₂.
Let N=ℚ with X acting as multiplication by 2. Projection p:M→N, p(a,b)=a, is ℚ[X]-linear because p(T(a,b))=2a=X·p(a,b).
Here ker p=ℚe₂ and im p=N. The induced map M/ℚe₂→N is an isomorphism of ℚ[X]-modules, not merely of vector spaces.

nonexample.title: One annihilator need not kill the module
nonexample.explanation: 3 kills [2] in ℤ/6ℤ but does not kill [1]. Inferring Ann(M)=Ann([2]) loses the distinction between one vector and the whole module.

proofSteps: Ann_R(m) is additive; if r kills m and s∈R, then (sr)m=s(rm)=0, so it is a left ideal.
Ann_R(M) is the kernel of the action homomorphism R→End_Z(M), hence two-sided; explicitly both sr and rs kill every x because r kills x and sx.
For multiplication by 2 on ℤ/6ℤ, solve 2x≡0 mod 6 to get kernel {0,3}; list outputs to get image {0,2,4}.
The first module isomorphism theorem identifies the quotient by that kernel with the image, and [x]+ker↦[2x] is well-defined by the kernel condition.
For operator modules, p(Tv)=2p(v) proves ℚ[X]-linearity for the projection to the eigenvalue-2 module; ker p=ℚe₂, so M/ker p≅ℚ as ℚ[X]-modules.

boundaryCheck.question: Why is Ann_R(M) two-sided although Ann_R(m) may only be left-sided?
choices: A scalar in Ann_R(M) kills every vector, including sx
boundaryCheck.explanation: For r killing all M, (rs)x=r(sx)=0 and (sr)x=s(rx)=0.

application.question: For M=ℤ/6ℤ, what are Ann([2]) and Ann(M)?
application.explanation: 2r≡0 mod 6 iff 3|r, while killing [1] requires 6|r.

transfer.question: For T=diag(2,1) on M=ℚ² and X acting as 2 on N=ℚ, what does p(a,b)=a identify with N?
choices: M/Ann(e₁) as a set without module structure
transfer.explanation: p(Tv)=2p(v) makes p a module map; its kernel is ℚe₂, and the first module isomorphism theorem gives M/ℚe₂≅N.

m3220-annihilator.connection: The module action board carries the same cyclic object through presentation, scalar action, submodule and exactness checks.

foundations-linear-algebra.hook: What does each matrix column do to a basis vector?
foundations-linear-algebra.objects: Over a specified field F, a linear map A:Fⁿ→Fᵐ is determined by its columns A e_j. Kernel and image are subspaces, rank–nullity is dim ker A+dim im A=n, and trace is the sum of diagonal entries of an endomorphism.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For a 2×3 matrix, what is the domain dimension?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: There is one column for each domain basis vector.

examples.title: Columns, kernel and image
steps: Over ℝ let A=[[1,1],[0,0]]. It maps e₁ and e₂ to e₁, so A(x,y)=(x+y,0).
ker A=span(1,−1) and im A=span(1,0). Both have dimension one, giving 1+1=2.

examples.title: Trace and an invariant line
steps: For B=diag(2,3) over ℝ, the coordinate axes are invariant eigenlines with eigenvalues 2 and 3.
tr B=5 is the sum of eigenvalues. In the basis e₁+e₂,e₂ the matrix changes but trace remains 5.

nonexample.title: A column is not a row
nonexample.explanation: The first row of A records the first output coordinate, not A(e₁). Confusing rows and columns gives the wrong image and often the wrong kernel.

proofSteps: For v=Σx_j e_j, linearity gives A(v)=Σx_j A(e_j); these images are exactly the columns.
The kernel solves Ax=0; the image is the span of the columns. Choose a basis of the kernel and extend it to a basis of the domain.
Images of the added basis vectors form a basis of im A, proving dim ker A+dim im A=dim domain.
A subspace W is invariant under B when BW⊆W; checking a basis of W suffices by linearity. Trace and eigenvalues require an endomorphism and a stated field.

boundaryCheck.question: When can trace be taken for A:Fⁿ→Fᵐ?
choices: When n=m and a basis identifies it with a square matrix
boundaryCheck.explanation: Trace is defined for an endomorphism, represented by a square matrix.

application.question: For A(x,y)=(x+y,0), what is ker A?
application.explanation: Solve x+y=0; the kernel has dimension one.

transfer.question: For a 3×3 matrix of rank 2, what is its nullity?
transfer.explanation: Rank–nullity gives nullity 3−2=1.

foundations-linear-algebra.connection: A group representation chooses invertible linear maps that respect multiplication.

ureca-linear-action.hook: Why must every group element act by an invertible matrix?
ureca-linear-action.objects: Use a left action on column vectors over F. A representation ρ:G→GL_F(V) satisfies ρ(gh)=ρ(g)ρ(h), so the rightmost matrix acts first; ρ(e)=I and dim_F V is stated.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For a left representation, which matrix acts first in ρ(gh)v?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Matrix multiplication applies the right factor first.

examples.title: Quarter-turn and reflection
steps: Over ℝ, V=ℝ², R=[[0,−1],[1,0]] and S=diag(1,−1) represent r and s of D₈ on columns.
R⁴=S²=I and SRS=R⁻¹. The generators therefore define a homomorphism D₈→GL₂(ℝ).

examples.title: From a set action to vectors
steps: If g permutes a finite set Ω, create a basis vector e_ω for each ω and define ρ(g)e_ω=e_{gω}, then extend linearly.
The action equation g(hω)=(gh)ω becomes ρ(g)ρ(h)e_ω=ρ(gh)e_ω on every basis vector.

nonexample.title: An arbitrary matrix assignment is not an action
nonexample.explanation: Assigning a singular matrix to a group generator fails: ρ(g)ρ(g⁻¹)=I forces every ρ(g) to be invertible.

proofSteps: A left group action by linear maps yields ρ(gh)v=g(hv)=ρ(g)ρ(h)v, so ρ is a homomorphism.
Conversely, a homomorphism ρ:G→GL(V) defines g·v=ρ(g)v; identity and associativity follow from ρ(e)=I and ρ(gh)=ρ(g)ρ(h).
For every g, ρ(g)ρ(g⁻¹)=ρ(e)=I, hence the inverse of ρ(g) is ρ(g⁻¹).
D₈ has presentation r⁴=s²=1, srs=r⁻¹; checking these matrices on generators verifies the displayed example.

boundaryCheck.question: Why is ρ(g) invertible?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The group inverse maps to an inverse linear operator.

application.question: For R=[[0,−1],[1,0]], what is R e₁?
application.explanation: The first column is (0,1)=e₂.

transfer.question: If an assignment satisfies the D₈ generator relations, what else identifies it as a representation?
choices: Its matrices act on one specified F-vector space with multiplication respected
One matrix per element with no relation checks
transfer.explanation: A presentation gives the homomorphism once all defining relations hold.

ureca-linear-action.connection: Permutation modules use one independent basis vector per point.

ureca-permutation-module.hook: Why do eight cube vertices give dimension eight, not three?
ureca-permutation-module.objects: For a finite G-set Ω over field F, F[Ω] has independent basis {e_ω:ω∈Ω}; the left action is ρ(g)e_ω=e_{gω}. Its dimension is |Ω|, separate from any spatial embedding dimension.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is dim F[Ω] when Ω is the eight cube vertices?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The module has one independent basis vector per vertex.

examples.title: A three-point action
steps: For C₃ acting cyclically on Ω={1,2,3}, ρ(r) sends e₁→e₂, e₂→e₃, e₃→e₁. Its columns are (0,1,0),(0,0,1),(1,0,0).
The vector 2e₁−e₃ moves to 2e₂−e₁, not to a single basis vector.

examples.title: Cube vertices
steps: For an eight-vertex cube, a symmetry g permutes eight labels, giving an 8×8 permutation matrix with exactly one 1 in each row and column.
The physical cube sits in ℝ³, while ℝ[Ω] is eight-dimensional; the all-ones vector spans a trivial subrepresentation.

Label vertices by three sign bits 0,…,7. A half-turn about the x-axis flips the y and z bits, acting on the eight basis vectors by (0 3)(1 2)(4 7)(5 6); this exact basis permutation specifies the full 8×8 matrix.

nonexample.title: Spatial dimension is not module dimension
nonexample.explanation: Treating the eight vertex labels as just three coordinate directions loses five independent basis vectors and cannot encode arbitrary vertex colourings.

proofSteps: Define ρ(g) on every basis vector and extend linearly: ρ(g)(Σa_ωe_ω)=Σa_ωe_{gω}.
Because g(hω)=(gh)ω, the equality ρ(g)ρ(h)=ρ(gh) holds on each e_ω and therefore on all F[Ω].
The inverse permutation gives ρ(g)⁻¹=ρ(g⁻¹), so these are invertible matrices.
The sum u=Σe_ω is fixed because g merely reorders its terms; its line is invariant over every field.

boundaryCheck.question: What determines permutation-module dimension?
choices: The number of independent point labels in Ω
The dimension of a drawing containing Ω
The order of the acting group
boundaryCheck.explanation: F[Ω] is free with basis indexed by Ω.

application.question: Under (123), where does 2e₁−e₃ go?
application.explanation: Move each basis vector by the same permutation, keeping its coefficient.

transfer.question: For a four-element G-set, what matrix size represents the action on F[Ω]?
transfer.explanation: There is one row and column for each point basis vector.

ureca-permutation-module.connection: Invariant subspaces include the constant line and sometimes a complementary sum-zero space.

ureca-invariant-subspaces.hook: Does a subspace remain stable even when its vectors move?
ureca-invariant-subspaces.objects: For ρ:G→GL_F(V), W≤V is invariant iff ρ(g)W⊆W for every g; it suffices to test generators. For a permutation module on three points, the constant line C=F(1,1,1) and sum-zero plane Z={x+y+z=0} are invariant.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Does invariant mean every vector is fixed pointwise?
choices: No, vectors may move within the subspace
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Setwise stability is weaker than pointwise fixation.

examples.title: Projection and adapted basis
steps: Over a field with 3 invertible, p_C(v)=((x+y+z)/3)(1,1,1) and p_Z(v)=v−p_C(v). Their images are C and Z.
The basis u=(1,1,1), v=(1,−1,0), w=(0,1,−1) is adapted to C⊕Z over characteristic not 3. A 3-cycle fixes u and moves v,w within Z.

examples.title: D₈ lines across fields
steps: For R=[[0,−1],[1,0]] over ℝ, no real line is R-invariant: the characteristic polynomial X²+1 has no real root.
Over ℂ, L+=ℂ(e₁+i e₂) is R-stable with eigenvalue −i, but S sends it to ℂ(e₁−i e₂), so L+ is not invariant under full D₈.

nonexample.title: Characteristic three boundary
nonexample.explanation: In characteristic 3, u=(1,1,1) lies in Z, and division by 3 is impossible. C and Z remain invariant, but the stated direct-sum projection and decomposition fail.

proofSteps: A generating set suffices: if each generator and its inverse preserves W, then every group word preserves W; in finite groups generator stability already gives inverse stability by equal dimensions.
For a permutation matrix, sum of coordinates is preserved, proving Z stable; the vector u is fixed, proving C stable.
When 3 is invertible, p_C and p_Z are idempotent, sum to I and have complementary images; every v decomposes uniquely as p_C(v)+p_Z(v).
In characteristic 3, C⊆Z, so C∩Z≠0 and the direct sum fails despite both subspaces remaining invariant.

boundaryCheck.question: When is the projection p_C(v)=Σv_i/3·u defined?
choices: Only if all vectors are fixed
boundaryCheck.explanation: The denominator 3 must exist in the field.

application.question: For the quarter-turn R over ℝ, which one-dimensional real subspace is invariant?
application.explanation: A real invariant line would give a real eigenvalue, but X²+1 has none.

transfer.question: Over ℂ, is L+=ℂ(e₁+i e₂) invariant under full D₈?
choices: No; S swaps it with L−
transfer.explanation: Check every generator of the full acting group.

ureca-invariant-subspaces.connection: An intertwiner carries actions between spaces and preserves kernels and images.

ureca-intertwiners.hook: Can one fixed matrix translate an entire representation?
ureca-intertwiners.objects: For left representations ρ_V:G→GL_F(V), ρ_W:G→GL_F(W), an intertwiner T:V→W satisfies Tρ_V(g)=ρ_W(g)T for every g. One T must work on a generating set; then it works on all group words.

prerequisiteCheck.question: May T depend on g when claiming two representations are equivalent?
choices: No, one invertible T must work for every g
Yes, choose a different T_g for each g
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Equivalence is a single change of basis respecting the whole action.

examples.title: A D₈ basis change
steps: Let ρ(r)=R=[[0,−1],[1,0]], ρ(s)=S=diag(1,−1), and ρ′(r)=R⁻¹, ρ′(s)=S over ℝ.
T=S satisfies TR=R⁻¹T and TS=ST on both generators. T is invertible, so it is an equivalence of the two representations.

examples.title: An equivariant projection
steps: Let V=F² carry ρ and let F carry the trivial action. On V⊕F, q(v,z)=z is equivariant since q(ρ(g)v,z)=z=g·q(v,z).
q is not invertible: ker q=V⊕0 is invariant, and im q=F. The first module isomorphism identifies (V⊕F)/ker q with F.

nonexample.title: Elementwise conjugacy is insufficient
nonexample.explanation: Finding a change of basis for r and a different one for s does not provide a single T satisfying both equations. The candidate I fails TR=R⁻¹T even though it commutes with S.

proofSteps: If T intertwines generators, multiply equations and use inverses to obtain Tρ(g)=ρ′(g)T for every word g.
For T=S, direct matrix multiplication gives SR=R⁻¹S and SS=SS; thus the two D₈ actions are equivalent.
If v∈ker T, then Tρ(g)v=ρ′(g)Tv=0, proving ker T invariant. If w=Tv, then ρ′(g)w=Tρ(g)v, proving im T invariant.

An invertible intertwiner is a representation equivalence. A noninvertible intertwiner may have proper kernel and image; Schur’s scalar conclusion needs irreducibility over an algebraically closed field.

boundaryCheck.question: What must be checked for the D₈ intertwiner T?
choices: The same T satisfies equations for r and s
A separate matrix for each generator
boundaryCheck.explanation: Generator equations propagate to all group elements.

application.question: For q:V⊕F→F, q(v,z)=z, what is ker q?
application.explanation: The scalar coordinate must be zero, while v is free.

transfer.question: If T is an intertwiner, what can be said of im T?
choices: It is invariant under the target action
It is always the full target
transfer.explanation: ρ′(g)Tv=Tρ(g)v remains in the image.

ureca-intertwiners.connection: Maschke and Schur need explicit field and irreducibility hypotheses.

representations-maschke.hook: Can averaging turn a chosen projection into an equivariant one?
representations-maschke.objects: Let G be finite and V a finite-dimensional representation over a field F with |G| invertible in F. For an invariant W≤V, start with any F-linear projection P₀:V→W and average P=(1/|G|)Σ_g ρ(g)P₀ρ(g)⁻¹. This is a left action on columns.

prerequisiteCheck.question: When can we divide by |G| in Maschke averaging?
choices: When char F does not divide |G|
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The group order must be a unit in the field.

examples.title: A non-equivariant projection becomes equivariant
steps: For C₂ swapping coordinates over ℚ, W=ℚ(1,1). Choose P₀(x,y)=(x,x), matrix [[1,0],[1,0]]. It fixes W but does not commute with the swap S.
The conjugate SP₀S=[[0,1],[0,1]]; their average P=[[1/2,1/2],[1/2,1/2]] maps (x,y) to ((x+y)/2,(x+y)/2).
P²=P, im P=W and ker P=ℚ(1,−1), an invariant complement.

examples.title: A nontrivial D₈ complement
steps: In the two-dimensional real D₈ representation, the full space is irreducible, so its only invariant subspaces are 0 and V; Maschke still applies but gives only trivial complements here.
On V⊕ℝ with a trivial last coordinate, projection onto the last coordinate is equivariant, and its kernel V⊕0 is invariant.

nonexample.title: Characteristic two obstruction
nonexample.explanation: For C₂ swapping coordinates on F₂², W=F₂(1,1) is invariant, but |G|=2=0 in F₂ so the average is undefined. The only nonzero invariant line is W, so W has no invariant one-dimensional complement.

proofSteps: For w∈W, every conjugate ρ(g)P₀ρ(g)⁻¹ fixes w, hence P|_W=id and im P=W.
Reindex g↦hg in the finite sum to show ρ(h)Pρ(h)⁻¹=P for every h; thus P commutes with G.
Since P has image W and fixes W, P²=P. Its kernel is invariant because P commutes with the action, and V=W⊕ker P.
The division by |G| requires char F∤|G|. The F₂ swap module exhibits failure when this hypothesis is removed.

boundaryCheck.question: Which hypothesis makes the average P available?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The scalar 1/|G| must exist.

application.question: For the C₂ swap over ℚ, what is P(2,0) after averaging?

transfer.question: Why is ker P invariant after averaging?
choices: Every kernel is automatically invariant under any action
transfer.explanation: Equivariance, not mere linearity, preserves the kernel under G.

representations-maschke.connection: Schur studies the equivariant maps between irreducible summands.

odyssey-schur.hook: What survives of an intertwiner between irreducible representations?
odyssey-schur.objects: For finite-dimensional left F-representations V and W, an intertwiner T obeys Tρ_V(g)=ρ_W(g)T. If V,W are irreducible, a nonzero T is an isomorphism. If F is algebraically closed and V=W, every T is scalar; over ℝ this last conclusion can fail.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What can a nonzero map between irreducibles have as kernel?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The kernel is invariant and cannot be all V for a nonzero map.

examples.title: Kernel and image first
steps: For nonzero equivariant T:V→W between irreducibles, ker T is invariant in V and im T invariant in W.
Irreducibility forces ker T=0 and im T=W, so T is an isomorphism without an algebraic-closure assumption.

examples.title: A real irreducible with nonscalar endomorphisms
steps: Let C₃ act on V=ℝ² by a rotation R through 120°. Its characteristic polynomial X²+X+1 has no real root, so it has no invariant real line and V is irreducible.
R itself commutes with every power of R, so it is a nonscalar real equivariant endomorphism. In fact End_{ℝ[C₃]}(V)≅ℂ via aI+bR.

nonexample.title: Scalar conclusion needs an eigenvalue
nonexample.explanation: Over ℝ, the nonscalar rotation endomorphism contradicts the claim that every irreducible endomorphism is a real scalar; no real eigenvalue exists to begin the usual scalar proof.

proofSteps: For equivariant T, ker T and im T are invariant: applying ρ to a kernel vector remains in ker, and acting on Tv remains in im.
When V,W are irreducible and T≠0, these invariant spaces force ker T=0 and im T=W; finite dimension gives an isomorphism.
If F is algebraically closed, T:V→V has an eigenvalue λ. The equivariant map T−λI has a nonzero kernel; irreducibility forces that kernel to be V, hence T=λI.
For ℝ² with a C₃ rotation, X²+X+1 has negative discriminant, so the eigenvalue step is unavailable over ℝ; R is a concrete nonscalar endomorphism.

boundaryCheck.question: What extra hypothesis gives the scalar endomorphism conclusion?
choices: An algebraically closed field (with finite-dimensional V)
boundaryCheck.explanation: The usual proof chooses an eigenvalue in F.

application.question: For nonzero T between irreducible V,W, what are ker T and im T?
application.explanation: Irreducibility leaves no proper nonzero invariant kernel or image.

transfer.question: Why can R on the real C₃ plane be nonscalar while V stays irreducible?
choices: R has no real eigenline but commutes with the action
Schur says every real endomorphism is scalar
transfer.explanation: The real endomorphism algebra may be larger than ℝ.

odyssey-schur.connection: Real and complex fields change which invariant lines exist.

representations-real-complex.hook: Can the same two-dimensional action be irreducible over ℝ but reducible over ℂ?
representations-real-complex.objects: Let C₃=⟨r | r³=1⟩ act from the left on column vectors in V=ℝ² by R=[[-1/2,−√3/2],[√3/2,−1/2]]. The complexification V_C=V⊗_ℝℂ has complex dimension 2, not 3.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the real dimension of the displayed C₃ rotation representation?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The displayed matrix is 2×2 and acts on the rotation plane.

examples.title: Over the real field
steps: R³=I and R²+R+I=0. Its characteristic polynomial X²+X+1 has no real root.
A proper nonzero invariant subspace of ℝ² would be a real eigenline, so V is irreducible over ℝ.

examples.title: After complexification
steps: Let ω=e^{2πi/3}. Over ℂ, e₁−i e₂ is an eigenvector of R with eigenvalue ω, and e₁+i e₂ has eigenvalue ω².
The two distinct eigenlines split V_C as ℂ(e₁−i e₂)⊕ℂ(e₁+i e₂), so the complexified representation is reducible.

nonexample.title: Do not borrow an ambient fixed axis
nonexample.explanation: A 3D picture with a fixed z-axis is a different representation: ℝ³ splits as axis⊕rotation plane. Its fixed axis cannot be used to claim that the 2D rotation plane is reducible over ℝ.

proofSteps: Compute det(XI−R)=X²+X+1, whose real discriminant is −3; there is no real eigenvalue or real invariant line.
The relation R²+R+I=0 implies R³=I, so the matrix defines a C₃ representation.
Over ℂ, factor X²+X+1=(X−ω)(X−ω²). The two displayed eigenvectors span distinct invariant lines and a direct sum.
Irreducibility therefore depends on the coefficient field even though the group, underlying real matrix and real dimension are fixed.

boundaryCheck.question: What changes when V=ℝ² is complexified?
choices: The field becomes ℂ and the complex dimension remains 2
boundaryCheck.explanation: Complexification preserves dimension while extending scalars.

application.question: What is the characteristic polynomial of the 120° rotation matrix?
application.explanation: Trace is −1 and determinant is 1.

transfer.question: Over ℂ, how many invariant eigenlines split this plane?
transfer.explanation: The two distinct complex roots give complementary eigenlines.

representations-real-complex.connection: Characters record the traces of these linear actions.

representations-characters.hook: Can a table row be built from a representation instead of memorised?
representations-characters.objects: A complex character χ_V(g)=tr ρ_V(g) is constant on conjugacy classes and additive on direct sums; products give tensor-product characters. For S₃, class sizes are 1,3,2 and inner products use (1/6)Σ_C|C|χ(C)overline{ψ(C)}.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the trace of a permutation matrix on F[Ω]?
choices: Its number of fixed basis points
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Only fixed basis vectors contribute diagonal 1 entries.

examples.title: Construct S₃ irreducible rows
steps: For S₃ acting on three letters over ℂ, the permutation trace is fixed-point count (3,1,0) on e, transpositions and 3-cycles.
The constant line contributes trivial (1,1,1), leaving standard (2,0,−1). Sign comes from parity: (1,−1,1). Weighted norms are 1 and pairwise inner products 0; 1²+1²+2²=6 proves completeness.

examples.title: Cube rotation and a genuinely complex row
steps: For a 90° cube rotation about z, the spatial matrix has trace 1, the permutation of eight vertices has two 4-cycles and trace 0, and the induced permutation of four body diagonals is a 4-cycle with trace 0. These are different representations of one motion.
On the five S₄ classes (e,(12),(12)(34),(123),(1234)), the vertex character is (8,0,0,2,0)=1+sgn+Std+(Std⊗sgn), each constituent with multiplicity one by class-weighted inner product.
For the one-dimensional complex C₃ representation r↦ω=e^{2πi/3}, χ(r)=ω and χ(r²)=ω² are nonreal. Thus character values need not be real.

nonexample.title: Equal dimension is not equivalence
nonexample.explanation: The trivial and sign representations both have dimension one but differ on transpositions. A character remembers trace by class, not every matrix entry; for finite groups over ℂ, equal characters do imply equivalence, unlike equal dimensions alone.

proofSteps: tr(ABA⁻¹)=tr B, so χ(hgh⁻¹)=χ(g): a character is a class function.
Trace adds on block direct sums and multiplies on tensor products, explaining the S₃ row constructions and χ_{V⊗W}=χ_Vχ_W.
For S₃, the standard row equals point-permutation trace minus trivial. Class-weighted inner products show its norm one and orthogonality to trivial and sign.
Degree-squared sum 1²+1²+2²=|S₃| accounts for all complex irreducibles. The orthogonality theorem itself needs proof from matrix coefficients, not merely this finite table.

boundaryCheck.question: What weights appear in S₃ character inner products?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The sum over all six elements groups equal class values by class size.

application.question: What is the standard S₃ character on e, transpositions and 3-cycles?
application.explanation: Subtract the trivial row from the three-point permutation trace.

transfer.question: Does a 90° cube rotation have the same trace on space and on vertices?
choices: No; spatial trace is 1 and vertex permutation trace is 0
Yes; trace depends only on the motion
transfer.explanation: Trace depends on the chosen representation, not just the group element.

representations-characters.connection: Character tables use these constructed rows to measure decomposition and induction.

odyssey-character-table.hook: How is a character table constructed, and which rows actually come from modules?
odyssey-character-table.objects: Work over ℂ with finite G. A character is the trace of an actual representation, an irreducible character comes from an irreducible representation, and a virtual character is an integer difference of actual characters. For S₃ the classes e,(12),(123) have sizes 1,3,2.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which S₃ row follows from its three-point permutation module after removing constants?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The permutation trace counts fixed points; subtract the trivial constant line.

examples.title: Build the complete S₃ table
steps: The trivial and sign rows are (1,1,1) and (1,−1,1). The three-point permutation character is (3,1,0), so the sum-zero standard row is (2,0,−1).
Weighting by sizes 1,3,2 gives each row norm one and distinct rows inner product zero. Their degrees satisfy 1²+1²+2²=6, exhausting the irreducibles.
Column orthogonality then gives Σ_χ χ(C)overline{χ(D)}=0 for different classes; for a class C the sum of squared absolute values is |C_G(g)|=6/|C|.

examples.title: Inflation from a quotient
steps: For N=A₃◁S₃, the quotient is C₂. Pulling its two one-dimensional characters back along q:S₃→C₂ yields the trivial and sign characters of S₃.
Exactly the irreducible S₃ characters whose kernels contain A₃ arise this way; the standard character does not, because its representation is faithful.

nonexample.title: A virtual row need not be an actual character
nonexample.explanation: Std−1=(1,−1,−2) is a virtual character, but its inner product with the trivial irreducible is −1, so it cannot be an actual character. A row-shaped class function is not automatically a representation trace.

proofSteps: Rows arise from explicit representations. For S₃, point-permutation trace minus the fixed constant line is the actual standard character, not an arbitrary formal subtraction.

On Hom(V,W), let g act by T↦ρ_W(g)Tρ_V(g)⁻¹. Over C for finite G, averaging these operators produces an idempotent P whose image is Hom_G(V,W): invariant maps are fixed by the average, and the average of any map is invariant.

The trace of this average is |G|⁻¹Σ_g χ_W(g)χ_V(g⁻¹)=⟨χ_W,χ_V⟩, since finite-order complex matrices have eigenvalues of modulus 1. An idempotent has trace equal to its image dimension. For irreducibles, Schur gives that dimension 1 for isomorphic V,W and 0 otherwise; this proves row orthogonality.

Maschke decomposes an actual representation into irreducibles. Character additivity and row orthogonality give its multiplicities as the weighted inner products; grouping the group sum by classes explains the class-size weights.

The irreducible character matrix is square because irreducibles and conjugacy classes have equal counts. Row orthogonality plus invertibility yields column orthogonality, with centralizer size on the diagonal.

For q:G→G/N, pullback of a quotient representation is irreducible exactly when the quotient representation is; conversely an irreducible G-representation with N in its kernel factors uniquely through q. Thus inflation is a bijection onto that subset, not every irreducible of G.
For S₃, the class sizes are (1,3,2), the standard character is (2,0,−1), and tensor characters multiply pointwise. Thus Std⊗Std has character (4,0,1).

Against trivial (1,1,1), sign (1,−1,1) and standard (2,0,−1), the weighted inner products are respectively (4+0+2)/6=1, (4+0+2)/6=1 and (8+0−2)/6=1. Their dimensions sum to 1+1+2=4, the tensor dimension. Hence the displayed direct-sum decomposition follows over C.

boundaryCheck.question: Which G-irreducibles are in the image of inflation from G/N?
choices: Exactly those with N in the representation kernel
boundaryCheck.explanation: Factoring through the quotient is equivalent to N acting trivially.

application.question: What is the standard S₃ row and its weighted norm?
application.explanation: (4+2)/6=1 using class sizes 1,3,2.

transfer.question: Can Std−1 be an actual S₃ character?
choices: No; its trivial multiplicity would be −1
Yes; every integer class function is actual
transfer.explanation: Actual characters have nonnegative integer inner products with irreducible rows.

odyssey-character-table.connection: Induction creates new representations from a subgroup; restriction checks them by reciprocity.

odyssey-induction.hook: What does one induced vector do when a group element crosses coset copies?
odyssey-induction.objects: Let G=S₃=⟨r=(123),s=(12)⟩, H=⟨s⟩≅C₂ and φ:H→ℂ× either trivial or sign. Choose left-coset transversal t₀=e,t₁=r,t₂=r². The induced left G-module Ind_H^G φ=ℂ[G]⊗_{ℂ[H]}ℂ_φ has basis u_i=t_i⊗1 and dimension [G:H]dim φ=3.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For g t_i=t_j h with h∈H, how does g act on u_i?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The subgroup correction h acts through the inducing character.

examples.title: Every generator matrix from the transversal
steps: r r^i=r^{i+1}, so r sends u₀→u₁→u₂→u₀. In the ordered basis its matrix is R=[[0,0,1],[1,0,0],[0,1,0]].
s r^i=r^{−i}s. For φ=sign_H, s sends u₀→−u₀, u₁→−u₂, u₂→−u₁, giving S=[[−1,0,0],[0,0,−1],[0,−1,0]]. For φ=trivial_H, remove those minus signs.
These matrices obey R³=S²=I and SRS=R⁻¹. The sign-induced trace on e, transpositions, 3-cycles is (3,−1,0).

examples.title: Character formula and reciprocity
steps: A fixed coset t_iH contributes tr φ(t_i⁻¹gt_i) when t_i⁻¹gt_i∈H; a moved coset contributes zero to the trace. For sign induction this gives (3,−1,0)=sgn_G+Std.
For target Std, ⟨Ind sign_H,Std⟩_G=(3·2+3·(−1)·0+2·0·(−1))/6=1. Restrict Std to H: character values (2,0), so ⟨sign_H,Res Std⟩_H=(2−0)/2=1.

nonexample.title: A lost subgroup correction changes the representation
nonexample.explanation: If the minus sign of φ(s) is omitted, the s matrix has trace +1 and describes Ind trivial_H, not Ind sign_H. Coset movement alone cannot recover the induced character.

proofSteps: The tensor balance relation (gh)⊗v=g⊗hv makes the formula g t_i=t_j h imply g·u_i=t_j⊗φ(h)1. It is independent of the chosen expression in the induced module.
The three coset basis vectors give dimension 3. The displayed R and S follow by applying r and s to each t_i; their relations verify the S₃ action.
For any g, the trace is the sum over fixed cosets, each weighted by the trace of its H-correction. This derives the induced-character formula for this transversal.
Frobenius reciprocity sends a G-map F:Ind_H^G V→W to the H-map v↦F(1⊗v); conversely an H-map f:V→Res_H^G W gives g⊗v↦g·f(v). The balance relation makes the inverse well-defined.

boundaryCheck.question: What determines the dimension of Ind_H^G V?
boundaryCheck.explanation: One copy of V occurs for each left coset.

application.question: What is the trace of s on Ind_H^G(sign_H)?
application.explanation: Only u₀ is fixed as a coset; its H-correction is s and sign_H(s)=−1.

transfer.question: Why do Hom_G(Ind sign_H,Std) and Hom_H(sign_H,Res Std) have equal dimension?
choices: Both are one by Frobenius reciprocity; the explicit characters confirm it
Because Ind and Res have equal dimensions
Because all S₃ representations are one-dimensional
transfer.explanation: The natural Hom-space isomorphism, not a numerical accident, is the theorem.

odyssey-induction.connection: Double cosets refine restriction of induced modules; H\G/H has H and HrH in this example.

algebra-wedderburn.hook: Is a matrix block the same size as its simple module?
algebra-wedderburn.objects: For an associative finite-dimensional unital F-algebra A, semisimple A is a product of matrix algebras over division F-algebras. If F is algebraically closed and the algebras are finite-dimensional over F, the division rings are F, so A≅∏_i M_{n_i}(F). In this split case D_i=F, the simple left module S_i has F-dimension n_i; its regular block contains S_i with multiplicity n_i. In general the simple module D_i^{n_i} has F-dimension n_i·dim_F(D_i), while the multiplicity is still n_i. For C as an R-algebra, n_i=1 but the simple module has real dimension 2.

prerequisiteCheck.question: For A=M₂(F), what is the dimension of its simple left module?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The column module F² is simple, and the regular module splits into two column copies.

examples.title: Matrix units and the regular module
steps: In M₂(F), E_ijE_kl=δ_jkE_il. The left ideals AE₁₁ and AE₂₂ are each isomorphic to the natural simple left module F², represented by one column.
A=AE₁₁⊕AE₂₂≅F²⊕F² as left modules. One block has F-dimension 4, its simple has dimension 2, and its regular multiplicity is 2.

examples.title: An explicit group-algebra block map
steps: Let C₂={1,g} and char F≠2. The central idempotents e_+=(1+g)/2 and e_-=(1−g)/2 are orthogonal and sum to 1.
The unital algebra map F[C₂]→F×F, a+bg↦(a+b,a−b), is bijective with inverse (x,y)↦((x+y)/2)+((x−y)/2)g. The regular module is trivial⊕sign.

nonexample.title: A semisimple quotient is not the original algebra
nonexample.explanation: For A=T₂(F), the upper-triangular 2×2 algebra, J(A)=FE₁₂ is nonzero and A/J(A)≅F×F. The quotient has two field blocks, but A is not their direct product and its natural module has a nonsplit extension.

proofSteps: Matrix units satisfy E_ijE_kl=δ_jkE_il by direct multiplication; the column left ideals AE_jj give n equivalent copies of the natural simple module in M_n(F).

For finite-dimensional semisimple unital A, simple isotypic components are two-sided ideals; their identity idempotents are central, and each component is a full matrix algebra over a division ring. Over algebraically closed F, finite-dimensional division F-algebras reduce to F.

For a left simple S, commuting A-endomorphisms form a division ring. Defining a right scalar action by s·d=d(s) reverses composition, so the opposite ring enters the double-centralizer step; do not silently identify these sides in the noncommutative case.
For F[C₂], e_+ and e_- are central orthogonal idempotents only when 2 is invertible. The displayed map sends the two idempotents to (1,0) and (0,1), certifying the block decomposition.

boundaryCheck.question: When may a finite-dimensional semisimple F-algebra be written as a product of M_n(F) without division rings?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The general blocks are matrix rings over division F-algebras.

application.question: How many copies of F² occur in the left regular M₂(F)-module?
application.explanation: Each column left ideal is a copy of F².

transfer.question: What fails in F₂[C₂] when trying the idempotents (1±g)/2?
choices: 2 is not invertible and the algebra has nonzero radical
The regular module has dimension one
transfer.explanation: In characteristic two, (g+1)²=0 and the split block map collapses.

algebra-wedderburn.connection: Radical filtrations expose the extension data a semisimple quotient forgets.

algebra-radical.hook: Can simple successive layers still form a nonsplit module?
algebra-radical.objects: Let A=T₂(F) be the finite-dimensional unital algebra of upper-triangular matrices [[a,b],[0,c]] over a field F. Its Jacobson radical J(A)=FE₁₂ has J²=0 and A/J≅F×F. On the natural left module V=F², Fe₁ is the socle and JV=Fe₁ is the module radical. For a finite-dimensional left A-module M, rad M is the intersection of its maximal proper submodules (intersection of an empty family means M); soc M is the sum of its simple submodules. Set soc⁰M=0 and define socʳM as the inverse image of soc(M/socʳ⁻¹M). The annihilator {m∈M:Jm=0} is an A-submodule because J is a two-sided ideal: J(am)=(Ja)m=0.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Does a filtration with simple quotients force the module to split?
choices: No; the extension may be nonsplit
Only if the algebra has an identity
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Composition factors do not record extension classes.

examples.title: The natural triangular module
steps: For [[a,b],[0,c]] acting on columns, Fe₁ is stable and simple: E₁₁ acts as 1, E₂₂ as 0. The quotient V/Fe₁ is a one-dimensional simple module on which E₂₂ acts as 1.
J(A)V=FE₁₂V=Fe₁. The only nonzero simple submodule is Fe₁, so soc(V)=Fe₁; also rad(V)=JV=Fe₁. The filtration 0<Fe₁<V has simple layers S₁ and S₂.
The exact sequence 0→S₁→V→S₂→0 does not split: every line complement contains e₂+c e₁, yet E₁₂(e₂+c e₁)=e₁ lies outside it.

examples.title: A characteristic-two group algebra
steps: In F₂[C₂], let ε=g+1. Then ε²=g²+2g+1=0, so J=(ε) and the quotient is F₂.
The regular module has two one-dimensional trivial composition factors but is not a direct sum of them; the nilpotent ε action records the extension.

nonexample.title: Layer dimensions do not identify the module
nonexample.explanation: The direct sum S₁⊕S₂ has the same simple layer dimensions as the natural T₂(F)-module, but E₁₂ acts as zero on the direct sum and nonzero on V. The extension data cannot be read from dimensions alone.

proofSteps: The map T₂(F)→F×F sending [[a,b],[0,c]]↦(a,c) is a surjective unital algebra map with kernel FE₁₂; that kernel squares to zero and is the Jacobson radical.
On V, E₁₂ sends e₂ to e₁ and e₁ to zero. Thus JV=Fe₁, and Fe₁ is the unique nonzero simple submodule.
A submodule complement to Fe₁ would be a stable line spanned by e₂+c e₁. E₁₂ sends that generator to e₁, not in the line, contradiction. Hence the extension is nonsplit despite simple layers.

The Artin–Wedderburn theorem applies to A/J, not to A when J≠0. Statements about unitization, spans of nilpotents and Morita equivalence of matrix rings are separate extensions, not consequences of this two-layer example.

For general finite-dimensional unital A, use the structure theorem that A/J(A) is semisimple. This result is imported here; the triangular example alone does not prove it. Since J annihilates every simple quotient M/L, JM lies in every maximal submodule L, so JM⊆rad M.

M/JM is a semisimple A/J-module. Its radical is zero: in a direct sum of simple modules, any nonzero vector survives a projection onto some simple summand and therefore lies outside the corresponding maximal kernel. Pulling these kernels back to M shows rad M⊆JM, proving equality.
Every simple submodule is annihilated by J, so soc M⊆{m:Jm=0}. Conversely that annihilator is an A/J-module and is semisimple; its simple summands are submodules of M, giving the reverse inclusion.

Define soc⁰M=0 and socʳM as the inverse image of soc(M/socʳ⁻¹M). By induction, m belongs to socʳM iff Jm⊆socʳ⁻¹M iff Jʳm=0. This proves the displayed socle-layer formula; finite-dimensionality supplies the semisimple-quotient input.

boundaryCheck.question: Which algebra here is semisimple?
choices: A because its natural module has simple factors
boundaryCheck.explanation: The radical must vanish for A itself to be semisimple.

application.question: What is J(A)V on V=F²?
application.explanation: E₁₂e₂=e₁ and E₁₂e₁=0.

transfer.question: Why does 0→Fe₁→V→V/Fe₁→0 fail to split?
choices: No complementary line is stable under E₁₂
transfer.explanation: The off-diagonal action sends a complementary generator into Fe₁.

algebra-radical.connection: The layer explorer compares this extension with actual semisimple blocks.

tensor-products.hook: Can a tensor product of two nonzero modules be zero?
tensor-products.objects: Let R be a unital ring, U a unital right R-module and V a unital left R-module. U⊗_R V is an abelian group with a balanced biadditive map τ:U×V→U⊗_R V, τ(u,v)=u⊗v. The typed balance law is (ur)⊗v=u⊗(rv). For every abelian group A and balanced biadditive b:U×V→A there is a unique homomorphism b̄:U⊗_R V→A with b=b̄∘τ.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which module sides type-check U⊗_R V over a noncommutative R?
choices: U right R and V left R
Both left R without further data
Both right R without further data
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The relation moves a scalar from the right of u to the left of v.

examples.title: A cyclic tensor by generators and relations
steps: For U=ℤ/2ℤ (right ℤ-module) and V=ℤ/4ℤ (left ℤ-module), every pure tensor is a multiple of t=[1]⊗[1]. The source relations impose 2t=0 and 4t=0.
Thus U⊗_ℤV is generated by t with 2t=0, so it is at most ℤ/2ℤ. The balanced map ([a],[b])↦[ab] in ℤ/2ℤ sends t to [1], proving no extra relation kills t and U⊗_ℤV≅ℤ/2ℤ.

examples.title: A zero tensor and a dual/Hom bridge
steps: For ℤ/2ℤ⊗_ℤℤ/3ℤ, t=[1]⊗[1] has 2t=3t=0. Since 1=3−2, t=0, so the entire tensor product is zero although both factors are nonzero.

For finite-dimensional F-spaces V and W, V*⊗_F W→Hom_F(V,W) sends φ⊗w to the rank-one map v↦φ(v)w. If e^i is the dual basis and f_j a basis of W, e^i⊗f_j maps to the matrix unit sending e_i to f_j and other e_k to zero; these form bases, proving the isomorphism.

nonexample.title: Not every tensor is pure
nonexample.explanation: In F²⊗_F F², e₁⊗f₁+e₂⊗f₂ corresponds to the rank-two identity matrix, so it cannot equal one pure tensor u⊗v, which has matrix rank at most one. Treating a sum as a decomposable tensor loses the rank obstruction.

proofSteps: Construct the free abelian group on pairs (u,v), then quotient by additivity in each input and by (ur,v)−(u,rv). This imposes the typed balancing relation and defines τ.

For a balanced biadditive b, send each generator (u,v) to b(u,v). Every defining relation maps to zero, so the homomorphism descends uniquely to U⊗_R V; uniqueness follows because pure tensors generate.
For cyclic ℤ/m and ℤ/n, t=[1]⊗[1] generates, mt=nt=0, and Bezout gives gcd(m,n)t=0. The balanced multiplication map to ℤ/gcd(m,n) sends t to 1, proving its order is exactly gcd(m,n).

Over F, a pure tensor u⊗v represents an outer-product matrix of rank at most one. The sum e₁⊗f₁+e₂⊗f₂ represents rank two and is not pure; the dual-basis matrix units prove V*⊗W≅Hom(V,W) when V,W are finite-dimensional.

boundaryCheck.question: What property must b:U×V→A have to factor through U⊗_R V?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The quotient imposes both additivity relations and the right/left balancing relation.

application.question: What is ℤ/4ℤ⊗_ℤℤ/6ℤ?
application.explanation: The cyclic generator has relations 4t=6t=0 and exact order gcd(4,6)=2.

transfer.question: How does π⊠ρ for G×H differ from an ordinary U⊗_R V construction?
choices: It is only a new spelling for the balancing relation
It always has the same kernel as π×ρ
transfer.explanation: External tensor product adds a product-group action on a field tensor; scalar matching controls its kernel.

tensor-products.connection: The URECA direct-product route uses the underlying field tensor but names the representation π⊠ρ and checks scalar-matching kernels separately.

mh2220-direct-product.hook: When do two independent subgroups really form a product inside a group?
mh2220-direct-product.objects: For groups H and K, H×K has componentwise multiplication. Internally the map (h,k)↦hk is an isomorphism exactly when H and K commute elementwise, intersect trivially, and generate G. Both factors are then normal in G.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the product of (1,0) and (0,1) in additive C₂×C₂?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Add each coordinate independently.

examples.title: C₂×C₃ inside C₆
steps: In C₆=⟨g⟩, H=⟨g³⟩ has order two and K=⟨g²⟩ has order three.
They commute, meet only at e and |HK|=|H||K|=6, so HK=C₆.
The map H×K→C₆, (h,k)↦hk, is an isomorphism; C₂×C₃ is cyclic.

examples.title: The square of involutions
steps: C₂×C₂ has four elements and every nonidentity element has order two.
The two coordinate subgroups commute, intersect trivially and generate it.
C₄ also has order four, but its generator has order four, so cardinality alone does not identify a product.

nonexample.title: A twisting complement in S₃
nonexample.explanation: A₃ and ⟨(12)⟩ intersect trivially and generate S₃, but they do not commute: (12)(123)(12)=(132). Hence S₃ is a semidirect, not a direct, product.

proofSteps: If H and K commute, (h,k)↦hk preserves multiplication: h₁k₁h₂k₂=h₁h₂k₁k₂.
If h₁k₁=h₂k₂, then h₂⁻¹h₁=k₂k₁⁻¹ lies in H∩K={e}; hence the map is injective.
HK=G makes it surjective. Conversely, the coordinate subgroups in an external product have these three properties.
For any (h,k) in a direct product, its order is lcm(|h|,|k|) when the coordinate orders are finite.

boundaryCheck.question: Why is S₃ not A₃×C₂ despite having the right subgroup orders?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The reflection conjugates a three-cycle to its inverse; the homomorphism step fails.

application.question: What is the order of (1,1) in C₂×C₄?
application.explanation: Its order is lcm(2,4)=4, not the size of the whole product.

transfer.question: Can C₄ be an internal direct product of two proper order-two subgroups?
choices: No, C₄ has only one order-two subgroup
transfer.explanation: The unique order-two subgroup cannot have trivial intersection with itself.

mh2220-direct-product.connection: Replacing commutation by a specified conjugation action leads to semidirect products.

mh2220-semidirect.hook: The factors C₃ and C₂ can make either C₆ or S₃. What changes?
mh2220-semidirect.objects: Let N=C₃ be additive and H=C₂=⟨s⟩. A left action α:H→Aut(N) gives (a,b)(c,d)=(a+α(sᵇ)c,b+d). Inversion α(s)c=−c is valid because inversion is an automorphism of C₃ and α(s)²=id.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which map C₃→C₃ is an automorphism of order dividing two?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Inversion preserves addition and its square is identity; the zero map is not invertible.

examples.title: Inversion builds S₃
steps: Use (a,b)(c,d)=(a+(−1)ᵇc,b+d), with coordinates mod 3 and mod 2.
r=(1,0) has order three and s=(0,1) has order two; srs=(−1,0)=r⁻¹.
The six normal forms rᵃsᵇ form S₃. The three order-two subgroups are ⟨s⟩, ⟨rs⟩ and ⟨r²s⟩.

examples.title: Trivial action builds C₆
steps: Set α(s)=id. Then (a,b)(c,d)=(a+c,b+d).
The element (1,1) has order lcm(3,2)=6, so C₃×C₂≅C₆.
The same underlying six pairs have a different multiplication law and subgroup structure.

nonexample.title: A nonsplit extension
nonexample.explanation: 1→C₂→C₄→C₂→1 has no complement to its order-two kernel. The only order-two subgroup is the kernel, so C₄ cannot be C₂⋊C₂. An extension is not automatically split.

proofSteps: The map α is a homomorphism: α(s)²=id. This equality is exactly what the C₂ relation s²=e requires.
Associativity follows by expanding ((n,h)(m,k))(p,l) and (n,h)((m,k)(p,l)); equality uses α(hk)=α(h)α(k).
If G=NH with N normal, H≤G and N∩H={e}, then each g has a unique nh form and conjugation hnh⁻¹ defines α(h).
The normal-form product is (n,h)(m,k)=(nα(h)(m),hk). This identifies G with N⋊H. It is direct precisely when α is trivial.

boundaryCheck.question: Does the map c↦0 define a C₂ action by automorphisms on C₃?
choices: Yes, it is a homomorphism of sets
No, it is not invertible and its square is not id
boundaryCheck.explanation: A group action here must land in Aut(C₃), and s²=e imposes α(s)²=id.

application.question: Under inversion, what is (0,1)(1,0)?
application.explanation: The left reflection coordinate applies inversion to the right rotation: 0−1=2 mod 3.

transfer.question: If N◁G, N∩H={e} and NH=G but H is not normal, what can be concluded?
transfer.explanation: A complement splits the extension. Trivial conjugation is the extra condition for a direct product.

mh2220-semidirect.connection: Action data also controls dihedral groups, order-six classification and split extensions.

mh2220-units.hook: When does multiplication on a clock become reversible?
mh2220-units.objects: Use $n\ge 2$ here. A unit is a residue with a multiplicative inverse. Bézout's identity turns a gcd calculation into an inverse calculation. For prime $p$ every nonzero residue is a unit. Composite moduli may have nonzero nonunits, so multiplication on all residues is not a group.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does [a] modulo n mean?
choices: All integers differing from a by multiples of n
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Congruence classes are sets; multiplying their representatives gives the class product.

examples.title: Invert seven modulo twelve
steps: The Euclidean identity 1=7−2·3=7−2(12−7)=3·7−2·12 gives inverse 3.
The units modulo twelve are 1,5,7,11: every other residue shares a prime factor with twelve.

examples.title: A group with no generator
steps: Modulo eight the units are 1,3,5,7. Their squares are all one.
The group has four elements but no element of order four, so it is not cyclic.

nonexample.title: A nonzero nonunit
nonexample.explanation: [2] modulo six is nonzero, but 2·3=0 and no product with 2 can be 1.

proofSteps: If au≡1 mod n, write au+nv=1; any common divisor of a,n divides one.
If gcd(a,n)=1, Bézout gives au+nv=1, so [u] is an inverse.
Units form a group: products of inverse pairs have inverses in reverse order.

boundaryCheck.question: Is every nonzero residue a unit?
choices: Only when the modulus is prime
boundaryCheck.explanation: For prime p every 1≤a

application.question: What is the inverse of [5] modulo twelve?
application.explanation: 25≡1 modulo twelve, so [5] is its own inverse.

transfer.question: Why does φ(p²)=p²−p for a prime p?
choices: Exactly p residues are divisible by p
transfer.explanation: The p multiples 0,p,…,(p−1)p are precisely the nonunits.

mh2220-units.connection: Produce an inverse modulo 15 and explain why a nonzero residue need not be a unit.

mh2220-permutations.hook: How can two individually simple swaps produce a three-cycle?
mh2220-permutations.objects: Follow a label until it returns to find a cycle, then repeat on unused labels. The resulting disjoint cycles are unique up to cyclic relabeling and reordering. Disjoint cycles commute; overlapping cycles usually do not. Inverse cycles run backward.

prerequisiteCheck.question: In στ, which permutation acts first?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Our convention is (στ)(x)=σ(τ(x)).

examples.title: Compose overlapping swaps
steps: Thus στ=(123); reversing the factors gives (132).

examples.title: Independent cycles return together
steps: The permutation (123)(4567) has two disjoint cycles of lengths three and four.
Its kth power is identity exactly when both 3 and 4 divide k. Its order is twelve.

nonexample.title: Repeated output
nonexample.explanation: The rule 1→2,2→2,3→3 is a function but not a permutation: it is not injective.

proofSteps: Disjoint cycles describe the orbits of repeated application of one permutation.
A power fixes a cycle of length ℓ exactly when ℓ divides the exponent.
A power fixes every point exactly when all cycle lengths divide it; take their least common multiple.

boundaryCheck.question: Must disjoint cycles have distinct lengths?
choices: They must all have length two
No; their moved point sets must be disjoint
boundaryCheck.explanation: (12)(34) has two disjoint cycles of the same length.

application.question: What is the order of (123)(45)?
application.explanation: The least common multiple of three and two is six.

transfer.question: Why can equal cycle type be changed by conjugation?
choices: A relabeling sends each cycle entry to its corresponding label
transfer.explanation: Conjugating (a₁…aₖ) by g yields (g(a₁)…g(aₖ)); matching disjoint cycles defines the relabeling.

mh2220-permutations.connection: Compose permutations from right to left.

mh2220-permutation-matrices.hook: Can the matrix and cycle diagram tell exactly the same story?
mh2220-permutation-matrices.objects: The jth column is the image of the jth basis vector. Permutation matrices have one 1 in each row and column. This construction is faithful: different permutations give different matrices. It is the first bridge from a group action to a linear representation.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does column j record?
choices: The inverse image of every vector
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A linear map is determined by its basis images, placed in columns.

examples.title: Read columns as images
steps: For σ=(123), the columns of Pσ are e₂,e₃,e₁.
Consequently Pσ(a,b,c)=(c,a,b); coefficients move with their original basis labels.

examples.title: Trace counts fixed labels
steps: For σ=(12) on three labels, e₁ and e₂ swap while e₃ stays fixed.
The diagonal is 0,0,1, giving trace one. Its determinant is −1.

nonexample.title: Wrong coordinate direction
nonexample.explanation: The rule (a,b,c)→(b,c,a) is the inverse three-cycle for the stated convention; it cannot be labelled P(123).

proofSteps: Both PσPτ and Pστ send eⱼ to eσ(τ(j)), so they agree on a basis.
Permutation columns are orthonormal; therefore PσᵀPσ=I.
A diagonal one occurs exactly when σ(j)=j, yielding the trace/fixed-point formula.

boundaryCheck.question: Does Pσ act by (vσ(1),…,vσ(n))?
choices: Generally no; output coordinate i is vσ⁻¹(i)
boundaryCheck.explanation: Coefficients move from j to σ(j), so recover the incoming label using σ⁻¹.

application.question: What is the trace of P(123) on three labels?
application.explanation: No basis label is fixed by the three-cycle.

transfer.question: Why is the representation faithful?
choices: If every basis vector is fixed then every label is fixed
transfer.explanation: Pσ=I forces σ(j)=j for every j. Trace alone need not determine σ.

mh2220-permutation-matrices.connection: Read matrix columns as images of basis vectors.

mh2220-alternating.hook: Does even describe the order of a permutation or how it is assembled?
mh2220-alternating.objects: A k-cycle can be expressed as $k-1$ transpositions, giving sign $(-1)^{k-1}$. The sign of a product is the product of signs, even for overlapping cycles. Thus every transposition decomposition has the same parity. $A_n$ contains the even permutations.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the determinant of a transposition matrix?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Swapping two basis columns reverses determinant sign.

examples.title: Two swaps make an even permutation
steps: The permutation (12)(34) has determinant (−1)(−1)=1.
It has order two, so even parity does not mean odd order.

examples.title: A cycle has a parity certificate
steps: A k-cycle can be written as k−1 transpositions.
A five-cycle is therefore even, while a four-cycle is odd. Determinants show the result cannot depend on the chosen factorization.

nonexample.title: Counting cycle length incorrectly
nonexample.explanation: A three-cycle is even: it requires two transpositions, not three.

proofSteps: Pστ=PσPτ and determinant multiplicativity give sgn(στ)=sgn(σ)sgn(τ).
The kernel of this homomorphism is the even permutations and is normal.
For n≥2, multiplication by a fixed transposition pairs even and odd permutations bijectively; each half has n!/2 elements.

boundaryCheck.question: For which n does |Aₙ|=n!/2 hold?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A₁ has one element; the pairing needs a transposition, which requires two labels.

application.question: What is the sign of (1234)(56)?
application.explanation: A four-cycle contributes −1 and the swap contributes −1, giving +1.

transfer.question: Why is Aₙ normal?
choices: It is the kernel of a homomorphism
Every even permutation commutes with every permutation
transfer.explanation: Kernels are preserved by conjugation; normality is setwise preservation, not centrality.

mh2220-alternating.connection: Determine sign from disjoint cycles and prove that the alternating group is a kernel.

mh2220-euler-fermat.hook: Why can a huge exponent become a small computation?
mh2220-euler-fermat.objects: Euler's theorem applies to units modulo $n$. Fermat's little theorem is its prime-modulus specialization. The coprimality condition matters: for a nonunit, repeated multiplication need not return to 1.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which residues form the unit group modulo n?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Bézout characterizes precisely the invertible residues.

examples.title: Reduce an exponent legitimately
steps: Modulo ten, [3] is a unit and φ(10)=4. Euler gives 3⁴≡1.
Since 1001=4·250+1, 3¹⁰⁰¹≡3 modulo ten.

examples.title: A prime separates two formulations
steps: For prime seven and a not divisible by seven, a⁶≡1.
Multiplying by a gives a⁷≡a. If seven divides a, the latter is also true because both sides vanish modulo seven.

nonexample.title: A missing coprimality premise
nonexample.explanation: 2⁴≡4 modulo ten, not one: gcd(2,10)≠1, so Euler does not apply.

proofSteps: When gcd(a,n)=1, [a] belongs to the finite unit group of size φ(n).
Its order divides φ(n) by Lagrange, giving [a]^φ(n)=[1].
For a prime p the unit group has p−1 elements. Include a divisible by p separately to obtain aᵖ≡a.

boundaryCheck.question: What premise is needed for a^φ(n)≡1 mod n?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Euler is a statement about a unit; primality of a is irrelevant.

application.question: What is 7⁸ modulo fifteen?

transfer.question: Does Fermat aᵖ≡a require p∤a?
choices: No, multiples of p satisfy it directly
transfer.explanation: The unit-group proof handles p∤a; the omitted case gives zero on both sides.

mh2220-euler-fermat.connection: Explain why Euler’s exponent cannot be applied to an arbitrary residue.

mh2220-real-circle.hook: What does a quotient forget when a line wraps around a circle?
mh2220-real-circle.objects: Addition of real parameters becomes multiplication on the unit circle. Choosing $t$ in [0,1) is a way to pick one representative per coset; the interval itself is not closed under ordinary addition. This is also the rotation group SO(2), through the usual rotation matrix.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is an element of R/Z?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A quotient element includes all representatives differing by integers.

examples.title: Same point after whole turns
steps: The real numbers 1/4 and 5/4 differ by one.
Both map to exp(πi/2)=i, so they represent the same point of R/Z.

examples.title: A homomorphism with infinite kernel
steps: The map t→exp(2πit) converts addition into multiplication.
Its kernel is all integers, and every unit complex number occurs as exp(2πit).

nonexample.title: Endpoints are not two points
nonexample.explanation: The representatives zero and one are distinct real numbers but determine the same quotient class and the same point on the circle.

proofSteps: The exponential identity proves preservation of addition.
Equality of exponentials occurs precisely when the difference is an integer.
Surjectivity follows by choosing an argument for each unit complex number; first isomorphism gives R/Z≅S¹ as groups.

boundaryCheck.question: Is the interval [0,1] literally a unique representative set?
choices: No class has a representative there
No; its endpoints represent the same class
boundaryCheck.explanation: [0,1) gives unique representatives; [0,1] duplicates the zero class.

application.question: What point corresponds to 1/2+Z?
application.explanation: exp(2πi·1/2)=exp(πi)=−1.

transfer.question: Why is t→exp(2πit) not injective on R?
choices: All integer translates have the same image
transfer.explanation: Its nontrivial kernel is Z. Quotienting by exactly this kernel removes the duplication.

mh2220-real-circle.connection: Identify the kernel of each map and explain why the two quotient descriptions are isomorphic.

mh2220-automorphism.hook: Which ways of renaming a group preserve every product?
mh2220-automorphism.objects: Automorphisms form a group under composition. Conjugations form its normal subgroup of inner automorphisms. An automorphism that is not inner is called outer. For a cyclic group, sending $g$ to $g^k$ is an automorphism precisely when $k$ is coprime to the group order.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is an automorphism?
choices: Any bijection of its underlying set
A bijective homomorphism from a group to itself
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Both structure preservation and bijectivity are necessary.

examples.title: Generators control cyclic automorphisms
steps: In C₈=⟨g⟩, sending g to g³ determines gᵏ→g³ᵏ.
Since gcd(3,8)=1 this is bijective; composing it with itself gives exponent nine, hence the identity modulo eight.

examples.title: Inner automorphisms can be invisible
steps: In an abelian group, gxg⁻¹=x for every pair, so every inner automorphism is identity.
C₅ nevertheless has four automorphisms, from the four possible generator images.

nonexample.title: A nongenerator image
nonexample.explanation: The map g→g² on C₈ preserves products but has image of order four, so it is not an automorphism.

proofSteps: An endomorphism of Cₙ is fixed by the image of its generator.
That endomorphism is invertible exactly when the image generates, equivalently gcd(k,n)=1.
Conjugation defines G→Aut(G), with kernel Z(G); first isomorphism identifies Inn(G) with G/Z(G).

boundaryCheck.question: Must every automorphism be inner?
choices: Only if the group is finite
No; abelian groups can have nontrivial automorphisms
boundaryCheck.explanation: Conjugation in an abelian group is always identity, but C₅ has nontrivial generator changes.

application.question: How many automorphisms does C₈ have?
application.explanation: The admissible exponents are 1,3,5,7.

transfer.question: Which group elements give the identity conjugation map?
choices: Every element of the commutator subgroup
transfer.explanation: Conjugation by g fixes every x exactly when g commutes with every x.

mh2220-automorphism.connection: Specify an automorphism by its effect on generators and check that all defining relations are preserved.

mh2220-centralizer-normalizer.hook: Can a motion preserve a subgroup while moving its individual elements?
mh2220-centralizer-normalizer.objects: The center consists of moves commuting with everything. The centralizer of a subgroup fixes it pointwise by conjugation, while the normalizer fixes it setwise. The normalizer is the largest subgroup of $G$ in which $H$ is normal.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does C_G(H) require?
choices: Commuting with every element of H
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Centralizing is a pointwise conjugation condition.

examples.title: Centralize one transposition
steps: In S₃, any permutation commuting with (12) must preserve its swapped pair and its unique fixed point.
Thus C_S₃((12))={e,(12)}, of order two.

examples.title: Normalize without centralizing
steps: A₃={e,(123),(132)} is normal in S₃, so its normalizer is S₃.
A transposition exchanges the two three-cycles by conjugation; the centralizer of A₃ is only A₃.

nonexample.title: Setwise is weaker than pointwise
nonexample.explanation: A transposition normalizes A₃ while failing to commute with its generator. Therefore normalizer and centralizer need not agree.

proofSteps: For g∈N_G(H), conjugation restricts to an automorphism of H.
These restrictions multiply by the composition law, giving a homomorphism N_G(H)→Aut(H).
Its kernel consists of elements commuting with every h∈H; quotient by C_G(H) embeds into Aut(H).

boundaryCheck.question: When is H normal in G?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Normalizer equality means every conjugation preserves H as a set.

application.question: What is N_S₃(A₃)?
application.explanation: A₃ is normal, so all six permutations normalize it.

transfer.question: Why is C_G(H) normal in N_G(H)?
choices: It is the kernel of the conjugation homomorphism
Every centralizer is normal in G
transfer.explanation: Kernel normality applies in the domain N_G(H); it need not apply in all G.

mh2220-centralizer-normalizer.connection: Produce an element that normalizes a subgroup without centralizing it.

mh2220-commutator.hook: What is the smallest information loss that makes all motions commute?
mh2220-commutator.objects: The subgroup generated by all commutators is normal. Quotienting by it makes every pair commute. This abelianization is the universal part of $G$ visible to homomorphisms into abelian groups.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which commutator convention is used?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The factor order is fixed throughout these lessons.

examples.title: A triangle has an abelian quotient
steps: In S₃, the sign map kills every commutator, so S₃′≤A₃.
For a three-cycle r and reflection s with srs=r⁻¹, [s,r]=r⁻²=r, so A₃≤S₃′. Thus S₃′=A₃.

examples.title: No loss for an abelian group
steps: If xy=yx then xyx⁻¹y⁻¹=e for every pair.
Hence the commutator subgroup of C₆ is trivial and its abelianization is C₆ itself.

nonexample.title: A commutator is not an arbitrary product
nonexample.explanation: The generating set of commutators need not itself be a subgroup. The derived subgroup is generated by them, not merely their list.

proofSteps: Conjugation sends [x,y] to [gxg⁻¹,gyg⁻¹], making the generated subgroup normal.
In G/N, xN and yN commute exactly when [x,y]∈N.
Therefore G/N is abelian exactly when G′≤N; every map to an abelian group factors through G/G′.

boundaryCheck.question: When is G/G′ trivial?
choices: When G is abelian and nontrivial
boundaryCheck.explanation: The quotient is trivial precisely when the derived subgroup is the whole group.

application.question: What is S₃/S₃′?
application.explanation: S₃′=A₃ has order three; the quotient has order two.

transfer.question: A homomorphism f:G→A has abelian target. What is forced?
transfer.explanation: Each commutator maps to the identity because its two target factors commute.

mh2220-commutator.connection: Show why every homomorphism to an abelian group kills the commutator subgroup.

mh2220-finite-abelian.hook: How many genuinely different arrangements of eight abelian motions exist?
mh2220-finite-abelian.objects: Here $G$ is finite abelian; the primes in the first product may repeat. These are elementary-divisor and invariant-factor descriptions. With nontrivial factors and standard ordering, the lists are unique. The course writes the invariant factors in the opposite order, an equivalent convention.

prerequisiteCheck.question: When is Cₘ×Cₙ cyclic of order mn?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The order of any pair divides lcm(m,n); it reaches mn exactly in the coprime case.

examples.title: The three partitions of three
steps: An abelian group of order eight has primary exponent three. Its partitions are 3,2+1,1+1+1.
The classification yields C₈, C₄×C₂, C₂³. Their maximum element orders are eight, four and two, proving they differ.

examples.title: Align different prime components
steps: For order twelve, the two-primary part is C₄ or C₂×C₂; the three-primary part is C₃.
Combining coprime cyclic factors gives C₁₂ or C₂×C₆. This uses classification for completeness and CRT for the isomorphisms.

nonexample.title: Order alone does not classify
nonexample.explanation: Q₈ is a group of order eight but is nonabelian, so it is outside the finite abelian classification.

proofSteps: The primary decomposition is obtained by separating prime powers using Bézout identities.
The primary cyclic decomposition and its uniqueness are imported structural results; this outline is not a complete proof of splitting.
Given the theorem, partitions enumerate candidates; element orders and the numbers killed by each pᵏ distinguish their invariants.

boundaryCheck.question: Which hypotheses does this classification require?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Nonabelian p-groups such as Q₈ are counterexamples to dropping commutativity.

application.question: How many abelian groups of order eight occur up to isomorphism?
application.explanation: The three partitions of the exponent three give the three primary decompositions.

transfer.question: Are C₄×C₃ and C₁₂ isomorphic?
choices: No, one has two displayed factors
transfer.explanation: The element (generator,generator) has order lcm(4,3)=12 and generates the whole product.

mh2220-finite-abelian.connection: List the abelian groups of a specified order and distinguish them using element orders.

mh2220-quaternion.hook: What distinguishes two different noncommutative groups with eight elements?
mh2220-quaternion.objects: In $Q_8$, we have $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$. There is exactly one element of order $2$, namely $-1$. The six elements $\pm i,\pm j,\pm k$ have order $4$. Its three cyclic subgroups of order $4$ meet in $\{1,-1\}$. Every subgroup of $Q_8$ is normal.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does index two imply for a subgroup?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The complementary coset is both the unique other left coset and the unique other right coset.

examples.title: Count involutions
steps: In Q₈, −1 is the unique element of order two; ±i,±j,±k have order four.
In D₄ the half-turn and all four reflections have order two, giving five involutions. Therefore Q₈ and D₄ are not isomorphic.

examples.title: See the shared quotient
steps: The center of Q₈ is {1,−1}.
The quotient has classes {±1},{±i},{±j},{±k}; its three nonidentity classes square to identity, so it is C₂×C₂.

nonexample.title: Same size is not enough
nonexample.explanation: Both Q₈ and D₄ are nonabelian of order eight. Their differing involution counts prevent an isomorphism.

proofSteps: The abelian order-eight groups are already classified as three possibilities.
For a nonabelian order-eight group, an element of order four gives a cyclic subgroup of index two. If none exists, all nonidentity elements have order two, forcing commutativity.
Choose a outside that cyclic subgroup. Noncommutativity forces inversion conjugation. Its square is identity or the unique involution of the cyclic subgroup, giving D₄ or Q₈ respectively.

boundaryCheck.question: Does Q₈ contain a subgroup generated by an involution outside its center?
boundaryCheck.explanation: i and j have order four; −1 is central and is the only order-two element.

application.question: How many involutions does D₄ have?
application.explanation: Count the four reflections and the half-turn.

transfer.question: Why is a group in which every element squares to e abelian?
choices: There can only be two elements
transfer.explanation: The inverse-of-product law gives ab=ba when each factor and their product is its own inverse.

mh2220-quaternion.connection: Distinguish D₄ from Q₈ without relying on their size or ordinary character table.

mh2220-conjugacy.hook: How does relabeling turn centralizers into a count of conjugacy classes?
