mh2220-conjugacy.objects: The stabilizer under conjugation is the centralizer. Central elements form singleton classes. In $S_n$, two permutations are conjugate exactly when their disjoint cycle types agree. This classification foreshadows characters, which are constant on conjugacy classes.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does conjugation by g do to (ab)?
choices: It changes the order to three
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Conjugation relabels the two moved points.

examples.title: The three kinds of permutations in S₃
steps: The conjugacy classes are {e}, the three transpositions, and the two three-cycles.
Their centralizer orders are six, two, three. Their indices are one, three, two, summing to six.

examples.title: A central class
steps: In Q₈, −1 commutes with every element. Its centralizer is all Q₈.
Its conjugacy class therefore has size 8/8=1; by contrast i and −i form a class of size two.

nonexample.title: Equal order need not mean conjugate
nonexample.explanation: In the abelian group C₂×C₂, the three nonidentity elements all have order two but each has a singleton conjugacy class.

proofSteps: Conjugation is a group action on G; the stabilizer at x is C_G(x).
Orbit–stabilizer gives |Cl(x)|=[G:C_G(x)].
The conjugacy orbits partition G; the singleton central orbits contribute |Z(G)| in the finite class equation.

boundaryCheck.question: What finiteness premise makes the class equation a sum of integers?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The orbit formula works as a coset bijection generally; the displayed integer counting uses finite G.

application.question: How large is a transposition class in S₃?
application.explanation: Its centralizer has order two, so the index is six divided by two.

transfer.question: When is Cl(x) a singleton?
choices: When x lies in any normal subgroup
transfer.explanation: gxg⁻¹=x for every g is exactly commutation with every group element.

mh2220-conjugacy.connection: Find a centralizer and use its index to calculate a conjugacy-class size.

mh2220-coset-action.hook: What information survives when a group moves only its cosets?
mh2220-coset-action.objects: The intersection is the core of $H$: the largest normal subgroup of $G$ contained in $H$. The action is defined even when $H$ is not normal, because left multiplication still permutes left cosets. For a finite-index subgroup, the image lies in a finite symmetric group.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What are the points acted on?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The action takes aH to gaH.

examples.title: A nonnormal stabilizer with faithful action
steps: Take H=⟨(12)⟩ in S₃. There are three left cosets.
The conjugate subgroups generated by (12),(13),(23) intersect in {e}. The coset action has trivial kernel.

examples.title: A normal stabilizer with invisible motions
steps: For H=A₃, there are two cosets and every conjugate of H equals H.
The core and action kernel are A₃; the induced quotient acts faithfully on two points.

nonexample.title: Coset action is not coset multiplication
nonexample.explanation: For nonnormal H, g·(aH)=gaH is well-defined even though (aH)(bH)=abH is not a well-defined quotient-group law.

proofSteps: If aH=bH, left multiplication gives gaH=gbH, proving the action is well-defined.
An element k fixes aH iff a⁻¹ka∈H; intersect over all a to obtain the core.
For finite index n, G/core embeds into Sₙ; its finite order therefore divides n! by Lagrange.

boundaryCheck.question: Does this action need H normal?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Left multiplication respects coset equality for every subgroup.

application.question: What is the core of ⟨(12)⟩ in S₃?
application.explanation: Intersect the three transposition subgroups; only identity remains.

transfer.question: If H has finite index n, what bounds [G:core(H)]?
transfer.explanation: The faithful induced action embeds G/core(H) into Sₙ, giving finite index dividing n!.

mh2220-coset-action.connection: Compute the action kernel and explain the factorial-index consequence.

mh2220-double-cosets.hook: What happens when one subgroup can move a representative from the left and another from the right?
mh2220-double-cosets.objects: Double cosets partition $G$, but they need not have equal sizes. Their sizes depend on the overlap between $H$ and $gKg^{-1}$. View them through the action of $H$ on the coset set $G/K$.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is HgK?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: It allows independent subgroup moves on both sides.

examples.title: Two double cosets in S₃
steps: Let H=⟨s⟩ with s=(12), and r=(123).
The double cosets are H={e,s} and HrH={r,r²,rs,r²s}; they have sizes two and four.

examples.title: Count through a stabilizer
steps: For HgK, let H act on the left coset gK.
Its stabilizer is H∩gKg⁻¹. Each point of this orbit is a left K-coset, so multiply the orbit count by |K|.

nonexample.title: Double cosets usually have unequal sizes
nonexample.explanation: The two double cosets above have sizes two and four; equal-size ordinary-coset intuition cannot be applied to them.

proofSteps: h fixes gK iff hgK=gK iff g⁻¹hg∈K.
Thus the H-orbit of gK contains [H:H∩gKg⁻¹] left K-cosets.
For finite groups, each such coset has |K| elements, yielding |HgK|=|H||K|/|H∩gKg⁻¹|.

boundaryCheck.question: Must double cosets have equal cardinality?
choices: Yes, all are translates of H
No, the intersection denominator can vary
boundaryCheck.explanation: The S₃ example gives different sizes already in a finite group.

application.question: If |H|=|K|=2 and |H∩gKg⁻¹|=1, what is |HgK|?
application.explanation: The product formula gives 2·2/1=4.

transfer.question: What happens if K={e}?
choices: Double cosets become ordinary right H-cosets Hg
transfer.explanation: Hg{e}=Hg. A set partition still does not require normality.

mh2220-double-cosets.connection: Compute both a double coset and its cardinality from the intersection formula.

mh2220-simple-composition.hook: Which irreducible group pieces survive a choice of decomposition?
mh2220-simple-composition.objects: A composition series is a finite chain in which each subgroup is normal in the preceding one and each successive quotient is simple. The Jordan–$H$ölder theorem says that any two such series have the same simple factors up to isomorphism and reordering. The source mentions this theorem without proving it.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What must a factor group Gᵢ/Gᵢ₊₁ require?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Normality in the immediately preceding term makes the quotient valid.

examples.title: The layers of S₄
steps: Use S₄≥A₄≥V₄≥C₂≥{e}; each term is normal in the preceding term.
The quotient orders are 2,3,2,2, so the simple factors are C₂,C₃,C₂,C₂.

examples.title: Simple does not mean no subgroups
steps: A₅ is nonabelian simple, yet it contains subgroups generated by three-cycles.
Those proper subgroups are not normal; simplicity excludes proper nontrivial normal subgroups only.

nonexample.title: Normality only at adjacent stages
nonexample.explanation: The selected C₂ inside V₄ is normal in V₄ but not in S₄. A composition series needs subnormal steps, not every term normal in the ambient group.

proofSteps: The displayed adjacent normality permits each factor quotient.
Prime-order factors are cyclic and have no proper nontrivial subgroup, so are simple.
Jordan–Hölder is imported: any two composition series of a finite group have the same multiset of simple factors. The example verifies its factors but does not prove that uniqueness theorem.

boundaryCheck.question: Can a simple group have proper nontrivial subgroups?
choices: Yes, provided they are not normal
boundaryCheck.explanation: Simplicity is a condition on normal subgroups.

application.question: What are the factor orders in the displayed S₄ series?
application.explanation: Take successive order ratios 24/12,12/4,4/2,2/1.

transfer.question: Does the multiset of composition factors determine a finite group?
choices: No; C₄ and C₂×C₂ both have two C₂ factors
transfer.explanation: Jordan–Hölder proves invariance of factors, not classification of how extensions assemble them.

mh2220-simple-composition.connection: Identify a composition series and distinguish its factors from its subgroups.

mh2220-p-groups.hook: Why must every finite prime-power group have an invisible central motion?
mh2220-p-groups.objects: Here G is a nontrivial finite p-group: |G|=p^a with a≥1. Every noncentral conjugacy class has size divisible by $p$. The identity is central, so the center cannot have size zero and must have at least $p$ elements. A simple finite $p$-group is therefore exactly a cyclic group of prime order.

prerequisiteCheck.question: How is a conjugacy-class size obtained?
choices: Index of the center in every case
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Orbit–stabilizer applies to conjugation.

examples.title: Read Q₈ modulo two
steps: Its conjugacy-class sizes are 1,1,2,2,2.
The noncentral terms are divisible by two. The two singleton classes form the center {1,−1}.

examples.title: A center need not be the whole group
steps: D₄ has center {e,r²}, with its half-turn commuting with every reflection.
Its noncentral rotations and reflections demonstrate that a nontrivial center does not imply abelianity.

nonexample.title: Finiteness matters
nonexample.explanation: The counting argument uses the integer order pᵃ. It is not a proof about arbitrary infinite groups whose elements have p-power order.

proofSteps: For |G|=p^a with a≥1, noncentral conjugacy classes have sizes [G:C_G(x)], positive p-powers greater than one.
The finite class equation modulo p therefore gives |Z(G)|≡0 mod p.
Identity belongs to the center, so its size is at least p. A simple p-group must equal its center, and a simple abelian finite group is Cₚ.

boundaryCheck.question: Which p-groups have to be simple?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A simple p-group is abelian by its center; an abelian simple group has prime order.

application.question: What is |Z(Q₈)|?
application.explanation: Only ±1 commute with all quaternion units.

transfer.question: Why is Cₚ² not simple?
choices: Its subgroup of order p is normal and proper
Its order is composite and every composite group is nonsimple
transfer.explanation: The actual subgroup ⟨gᵖ⟩ supplies the normal-subgroup witness.

mh2220-p-groups.connection: Explain why a finite p-group has nontrivial center but need not be abelian.

mh2220-finite-matrices.hook: How do independent columns reveal a maximal prime-power subgroup?
mh2220-finite-matrices.objects: The first column can be any nonzero vector; each later column must avoid the span of its predecessors. In the unitriangular subgroup there are $n(n-1)/2$ arbitrary entries above the diagonal. It captures the entire $p$-part of the general linear group order. Every finite $p$-group $G$ embeds into $U_|G|(F_p)$, although this construction can use a much larger dimension than necessary.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What makes a square matrix invertible over a field?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Independence means the corresponding linear map is bijective.

examples.title: Count GL₂(F₃)
steps: The first column is any nonzero vector: eight choices.
The second must avoid its three-element span: six choices. Hence GL₂(F₃) has 48 elements.

examples.title: Count unitriangular matrices
steps: In U₃(F₂), three entries above the diagonal can independently be zero or one.
The subgroup has eight elements. GL₃(F₂) has (8−1)(8−2)(8−4)=168 elements, whose two-part is eight.

nonexample.title: Nonzero columns can still be dependent
nonexample.explanation: The matrix with both columns (1,0) has nonzero columns but zero determinant. Each new column must avoid the span of all previous ones.

proofSteps: Choose column i+1 outside the pⁱ-element span of the previous i columns, obtaining ∏(pⁿ−pⁱ).
Factor pⁱ from each term; the remaining factors pⁿ⁻ⁱ−1 are prime to p. The p-part is p raised to n(n−1)/2.

Upper-unitriangular matrices form a subgroup with exactly that order, hence a Sylow p-subgroup. Cayley embeds any finite p-group into permutation matrices, and Sylow containment conjugates it into a unitriangular subgroup.

boundaryCheck.question: Why restrict the coefficient field to Fₚ here?
choices: Every finite field has p elements
The p-part computation and Cayley embedding use characteristic p
boundaryCheck.explanation: The general q-element column formula also exists; this argument specifies the prime-field case.

application.question: How many matrices are in U₃(F₂)?
application.explanation: There are three free binary upper entries.

transfer.question: Why does Cayley plus Sylow containment produce a unitriangular embedding?
choices: The permutation matrices form a p-subgroup of GL and lie in a conjugate Sylow
Every permutation matrix is already upper triangular
transfer.explanation: Changing basis by that conjugation keeps the map injective while placing its image in U.

mh2220-finite-matrices.connection: Count GL₂(𝔽₃) by independent columns and identify its p-part.

m3220-subrings.hook: Must a smaller ring inherit the identity of its parent?
m3220-subrings.objects: The even integers form a ring without identity under ordinary operations. In the matrix ring, the corner matrices diag(a,0) form a unital subring whose identity is diag(1,0), not the ambient identity.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What additive test is used for subrings?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Differences ensure additive identity and inverses.

examples.title: An identity changes
steps: Inside M₂(R), the matrices diag(a,0) form a ring under inherited operations.
Its identity is diag(1,0), not I₂.

examples.title: A ring without an identity
steps: The even integers are closed under differences and products.
No even integer e satisfies e·2=2, so this subring of Z has no identity.

nonexample.title: A set closed under multiplication only
nonexample.explanation: Positive integers are multiplicatively closed but are not closed under differences, so are not a subring.

proofSteps: Difference closure and nonemptiness give an additive subgroup.
Multiplicative closure gives the second operation; associativity and distributivity are inherited.
An identity, when required, must be checked separately under the declared subring convention.

boundaryCheck.question: Must a subring contain 1 of the parent in this course convention?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The course permits nonunital rings and subrings with a different identity.

application.question: What is the identity of {diag(a,0)}?
application.explanation: Multiplying either side by diag(1,0) leaves diag(a,0) fixed.

transfer.question: Why is 2Z a subring but not a field?
choices: It has no multiplicative identity and nonzero elements are not invertible there
It is not closed under products
It is not closed under subtraction
transfer.explanation: Its operations close, but the field axioms fail.

m3220-subrings.connection: Decide whether an inclusion preserves identity and explain why that question is separate from additive/multiplicative closure.

m3220-characteristic.hook: Why does a finite field always contain a prime clock?
m3220-characteristic.objects: If a finite field has characteristic $p$, the copies of its identity form a copy of the prime field. The whole field is a finite-dimensional vector space over that subfield, so its cardinality is a power of $p$.

prerequisiteCheck.question: How is n1 formed?
choices: By adding the identity to itself n times
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Characteristic concerns additive repetition.

examples.title: Two different twelves
steps: Z/12Z has characteristic twelve since twelve copies of one first give zero.
It is not a domain: [3][4]=[0] with both factors nonzero.

examples.title: Four elements, characteristic two
steps: F₄ is two-dimensional over its prime subfield F₂.
Its additive identity satisfies 1+1=0, while its cardinality is 2²=4.

nonexample.title: Size is not characteristic
nonexample.explanation: F₄ has characteristic two, not four. Cardinality is a prime power; characteristic is the prime.

proofSteps: The map Z→R sending n to n1 is a ring map for a unital ring; its kernel is dZ.
If positive d factors as ab with 1<a,b<d, both a1,b1 are nonzero while their product vanishes; a domain therefore has prime characteristic.
A finite field is a finite-dimensional vector space over Fₚ; k basis coefficients give pᵏ elements.

boundaryCheck.question: Can a domain have characteristic six?
choices: Yes if it has six units
boundaryCheck.explanation: Then (2·1)(3·1)=0 with both factors nonzero.

application.question: What is char(Z/8Z)?
application.explanation: Eight is the least positive multiple of one equal to zero.

transfer.question: A finite field has 27 elements. What is its characteristic?
transfer.explanation: Its cardinality is 3³, so its prime subfield has characteristic three.

m3220-characteristic.connection: Distinguish cardinality from characteristic and explain why a finite field is a vector space over its prime field.

m3220-domains.hook: When does cancellation force every nonzero number to be invertible?
m3220-domains.objects: A division ring requires inverses for every nonzero element but may be noncommutative. A field is a commutative division ring. Finiteness closes the gap between cancellation and invertibility.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does a domain exclude?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Domains are nonzero commutative unital rings without nonzero zero divisors.

examples.title: A finite domain
steps: In F₂[X]/(X²+X+1), the nonzero elements 1,α,α+1 are units.
α(α+1)=1 verifies the two nontrivial inverses.

examples.title: An infinite domain
steps: Z has no nonzero zero divisors, so multiplication by two is injective.
It is not surjective: one has no integer preimage. Therefore Z is not a field.

nonexample.title: Finite ring is insufficient
nonexample.explanation: Z/6Z is finite but not a domain; [2][3]=[0]. Its nonzero [2] has no inverse.

proofSteps: For nonzero a in a domain, ax=ay implies a(x−y)=0 and hence x=y.
On a finite set this injective map is surjective.
Find x with ax=1; commutativity gives xa=1 as well. Thus every nonzero a is a unit.

boundaryCheck.question: Which premise converts injectivity to surjectivity?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Injective maps on infinite sets can miss targets.

application.question: Is Z/5Z a field?
choices: No, zero is not a unit
application.explanation: It is a finite domain; all four nonzero classes have inverses.

transfer.question: Why does the argument fail for Z?
choices: Multiplication by two is injective but misses one
transfer.explanation: The lost premise is finiteness, not cancellation.

m3220-domains.connection: Distinguish cancellation from existence of inverses.

m3220-algebraic.hook: How can one new number produce a closed field?
m3220-algebraic.objects: An algebraic number satisfies a nonzero integer polynomial. An algebraic integer satisfies a monic integer polynomial. In a quadratic field, multiplication reduces every occurrence of the square of the new root to $D$.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What field are the coefficients a,b in?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Q(√D) is described using rational coefficients.

examples.title: Invert a quadratic number
steps: For x=1+√2, multiply by 1−√2 to obtain −1.
Thus x⁻¹=√2−1, still in Q(√2).

examples.title: Multiply in two coordinates
steps: (a+b√D)(c+d√D)=(ac+Dbd)+(ad+bc)√D.
If D=−1 this is the usual rational complex arithmetic, with basis 1,i.

nonexample.title: A rational square collapses the basis
nonexample.explanation: For D=1, a+b√D is just a+b; two coordinates are no longer unique. The quadratic-field premise excludes this.

proofSteps: A square-free D≠0,1 is not a square in Q, so 1 and √D are linearly independent.
The multiplication formula closes the two-dimensional space.
The conjugate product a²−Db² cannot vanish for a nonzero pair, so conjugate divided by norm provides an inverse.

boundaryCheck.question: Why require D not a rational square?
boundaryCheck.explanation: If √D is rational, the extension has degree one.

application.question: What is (1+√2)⁻¹?
application.explanation: Their product is 2−1=1.

transfer.question: What is the norm of 3+2√2?

m3220-algebraic.connection: Relate minimal polynomial, quotient and extension degree.

m3220-quadratic-integers.hook: Why do some integer lattices need a half-step?
m3220-quadratic-integers.objects: Here $D$ is square-free and different from 0 and 1. For negative $D$ the complex embedding draws the lattice faithfully. For positive $D$ the coefficient plane is a coordinate model; the two real embeddings give a different geometric view.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What defines an algebraic integer?
choices: Any number with integer norm only
A root of a monic polynomial in Z[X]
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Monicity and integer coefficients are both essential.

examples.title: A hidden integral half-step
steps: For D=5, ω=(1+√5)/2 satisfies ω²−ω−1=0.
It is an algebraic integer although its coordinates in the basis 1,√5 are halves. O_K=Z[ω].

examples.title: An ordinary integer lattice
steps: For D=−1, D≡3 mod 4 and the ring is Z[i].
Every a+bi with integer a,b satisfies X²−2aX+(a²+b²)=0.

nonexample.title: Wrong integral basis
nonexample.explanation: Z[√5] omits the integral ω. It is a subring of the full integer ring, not the full ring.

proofSteps: The displayed ω satisfies a monic integer quadratic, so Z[ω] consists of algebraic integers.
The converse uses integrality of trace and norm and their parity constraints; the integral-basis classification is imported, with this outline showing its mechanism.
For D≡1 mod 4 the relation ω²=ω+(D−1)/4 closes multiplication; otherwise √D²=D does.

boundaryCheck.question: What assumptions does the displayed integral-basis theorem use?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A genuine quadratic field requires a nonsquare radicand.

application.question: What is ω² when ω=(1+√5)/2?
application.explanation: Substitute D=5 in ω²=ω+(D−1)/4.

transfer.question: Is the coefficient plane for positive D a complex lattice picture?
choices: No quadratic field has geometric embeddings
No; it is a coordinate model, with two real embeddings
transfer.explanation: For positive D both embeddings are real; a coefficient drawing must be labelled accordingly.

m3220-quadratic-integers.connection: Determine the correct integral basis and verify that a proposed element is an algebraic integer.

m3220-norm-trace.hook: How does conjugation certify that an integer is a unit?
m3220-norm-trace.objects: For Gaussian integers the norm is squared Euclidean distance from zero. For positive $D$ it is an indefinite quadratic expression, so it must not be presented as ordinary length. On the quadratic integer ring, both norm and trace are integers.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the conjugate of a+b√D?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The nontrivial field automorphism changes the sign of √D.

examples.title: A Gaussian unit
steps: N(i)=i(−i)=1. The conjugate −i is its inverse.
In Z[i], norm-one elements are ±1,±i.

examples.title: A real quadratic unit
steps: For 1+√2, the norm is 1−2=−1.
Its inverse is −(1−√2)=√2−1, so negative norm is compatible with being a unit.

nonexample.title: Small-looking is not invertible
nonexample.explanation: N(1+i)=2, so 1+i is not a unit of Z[i], though it has an inverse in Q(i).

proofSteps: Conjugation respects sums and products; x·conjugate(x) is the norm.
If u and v are inverse algebraic integers, their integer norms multiply to one, forcing N(u)=±1.
Conversely N(u)=±1 gives u⁻¹=conjugate(u)/N(u), an algebraic integer in the same ring.

boundaryCheck.question: Is norm always positive in a real quadratic field?
choices: It is never zero or negative
boundaryCheck.explanation: N(√2)=−2. Positivity of a²+b² is particular to Gaussian integers.

application.question: What are trace and norm of 3+2√2?
application.explanation: Trace adds the conjugates; norm multiplies them: 6 and 9−8=1.

transfer.question: Why does norm one certify an inverse in O_K?
choices: The conjugate is integral and is the inverse
Every nonzero field element is an integer unit
transfer.explanation: Conjugation preserves O_K; multiplying by the conjugate produces one.

m3220-norm-trace.connection: Decide whether a quadratic integer is a unit and give its inverse when it is.

m3220-ideal-arithmetic.hook: Why does ideal multiplication differ from intersection?
m3220-ideal-arithmetic.objects: For a commutative unital ring, the ideal generated by a finite set consists of linear combinations with ring coefficients. The product of ideals consists of finite sums of products; it always lies inside their intersection.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does membership in I+J mean?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Sums produce an ideal; the union generally does not.

examples.title: Three operations on integer ideals
steps: (4)+(6)=(2), since 2=6−4 and every sum is even.

examples.title: Comaximal ideals agree at the bottom
steps: Here (3)∩(4)=(12)=(3)(4); coprimality explains the agreement.

nonexample.title: Product need not equal intersection
nonexample.explanation: The integer twelve belongs to (4)∩(6) but not (4)(6)=(24).

proofSteps: A product ideal consists of finite sums of products ab with a∈I,b∈J.
Each product is absorbed by both ideals, giving IJ⊆I∩J.
In Z, Bézout gives the sum generator gcd; common multiples give intersection generator lcm; product generator is ab.

boundaryCheck.question: Is IJ always I∩J?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The ideals (4),(6) give a strict inclusion.

application.question: What is (6)+(10) in Z?
application.explanation: gcd(6,10)=2, realized by 2=2·6−10.

transfer.question: Why does I+J=R imply I∩J⊆IJ in a commutative unital ring?
choices: Because ideal generators must be coprime integers
transfer.explanation: xi uses x∈J and i∈I; xj uses x∈I and j∈J.

m3220-ideal-arithmetic.connection: Compute all three operations and state when intersection equals product.

m3220-ring-correspondence.hook: How do ideals survive when one ideal is made invisible?
m3220-ring-correspondence.objects: In the first formula $I$ is a two-sided ideal and $S$ is a subring. In the second $I$ and J are two-sided ideals. Taking inverse images under the quotient map recovers subrings and one-sided or two-sided ideals, with inclusion preserved.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which ideals participate in the correspondence?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The inverse-image operation automatically includes the kernel I.

examples.title: Ideals above (12)
steps: The ideals of Z containing (12) are (d) for d dividing twelve.
Their images are exactly the ideals of Z/12Z; inclusion reverses divisibility of d.

examples.title: Quotient in stages
steps: In Z, (12)⊆(4). In Z/12Z the image (4)/(12) has three elements.
Quotienting by it gives a ring with four elements, canonically Z/4Z.

nonexample.title: An ideal below the kernel loses information
nonexample.explanation: The images of (12) and (24) in Z/12Z are both zero. Only ideals containing the kernel participate bijectively.

proofSteps: Inverse images of ideals under the quotient map are ideals containing its kernel.
If I⊆K, the inverse image of K/I is exactly K; conversely the image of the inverse image is the original quotient ideal.
Compose quotient maps to identify (R/I)/(J/I) with R/J when I⊆J.

boundaryCheck.question: What makes (R/I)/(J/I) meaningful?
choices: J is merely an additive subgroup
I⊆J and both are ideals of R
boundaryCheck.explanation: The image J/I must be an ideal of the first quotient.

application.question: How many elements are in (Z/12Z)/((4)/(12))?
application.explanation: The kernel ideal has three elements, so the quotient has 12/3=4.

transfer.question: Why can two ideals have the same image without containing I?
choices: Their inverse images after projection are K+I
Every ideal is mapped to zero
transfer.explanation: The image forgets differences inside the kernel; containing I removes that ambiguity.

m3220-ring-correspondence.connection: Lift an ideal from a quotient and apply the correct isomorphism theorem rather than match a memorized pattern.

m3220-maximal.hook: How does a quotient recognize that no larger proper ideal exists?
m3220-maximal.objects: Every proper ideal in a nonzero unital ring lies in a maximal ideal. The proof uses Zorn's lemma: a union of a chain of proper ideals stays proper because otherwise one member would already contain 1.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does proper ideal mean?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A proper unital-ring ideal cannot contain one.

examples.title: A prime modulus
steps: In Z, (5) is maximal because Z/5Z is a field.
Every nonzero class has an inverse; no nonzero proper quotient ideal can remain.

examples.title: A composite modulus
steps: (6)⊊(2)⊊Z, so (6) is not maximal.
The quotient Z/6Z contains the proper nonzero ideal {0,2,4}.

nonexample.title: The whole ring is excluded
nonexample.explanation: R is not a maximal ideal of itself. Its quotient is the zero ring, excluded from the definition of a field.

proofSteps: Assume R commutative unital and M proper. For a∉M, maximality gives M+(a)=R.
Write 1=m+ab; modulo M, [b] is the inverse of [a], so R/M is a field.
Conversely any ideal properly containing M has a nonzero quotient class; its field inverse forces the ideal to contain one and equal R.

boundaryCheck.question: Which ring hypotheses are used in the field-quotient characterization?
boundaryCheck.explanation: In noncommutative rings maximal left ideals yield simple modules, not generally field quotients.

application.question: Is (7) maximal in Z?
application.explanation: Z/7Z is a field.

transfer.question: Does maximal mean the ideal has maximal cardinality?
choices: No; it means no strictly larger proper ideal
transfer.explanation: The definition is ordered by inclusion, not by set size.

m3220-maximal.connection: Translate maximality into invertibility of every nonzero quotient class.

m3220-prime.hook: What can a zero product tell us after passage to a quotient?
m3220-prime.objects: For commutative unital rings, primality is equivalent to the quotient being an integral domain. Every maximal ideal is prime. The zero ideal of the integers is prime but not maximal, and (X) in the integer polynomial ring is another prime, nonmaximal ideal.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is a zero divisor?
choices: A nonzero element with a nonzero annihilating partner
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The two nonzero factors witness failure of cancellation.

examples.title: A prime ideal which is not maximal
steps: (0) is prime in Z because Z is a domain.
It is not maximal: (0)⊊(2)⊊Z. Thus prime does not imply maximal.

examples.title: An ordinary prime modulus
steps: (3) is prime since ab divisible by three forces one factor divisible by three.
Equivalently Z/(3)=F₃ has no nonzero zero divisors.

nonexample.title: A composite ideal fails
nonexample.explanation: In Z, 2·3∈(6) but neither 2 nor 3 lies in (6). Thus (6) is not prime.

proofSteps: Require R commutative unital and P proper.
A product of quotient classes is zero exactly when the representatives multiply into P.
The prime test therefore says precisely that R/P is a nonzero domain; fields are domains, so maximal ideals are prime.

boundaryCheck.question: Must a prime ideal be proper?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Without properness the implication is vacuous and the quotient is the zero ring.

application.question: Is (0) prime in Z?
choices: No because it is not maximal
application.explanation: The quotient by zero is Z, a domain.

transfer.question: Why is every maximal ideal prime in this setting?
choices: Its field quotient is a domain
transfer.explanation: Use the quotient characterizations with the commutative unital hypotheses.

m3220-prime.connection: Exhibit a prime ideal that is not maximal and explain its quotient.

m3220-crt.hook: When can one arithmetic problem become independent coordinates?
m3220-crt.objects: Here $R$ is commutative and unital, and the family of pairwise comaximal ideals is finite. For integers modulo 12, recording residues modulo 3 and 4 places every element into exactly one cell of a 3-by-4 grid. Addition and multiplication can be performed coordinatewise.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the kernel of x→(x mod 3,x mod 4)?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Both congruences vanish exactly for multiples of lcm(3,4)=12.

examples.title: Find a residue from two coordinates
steps: Solve x≡2 mod 3, x≡1 mod 4. Checking the four classes 2,5,8,11 modulo twelve gives x=5.
Its residue pair is (2,1); coordinate addition and multiplication agree with arithmetic modulo twelve.

examples.title: Build the inverse map
steps: Since 4≡1 mod 3 and 9≡1 mod 4, the expression 4a+9b has residues (a,b).
For (a,b)=(2,1), 4·2+9=17≡5 modulo twelve.

nonexample.title: Incompatible noncoprime coordinates
nonexample.explanation: There is no integer congruent to zero modulo four and one modulo six, since their residues disagree modulo two.

proofSteps: For comaximal I,J choose i+j=1 with i∈I,j∈J; si+rj has residues (r,s).
This proves surjectivity of R→R/I×R/J, with kernel I∩J.
First isomorphism gives the quotient product; the same identity gives I∩J=IJ. Induct for a finite pairwise comaximal family.

boundaryCheck.question: What hypothesis makes the ordinary CRT map surjective?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Comaximality constructs arbitrary residue pairs.

application.question: What solves x≡2 mod 3 and x≡1 mod 4 modulo twelve?
application.explanation: Five has the required two remainders.

transfer.question: Why are Z/12Z and Z/3Z×Z/4Z isomorphic as rings?
choices: The bijection preserves both operations coordinatewise
transfer.explanation: Reduction preserves sums and products; CRT proves bijectivity.

m3220-crt.connection: Construct a residue from coprime components.

m3220-localization-variants.hook: Can making a zero divisor invertible destroy other elements?
m3220-localization-variants.objects: Laurent polynomials have only finitely many terms. For a general multiplicative set with zero divisors, the correct fraction relation asks for some denominator $u$ with $u(at-bs)=0$. The natural ring map then need not be injective.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is a Laurent polynomial?
choices: A finite sum with positive and negative integer powers of X
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Only finitely many coefficients are nonzero.

examples.title: Invert three modulo six
steps: In R=Z/6Z, invert S={1,3}. Since 3·2=0 and 3 becomes a unit, two becomes zero.
Reduction modulo two sends both denominators to one and identifies S⁻¹R with F₂.

examples.title: Allow negative polynomial exponents
steps: Localizing F[X] at {1,X,X²,…} gives Laurent polynomials.
X⁻¹ exists, but (X+1)⁻¹ generally does not: only powers of X have been inverted.

nonexample.title: Fraction equality needs an annihilator
nonexample.explanation: For zero-divisor denominators, plain cross-multiplication is not the complete localization relation. Equality allows an s∈S annihilating the cross-product difference.

proofSteps: For a commutative unital ring use (a,s)~(b,t) iff some u∈S has u(at−bs)=0.
The universal property forces elements annihilated by denominators to become zero.
In the six-element example the quotient modulo two already makes all S units, and its two classes exhaust the localization.

boundaryCheck.question: Must a localization map be injective?
choices: Only if the ring is finite
No, denominators can annihilate nonzero elements
boundaryCheck.explanation: Regular denominators ensure injectivity; zero divisors can destroy it.

application.question: What does 2/1 become when three is inverted in Z/6Z?
application.explanation: 3·2=0 and invertibility of three force 2=0.

transfer.question: Why is F[X,X⁻¹] smaller than F(X)?
transfer.explanation: The first ring inverts powers of X; the fraction field inverts every nonzero polynomial.

m3220-localization-variants.connection: Explain why localization can identify a nonzero element with zero.

m3220-gaussian-division.hook: Why does rounding in a square lattice guarantee Euclidean descent?
m3220-gaussian-division.objects: Compute $z/w$ in the complex plane and round its real and imaginary coordinates to integers. The error in each coordinate is at most one half, so its squared length is at most one half.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is N(a+bi) in Z[i]?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: It is the squared complex absolute value.

examples.title: A small nonzero remainder
steps: The product (2+i)(2−i)=5; the remainder is i with norm one, below divisor norm five.

nonexample.title: Rounding one coordinate is insufficient
nonexample.explanation: The guarantee uses distance at most one-half in each coordinate. A quotient approximation with an uncontrolled imaginary coordinate has no norm bound.

proofSteps: Round real and imaginary parts of z/w to nearest integers to obtain q.
The error ε has norm at most (1/2)²+(1/2)²=1/2.
Since r=wε and norm is multiplicative, N(r)≤N(w)/2<N(w), proving Euclidean division for w≠0.

boundaryCheck.question: What premise is needed to divide z/w?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The Euclidean algorithm permits any nonzero divisor.

application.question: For z=3,w=1+i,q=2−i, what is r?

transfer.question: Why is Z[i] a PID?
choices: Its norm gives a Euclidean algorithm, which forces every ideal principal
Every complex number lies in it
transfer.explanation: Choose a nonzero ideal element of least norm and divide every other member by it.

m3220-gaussian-division.connection: Produce a valid quotient/remainder pair and justify the strict norm decrease.

m3220-prime-irreducible.hook: Why can something resist factoring yet fail to detect a factor?
m3220-prime-irreducible.objects: Both definitions require a nonzero nonunit in a domain. Primes are always irreducible. In a PID the converse holds because an ideal lying above an irreducible principal ideal would provide a factorization.

prerequisiteCheck.question: When are two elements associates?
choices: When they differ by multiplication by a unit
When they have equal absolute value in every ring
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Factorization uniqueness permits associates.

examples.title: Three resists factorization
steps: In Z[√−5], N(3)=9. A product of two nonunits would require norms three and three.
a²+5b²=3 has no integer solutions, so three is irreducible.

examples.title: Three fails the divisibility test
steps: (1+√−5)(1−√−5)=6 is divisible by three.
Neither factor is divisible by three, since its two integer coordinates are not both multiples of three. Thus three is not prime.

nonexample.title: Units and zero are excluded
nonexample.explanation: Prime and irreducible elements are required to be nonzero nonunits. Otherwise the displayed implication-only tests admit misleading cases.

proofSteps: In a domain, if prime p=ab, then p divides one factor. Cancel p to show the other factor is a unit.
In a PID an ideal above (p) is (a), yielding p=ab. Irreducibility leaves only (p) or the whole ring.
Thus (p) is maximal and prime, so p is prime. The converse fails outside this stronger setting.

boundaryCheck.question: What is required of a prime or irreducible element?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Units are deliberately excluded from both definitions.

application.question: Is three prime in Z[√−5]?
choices: Yes because three is a prime integer
No because it is a unit
application.explanation: It divides the product six but neither factor 1±√−5.

transfer.question: Why do irreducibles become prime in a PID?
choices: Their principal ideals are maximal, hence prime
transfer.explanation: A larger principal ideal yields a forbidden nonunit factorization.

m3220-prime-irreducible.connection: Identify which implication holds in a domain and why the reverse needs extra structure.

m3220-polynomial.hook: Why are polynomials coefficient data rather than merely functions?
m3220-polynomial.objects: Over a domain the product of leading coefficients cannot vanish, so degrees add. Over a ring with zero divisors the top coefficient can disappear and the degree can drop.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does a polynomial store?
choices: An infinite mandatory list of nonzero terms
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Formal coefficient data define a polynomial even when function evaluation is not injective.

examples.title: Multiply coefficient lists
steps: (1+2X)(3+X) has constant 3, linear coefficient 1+6=7, and quadratic coefficient 2.
The coefficient convolution gives 3+7X+2X².

examples.title: A nonzero polynomial function can vanish everywhere
steps: Over F₂, f=X²−X is a nonzero formal polynomial of degree two.
At both inputs zero and one its value is zero. Distinct coefficient data can give the same finite-field function.

nonexample.title: Degree can drop with zero divisors
nonexample.explanation: In (Z/4Z)[X], (2X)(2X)=0. Degree-addition requires a domain or another suitable leading-coefficient condition.

proofSteps: The Xᵏ coefficient of a product is the sum of aᵢbⱼ over i+j=k.
For nonzero polynomials over a domain the top coefficient is the product of two nonzero leading coefficients.
That product stays nonzero, so degree(fg)=degree f+degree g; over rings with zero divisors the conclusion can fail.

boundaryCheck.question: When does degree addition hold for nonzero factors as stated?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The leading-coefficient product must stay nonzero.

application.question: What is the X coefficient of (1+2X)(3+X)?
application.explanation: The contributions are 1·1 and 2·3.

transfer.question: Why does X²−X over F₂ refute polynomial/function identification?
choices: It is nonzero data but evaluates to zero at all two inputs
transfer.explanation: Finite-field evaluation can identify distinct formal polynomials.

m3220-polynomial.connection: Distinguish a formal polynomial from its induced function.

m3220-roots.hook: What does a root certify, and why can a ring have too many?
m3220-roots.objects: The factor theorem holds over every commutative unital ring. For nonzero polynomials over a domain, the total multiplicity of roots is bounded by the degree. An algebraically closed field is one where every nonconstant polynomial splits into linear factors.

prerequisiteCheck.question: When does X−a divide f?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Monic division leaves constant remainder f(a).

examples.title: A repeated root
steps: Over Q, f=(X−1)²(X+2) has root one of multiplicity two and root −2 of multiplicity one.
The total multiplicity is three, equal to its degree.

examples.title: Too many roots over a non-domain
steps: In Z/8Z, X²−1 has roots 1,3,5,7.
It has degree two but four distinct roots: the domain hypothesis is essential.

nonexample.title: Zero polynomial boundary
nonexample.explanation: The zero polynomial vanishes everywhere but has no finite root-multiplicity bound of this form; the theorem assumes f≠0.

proofSteps: Divide by the monic X−a: the constant remainder is f(a), proving the factor theorem.
Repeated division counts the multiplicity until the remaining factor is nonzero at a.
Over a domain, removing a different linear factor does not destroy the other roots; degree addition bounds the sum of all multiplicities by degree f.

boundaryCheck.question: Which hypotheses bound the sum of root multiplicities?
choices: R a domain and f nonzero
boundaryCheck.explanation: A non-domain can have too many roots, and zero is excluded.

application.question: What is the multiplicity of one in (X−1)²(X+2) over Q?
application.explanation: The remaining factor evaluates to three at one, so two is exact.

transfer.question: Why can X²−1 have four roots modulo eight?
choices: Zero divisors invalidate the domain root bound
transfer.explanation: Distinct root factors cannot be counted using cancellation as in a domain.

m3220-roots.connection: Explain why a polynomial over a ring with zero divisors can have more roots than its degree.

m3220-polynomial-ufd.hook: Why does unique factorization not make every ideal principal?
m3220-polynomial-ufd.objects: Factor the integer content uniquely, then use unique factorisation over the rational polynomial ring and Gauss's lemma for the primitive part. This gives unique factorisation of every nonzero nonunit integer polynomial.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is a unit of Z[X]?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: An integer constant is invertible only when it is ±1.

examples.title: A nonprincipal ideal
steps: In Z[X], let I=(2,X). Any generator f of I would divide the constant two, so f is constant.
Since f also divides X, it must be ±1. But I has only even constant terms and is proper, contradiction.

examples.title: A field changes the ideal story
steps: Q[X] admits polynomial division by any nonzero polynomial because its leading coefficient is invertible.
It is Euclidean and hence a PID; the ideal (2,X) is the whole ring since two is a unit.

nonexample.title: UFD is weaker than PID
nonexample.explanation: Z[X] is a UFD by Gauss but (2,X) is not principal. Factorization controls elements, not all ideals.

proofSteps: Separate any integer polynomial into content and a primitive part.
Gauss transports primitive factorizations from Q[X] to Z[X] and gives uniqueness up to units and factor order.
For a general domain R, if R[X] is a PID, the ideal (a,X) for any nonzero a forces a to be a unit; thus R is a field.

boundaryCheck.question: Does being a UFD imply being a PID?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The ideal (2,X) in Z[X] disproves it.

application.question: Why is (2,X) proper in Z[X]?
choices: Every element has degree at least two
Every element has even constant term
application.explanation: A sum 2a(X)+Xb(X) always has even constant coefficient.

transfer.question: For a domain R, when is R[X] a PID?
choices: Exactly when R is a field
transfer.explanation: The forward ideal argument forces every nonzero constant to be invertible; the reverse uses Euclidean division.

m3220-polynomial-ufd.connection: Distinguish unique factorization of elements from every ideal being principal.

m3220-hilbert.hook: Why do finitely many polynomial variables preserve finite generation?
m3220-hilbert.objects: Quotients by proper ideals preserve the ascending chain condition through ideal correspondence. In particular every proper quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over a field is Noetherian.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does Noetherian mean for ideals?
choices: The ring has finitely many elements
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Finite generation is equivalent to ACC.

examples.title: Finite-variable inheritance
steps: Z is Noetherian because every ideal is principal.
Hilbert gives Z[X,Y] Noetherian, though the ideal (2,X) already shows it is not a PID.

examples.title: An infinite-variable obstruction
steps: In F[X₁,X₂,…], the ideals (X₁)⊊(X₁,X₂)⊊… never stabilize.
A fresh variable is not in the previous ideal, as setting earlier variables to zero verifies.

nonexample.title: Noetherian is not principal
nonexample.explanation: Hilbert guarantees a finite list of generators for each ideal, not a single generator or a finite ring.

proofSteps: The leading coefficients arising from an ideal form a coefficient ideal; the Noetherian premise gives a finite list.
Lift generators to polynomials and control the finitely many lower degrees to reduce any member by degree.
This is the proof roadmap, not the full lower-degree argument. Iterating the theorem covers finitely many variables; no infinite iteration is claimed.

boundaryCheck.question: Does Hilbert apply to infinitely many variables?
choices: Yes by iteration without a limit argument
boundaryCheck.explanation: The fresh-variable ascending chain is a counterexample.

application.question: Is Z[X,Y] Noetherian?
choices: Only if all its ideals are principal
application.explanation: Apply Hilbert twice from Z.

transfer.question: Why can an infinite variable ring fail ACC even over a field?
choices: Each new variable enters a strictly larger ideal
transfer.explanation: Every polynomial has finite support; the unbounded number of variables creates the chain.

m3220-hilbert.connection: Explain why controlling leading coefficients alone is not the whole proof.

m3220-krull.hook: Does a drawn prime chain prove a dimension or only a lower bound?
m3220-krull.objects: A field has only its zero prime ideal, so its dimension is zero. In a PID that is not a field, every nonzero prime ideal is maximal; the longest chain is the zero ideal followed by a nonzero prime.

prerequisiteCheck.question: How long is p₀⊊p₁⊊p₂?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Length counts strict inclusions.

examples.title: Dimension of Z
steps: The prime ideals are (0) and (p) for prime integers p.
Every nonzero prime is maximal, so (0)⊊(p) has length one and no chain is longer.

examples.title: A two-step witness
steps: In F[X,Y], (0)⊊(X)⊊(X,Y) is a prime chain.
The quotients are F[X,Y], F[Y], F, respectively. This proves dimension at least two; equality additionally needs a dimension theorem.

nonexample.title: Count inclusions, not nodes
nonexample.explanation: The chain (0)⊊(p) contains two ideals but has length one.

proofSteps: Krull dimension is the supremum of the number of strict inclusions in prime chains.
A field has only its zero prime ideal, so dimension zero.
A nonfield PID has a nonzero prime generated by an irreducible, and every nonzero prime is maximal. Thus its maximum chain length is one.

boundaryCheck.question: Does one length-two chain alone prove dimension exactly two?
choices: No, it proves at least two
boundaryCheck.explanation: A separate upper bound excludes longer chains.

application.question: What is dim Z?
application.explanation: Zero is prime and nonzero primes are maximal.

transfer.question: Why is a field dimension zero?
choices: Its only proper ideal is zero
Its underlying set must be finite
transfer.explanation: The zero ideal is prime in a field; there are no strict prime inclusions.

m3220-krull.connection: Recognize when a diagram establishes only a lower bound.

m3220-jacobson.hook: Which elements stay hidden from every simple field quotient?
m3220-jacobson.objects: For the integers the radical is zero. For a local ring it is its unique maximal ideal. In integers modulo 12, the maximal ideals are generated by 2 and by 3; their intersection is generated by 6.

prerequisiteCheck.question: How is J(R) defined here?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Intersections preserve the ideal property; unions generally do not.

examples.title: Intersect maximal ideals modulo twelve
steps: The maximal ideals of Z/12Z are (2) and (3).
Their intersection is {0,6}; hence J=(6).

examples.title: A domain can have a nonzero radical
steps: In the local domain Z₍₃₎, the unique maximal ideal is 3Z₍₃₎.
Thus J=3Z₍₃₎ although its nilradical is zero. Jacobson radical and nilradical need not agree.

nonexample.title: Nonunit is not the same as radical
nonexample.explanation: Modulo twelve, two is a nonunit but is not in (3), so is not in the Jacobson radical.

proofSteps: Assume a commutative unital ring. If x is in every maximal ideal, a nonunit 1−rx would belong to a maximal ideal and force that ideal to contain one.
If x is outside a maximal ideal M, write 1=m+rx; then 1−rx=m is a nonunit.
These two directions establish x∈J iff every 1−rx is a unit.

boundaryCheck.question: Must every radical element be nilpotent?
choices: Not in a general commutative ring
boundaryCheck.explanation: Three in Z₍₃₎ lies in J and is nonnilpotent.

application.question: What is J(Z/12Z)?
application.explanation: Intersect multiples of two and three modulo twelve.

transfer.question: Why is 1−rx a unit for all r when x∈J?
choices: A maximal ideal containing it would also contain rx and then one
transfer.explanation: Containment in every maximal ideal supplies the contradiction.

m3220-jacobson.connection: Test whether an element is in J(R) using the displayed criterion with the correct quantifier.

m3220-nilradical.hook: What can vanish after repeated multiplication but remain visible initially?
m3220-nilradical.objects: Throughout, the ring is commutative and unital. Its nilpotent elements form an ideal contained in every maximal ideal. If the ring is also Artinian, its Jacobson radical is nilpotent and equals the nilradical. In integers modulo 8, the ideal generated by 2 reaches zero after three powers.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does nilpotent mean?
choices: The element is a nonunit only
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A nonzero nilpotent such as six modulo twelve may vanish after several products.

examples.title: A nilpotent residue
steps: In Z/12Z, six is nonzero and 6²=0.
The nilradical is {0,6}; it agrees with the Jacobson radical in this finite Artinian ring.

examples.title: An element in J that never vanishes
steps: Three belongs to J(Z₍₃₎).
Every positive power of three is nonzero in that domain, so three is not nilpotent.

nonexample.title: Nilpotent ideal needs a uniform exponent
nonexample.explanation: Knowing each element is nilpotent does not generally provide one exponent annihilating the entire ideal; finite Artinian structure supplies additional information.

proofSteps: If xⁿ=0 lies in a prime P, repeated primality gives x∈P.
The reverse inclusion imports a maximality lemma constructing a prime disjoint from the powers of a nonnilpotent x.
For commutative Artinian rings, radical nilpotence is another imported result. Stabilization of powers alone does not prove the stable ideal is zero.

boundaryCheck.question: Is Nil(R)=J(R) for every commutative ring?
choices: No; it holds here under Artinian hypotheses
boundaryCheck.explanation: The local domain Z₍₃₎ has zero nilradical but nonzero Jacobson radical.

application.question: What is 6² modulo twelve?
application.explanation: Thirty-six is divisible by twelve.

transfer.question: Why is using finite-generation Nakayama before proving finite generation invalid?
choices: It assumes a needed premise and can create a circular proof
transfer.explanation: The imported radical theorem keeps the Artinian⇒Noetherian argument independent.

m3220-nilradical.connection: Explain why a collection of nilpotent elements need not have one common vanishing power without extra hypotheses.

m3220-artinian.hook: Why do ascending and descending chains tell different stories?
m3220-artinian.objects: The condition is equivalent to every nonempty collection of ideals having a minimal member. Finite rings are examples, but an Artinian ring need not be a finite set: every field is Artinian.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which direction does DCC examine?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Artinian means every descending ideal chain eventually stabilizes.

examples.title: Integers descend forever
steps: (2)⊋(4)⊋(8)⊋… in Z, since 2ᵏ is not divisible by 2ᵏ⁺¹.
Z is Noetherian because all ideals are principal, yet this descending chain proves it is not Artinian.

examples.title: An infinite Artinian ring
steps: A field such as Q has only ideals zero and Q.
Every descending ideal chain stabilizes even though Q has infinitely many elements.

nonexample.title: Finite cardinality is sufficient, not necessary
nonexample.explanation: Every finite ring is Artinian, but infinite fields show that Artinian does not mean finite as a set.

proofSteps: Artinian is DCC on ideals; Noetherian is ACC, so the definitions use opposite directions.
In Z, the powers-of-two ideals are strictly descending by divisibility, disproving DCC.
In a field every nonzero ideal contains a unit and hence one, so there are only two ideals and DCC holds.

boundaryCheck.question: Does Noetherian imply Artinian?
choices: Only if the ring is infinite
boundaryCheck.explanation: Z is the explicit counterexample.

application.question: Which is properly contained in (4) inside Z?
application.explanation: Multiples of eight are multiples of four, but four is not a multiple of eight.

transfer.question: Why is Q Artinian although infinite?
choices: Its only ideals are zero and Q
transfer.explanation: Any nonzero ideal in a field contains an inverse multiple giving one.

m3220-artinian.connection: Identify which finite-generation claims have actually been proved at each stage.

m3220-artinian-decomposition.hook: How does a finite collection of local pieces reconstruct a ring?
m3220-artinian-decomposition.objects: Assume throughout this result that $R$ is a nonzero commutative unital Artinian ring. The first factors are fields. The second factors are Artinian local rings. Every prime ideal is maximal, so the Krull dimension is zero. For integers modulo 12, the local decomposition is into residues modulo 4 and modulo 3.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What makes a ring local?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Local refers to maximal-ideal structure.

examples.title: Split twelve into local pieces
steps: Z/12Z≅Z/4Z×F₃ by CRT.
The first factor is local with maximal ideal {0,2}; the second is a field and local with zero maximal ideal.

examples.title: Separate the radical quotient
steps: J(Z/12Z)={0,6}. Quotienting removes its nilpotent direction.
The resulting six-element ring is F₂×F₃, not the original twelve-element ring.

nonexample.title: Semisimple quotient is not the original ring
nonexample.explanation: The sizes twelve and six distinguish R from R/J. Recovering nilpotent layers requires higher powers of maximal ideals.

proofSteps: For a commutative unital Artinian ring, import finiteness of the maximal ideals and nilpotence of J.
Distinct maximal ideals are comaximal, and sufficiently high powers remain comaximal.
Their high-power intersection is zero; CRT gives a product of local quotients. The general structure theorems are not proved by the integer example.

boundaryCheck.question: May R be replaced by R/J without losing data?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Equality with the radical quotient requires J=0.

application.question: Which local factors reconstruct Z/12Z?
application.explanation: The coprime factors four and three preserve all twelve classes.

transfer.question: Why does an Artinian ring have dimension zero?
transfer.explanation: The imported Artinian structure theorem leaves no strict prime inclusions.

m3220-artinian-decomposition.connection: Recover a ring element from its local-factor coordinates and distinguish R from R/J(R).

m3220-module-chains.hook: How do finite layers turn a descending-chain premise into an ascending-chain conclusion?
m3220-module-chains.objects: The Noetherian condition is preserved and reflected by a submodule and its quotient together. For an Artinian local ring with maximal ideal $m$, a finite power of $m$ is zero; the successive layers $\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}$ are finite-dimensional over the residue field.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is a module subobject?
choices: Any additive subgroup without further conditions
A submodule stable under every scalar
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Chain conditions apply to submodules, not arbitrary subsets.

examples.title: A finite-dimensional vector space
steps: In F³, every strict subspace inclusion changes dimension by at least one.
Both ascending and descending chains therefore have at most three strict steps.

examples.title: An infinite-dimensional obstruction
steps: A vector space with basis e₁,e₂,… has ascending spans ⟨e₁,…,eₙ⟩.
The tails ⟨eₙ,eₙ₊₁,…⟩ descend strictly. It is neither Noetherian nor Artinian.

nonexample.title: Layers need not split
nonexample.explanation: A filtration with finite-dimensional quotients can establish chain conditions without asserting a direct-sum decomposition of the module.

proofSteps: For commutative unital Artinian rings, use the imported local decomposition and nilpotent radical to obtain a finite filtration.
Each radical layer is an Artinian vector space over a residue field, hence finite-dimensional and Noetherian.
Noetherianity passes through a submodule–quotient extension and finite products; lift it through these finite layers to prove Artinian⇒Noetherian without circular use of Nakayama.

boundaryCheck.question: Does Artinian imply Noetherian for every module?
choices: No; the ring theorem needs its structural premises
Only for vector spaces over finite fields
boundaryCheck.explanation: The lesson proves the commutative Artinian ring result; arbitrary Artinian modules need not be Noetherian.

application.question: What bounds strict subspace steps in F³?
application.explanation: Each strict inclusion changes dimension.

transfer.question: Why must the filtration used in the proof be finite?
choices: A finite extension of Noetherian layers stays Noetherian; an infinite chain may not
transfer.explanation: Infinite direct sums of one-dimensional spaces give a counterexample to unrestricted iteration.

m3220-module-chains.connection: Explain why finite length supplies both chain conditions, and identify which converse hypotheses are needed.

m3220-nakayama.hook: Can a finite generating list be swallowed entirely by the radical?
m3220-nakayama.objects: The notes first prove this for finitely generated ideals and then ask for the module version. It explains why generators can be detected after reducing modulo the radical, especially over local rings.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does finite generation supply?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Modules need not be free; only a finite generating set is required.

examples.title: Reduce a generating list
steps: For a finitely generated module M over local R with maximal ideal m, M=mM forces M=0.
If mₙ=Σrᵢmᵢ with rᵢ∈m, then 1−rₙ is a unit; solve for mₙ using the earlier generators, contradicting minimality.

examples.title: A missing finite-generation premise
steps: Over Z₍₃₎, Q=3Q because each q equals 3(q/3).
Yet Q≠0. This module is not finitely generated over Z₍₃₎; finitely many denominators have bounded powers of three.

nonexample.title: A unit coefficient changes the argument
nonexample.explanation: The unit 1−r is guaranteed by r∈J(R). An arbitrary coefficient outside the radical need not have this property.

proofSteps: Assume M nonzero finitely generated and choose a generating set of least size.
If J(R)M=M, express its last generator with radical coefficients.
Move its own coefficient to the left, invert 1−rₙ, and remove that generator; contradiction proves M=0.

boundaryCheck.question: Can finite generation be omitted?
choices: No; Q=3Q over Z₍₃₎ is a counterexample
boundaryCheck.explanation: Division by three is possible in Q, but Q is not finitely generated over this local ring.

application.question: Why is 1−rₙ invertible for rₙ∈J(R)?
choices: Every nonzero ring element is a unit
application.explanation: The radical is exactly the set whose 1−rx expressions are units.

transfer.question: If M/N=m(M/N) and M/N is finitely generated over local R, what follows?
transfer.explanation: Apply Nakayama to the quotient, obtaining M/N=0.

m3220-nakayama.connection: Explain every hypothesis and use M/𝔪M to lift a generating set.

m3220-dvr.hook: Why do powers of one uniformizer order every ideal?
m3220-dvr.objects: Set $v(0)=\infty$. If $t$ has value 1, every nonzero field element is a unit times an integer power of $t$. The resulting valuation ring is a local PID and has Krull dimension one. For the rational numbers, counting powers of $p$ gives the localization of the integers at $p$.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What value do we assign to zero?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The initial map is on F×; the infinity convention includes zero in R.

examples.title: A rational valuation
steps: For v₃ on Q, 18/5 has value two and 2/9 has value minus two.
The first lies in Z₍₃₎ and is a nonunit; the second lies outside it.

examples.title: Ideal inclusion reverses exponent
steps: A larger valuation requires more divisibility and therefore gives a smaller ideal.

nonexample.title: Two valuation meanings
nonexample.explanation: This additive valuation on F× differs from a Euclidean descent function. Set v(0)=∞ separately to include zero in the valuation ring.

proofSteps: Choose t with v(t)=1 by surjectivity. For nonzero x, x/tᵛ⁽ˣ⁾ has valuation zero and is a unit.
A nonzero ideal has a least valuation n among its nonzero elements, since these are nonnegative integers.
An element of valuation n generates the ideal: every other element is a multiple by an element of nonnegative valuation.

boundaryCheck.question: What does v(x)=0 mean for nonzero x in the valuation ring?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Both x and its inverse have nonnegative valuation.

application.question: What is v₃(18/5)?
application.explanation: Eighteen has two factors of three; five has none.

transfer.question: Which ideal is smaller: (t²) or (t³)?
transfer.explanation: Every t³ multiple is a t² multiple; t² itself has insufficient valuation for (t³).

m3220-dvr.connection: Determine units and ideal inclusion from valuations, with the direction of inclusion correct.

m3220-finite-field-four.hook: Why is a four-element field different from arithmetic modulo four?
m3220-finite-field-four.objects: The defining quadratic has no root in the two-element field and is therefore irreducible. Its ideal is maximal, so the quotient is a field. Addition uses binary coefficients; multiplication first expands and then replaces each square of alpha by alpha+1.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What are the possible coefficients a,b?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: There are two choices for each of two coefficients.

examples.title: Build the relation
steps: Over F₂, X²+X+1 evaluates to one at both zero and one. It is irreducible.
In the quotient α²=α+1, so α(α+1)=α²+α=1.

examples.title: List every element
steps: Monic division reduces every polynomial to a+bα with a,b∈F₂.
The four distinct elements are 0,1,α,α+1. Their characteristic is two, and the nonzero group has order three.

nonexample.title: Z/4Z is not F₄
nonexample.explanation: [2] modulo four is a nonzero zero divisor. F₄ has no nonzero zero divisors and has characteristic two.

proofSteps: A degree-two polynomial over a field is irreducible exactly when it has no root.
The irreducible ideal is maximal, so its quotient is a field.
Monic division gives a unique remainder of degree below two, hence exactly four classes. The relation directly verifies all nonzero inverses.

boundaryCheck.question: Is a four-element field the same ring as Z/4Z?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Characteristic and zero divisors distinguish them.

application.question: What is α(α+1) in F₄?
application.explanation: Use α²=α+1 and characteristic two.

transfer.question: Why is every quotient class represented by a+bα?
choices: Monic division gives a unique remainder of degree below two
transfer.explanation: The defining relation reduces higher powers, and uniqueness ensures four distinct classes.

m3220-finite-field-four.connection: Compute a nontrivial inverse in a finite field.

odyssey-linear-groups.hook: What does a determinant remember after all other matrix data are forgotten?
odyssey-linear-groups.objects: Here $n$ is a positive integer and $F$ is a field. Over the real numbers, the absolute determinant gives volume scaling and its sign gives orientation. The determinant homomorphism forgets the details of the deformation and remembers one scalar. Special orthogonal matrices preserve both inner products and orientation, a stronger condition than determinant one: a shear can belong to SL without preserving lengths.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Which columns form an invertible matrix over F?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Independence is equivalent to full rank.

examples.title: Count invertible matrices over F₂
steps: The first column has three nonzero choices; the second has two choices outside its span.
Thus GL₂(F₂) has six elements. F₂× has only one element, so all six have determinant one.

examples.title: A determinant fiber
steps: Over Q, diag(2,1) has determinant two and lies in GL₂ but not SL₂.
Multiplying by any determinant-one matrix stays in the determinant-two fiber.

nonexample.title: Nonzero determinant is field-specific invertibility
nonexample.explanation: Over Z, diag(2,1) has nonzero determinant but no integer inverse. The GLₙ(F) definition here assumes a field.

proofSteps: The determinant is multiplicative and sends diag(a,1,…,1) to every a∈F×.
Its kernel is SLₙ(F). First isomorphism gives GLₙ(F)/SLₙ(F)≅F×.
Over a q-element field, the successive forbidden column spans have qⁱ elements, yielding the product count.

boundaryCheck.question: Which coefficient premise supports det≠0 as the inverse test?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Over a general commutative ring the determinant must be a unit.

application.question: What is |GL₂(F₂)|?
application.explanation: Count three first columns and two possible second columns.

transfer.question: What distinguishes two matrices in the same SL coset?
transfer.explanation: The quotient map is determinant; equality of images is equality of kernel cosets.

odyssey-linear-groups.connection: Exhibit an SL matrix that is not orthogonal and explain the quotient by SL.

odyssey-flags.hook: Why does preserving a nested collection of spaces force triangular matrices?
odyssey-flags.objects: We use column vectors and left actions throughout. Preserving the first line forces the first column to have only its first entry nonzero. Preserving the first plane forces the third entry of the second column to vanish. Invertibility then makes every diagonal entry nonzero. A partial flag omits some intermediate dimensions; its stabilizer is a parabolic subgroup.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does a complete flag in F³ include?
choices: A line contained in a plane
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Nested subspaces, not ordered vectors, form a flag.

examples.title: Preserve the standard flag
steps: A matrix preserving ⟨e₁⟩ has its first column in that line.
Preserving ⟨e₁,e₂⟩ also keeps the second column in that plane, forcing all entries below the diagonal to zero.

examples.title: Move to another flag
steps: Choose a basis v₁,v₂,v₃ adapted to a line L inside a plane P.
The matrix with these columns sends the standard flag to L⊂P⊂F³, so the GL₃ action is transitive.

nonexample.title: Flags are nested
nonexample.explanation: A line outside a chosen plane is not a line-in-plane flag; the incidence relation is part of the object.

proofSteps: Preservation of each standard subspace gives the triangular column conditions.
Nonzero diagonal product ensures the matrix is invertible, describing the stabilizer B.
An adapted basis gives transitivity; gB→g·F₀ is the orbit–stabilizer coset bijection. This is a G-set, not a quotient group unless B is normal.

boundaryCheck.question: Is GL₃/B generally a quotient group?
choices: No; it is a coset set with a G-action
Only when the field is infinite
boundaryCheck.explanation: Normality would be needed for coset multiplication.

application.question: Which matrices stabilize the standard flag?
application.explanation: Upper triangular columns preserve the standard prefixes.

transfer.question: Why is the action transitive?
choices: Every flag has an adapted basis
transfer.explanation: An adapted basis constructs a matrix carrying one flag to another.

odyssey-flags.connection: Determine the stabilizer shape of a specified partial flag.

odyssey-frobenius.hook: Can a map out of an induced representation be recovered from one coset copy?
odyssey-frobenius.objects: The Hom-space statement works over any field. Given an $H$-equivariant map $f$ from $W$ to the restricted module $V$, extend it by $a\otimes w\mapsto a\cdot f(w)$. Conversely evaluate a $G$-equivariant map on $1\otimes w$. Over the complex numbers for finite groups, taking dimensions gives the familiar equality of character multiplicities.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What relation defines the balanced tensor here?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The FH action can move between the two tensor factors.

examples.title: Recover the map from the identity copy
steps: For a G-map F:FG⊗_FH W→V, define f(w)=F(1⊗w).
For h∈H, F(1⊗hw)=F(h⊗w)=hF(1⊗w), so f is H-equivariant.

examples.title: An explicit character count
steps: In S₃ with H=⟨(12)⟩, the induced sign has character (3,−1,0).
Its inner product with Std=(2,0,−1) is (6+0+0)/6=1. Restricting Std to H has multiplicity (2−0)/2=1 for sign.

nonexample.title: An equality of numbers is not the theorem
nonexample.explanation: Matching dimensions in one example illustrates reciprocity. The natural Hom-space isomorphism explains why the equality holds generally.

proofSteps: Extend an H-map f by F(a⊗w)=a·f(w).
The relation ah⊗w=a⊗hw is respected because f(hw)=h·f(w).
Evaluation at 1⊗w and extension undo each other. For finite complex characters, dimensions of these Hom spaces give the inner-product identity.

boundaryCheck.question: Does the Hom-space version require complex semisimple representations?
choices: No; the algebraic adjunction is more general
boundaryCheck.explanation: The character inner-product formula uses finite complex representation theory; the Hom construction is algebraic.

application.question: What is the sign multiplicity in Res_H Std for H=C₂ in S₃?
application.explanation: On H the standard character is (2,0); the inner product with (1,−1) is one.

transfer.question: Why is evaluation at the identity copy sufficient?
choices: Every group element belongs to H
transfer.explanation: All other coset copies are G-translates.

odyssey-frobenius.connection: Compute a decomposition using restriction data and verify its total dimension.

ureca-group-algebra.hook: What changes when symmetries may be added as well as composed?
ureca-group-algebra.objects: Here $G$ is finite and $F$ is a field, so $FG$ has dimension $|G|$. A group representation extends to an algebra action by sending a weighted sum of group elements to the same weighted sum of their matrices. The regular left action permutes the basis $G$ by left multiplication. General algebra elements need not act invertibly.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the dimension of FG for finite G?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Each group element labels one independent basis vector.

examples.title: Expand a formal product
steps: In F[C₂], write g²=1. Then (a+bg)(c+dg)=(ac+bd)+(ad+bc)g.
The symbols 1 and g are independent basis elements, even if a particular representation sends both to identity.

examples.title: Extend a representation linearly
steps: For a swap matrix S, a+bg acts as aI+bS.
The equation S²=I ensures multiplication of formal group-algebra elements agrees with multiplication of their operators.

nonexample.title: A representation need not embed the algebra
nonexample.explanation: The trivial representation sends every g to one. Distinct formal sums can act identically, so faithful group action and faithful algebra action are different questions.

proofSteps: The group basis multiplication is extended bilinearly. Associativity follows by expanding triples and using associativity in G.
The linear extension of ρ respects products because ρ(gh)=ρ(g)ρ(h).
Conversely a unital FG-module restricts to G, whose basis elements act invertibly because g⁻¹ supplies an inverse.

boundaryCheck.question: Must formal group basis symbols have distinct operators in every module?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A module action may have a nontrivial algebra kernel.

application.question: What is (1+g)² in F₂[C₂]?
application.explanation: Expansion gives 1+2g+g²=0 in characteristic two.

transfer.question: Why must FG-modules be unital to recover a representation?
choices: The identity group element must act as I
Every module must be finite as a set
transfer.explanation: The group identity basis element is the algebra identity; unitality makes it the identity operator.

ureca-group-algebra.connection: Multiply algebra elements and identify the averaging idempotent.

ureca-cyclic-eigenvalues.hook: How can one cyclic subgroup reveal the frequencies inside a representation?
ureca-cyclic-eigenvalues.objects: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex representation and $r$ an element of finite order $m$. On $V\lambda$ every power $r^{k}$ acts by $\lambda ^{k}$; its dimension is the multiplicity of that one-dimensional cyclic representation. In the natural three-dimensional cube representation, a quarter-turn about the vertical axis has eigenvalues 1, $i$ and $-i$. The real horizontal plane splits into two lines only after complexification.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is an eigenline?
choices: A one-dimensional subspace preserved by the operator
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: An operator may multiply a line by a nontrivial scalar.

examples.title: A three-cycle has three frequencies
steps: The permutation matrix of (123) has eigenvalues 1,ω,ω² over C.
The constant line has eigenvalue one; the sum-zero plane complexifies into the other two eigenlines.

examples.title: Trace of a power
steps: For eigenvalues 1,i,−i, the trace at the generator is one.
At its square the eigenvalues become 1,−1,−1, giving trace −1.

nonexample.title: Characteristic can block diagonalization
nonexample.explanation: In characteristic p, Xᵖ−1=(X−1)ᵖ. A nonidentity unipotent operator can have order p without splitting into eigenlines.

proofSteps: For an element r of finite order m, ρ(r)ᵐ=I, so the minimal polynomial divides Xᵐ−1.
Over C this polynomial splits into distinct roots, giving a direct sum of eigenspaces.
Each power rᵏ acts by λᵏ on its eigenspace; summing multiplicity-weighted eigenvalues gives the character formula.

boundaryCheck.question: What makes the displayed complex decomposition valid?
choices: All fields have every mth root
Xᵐ−1 splits with distinct roots over C
The matrix is diagonal in every basis
boundaryCheck.explanation: Separability and splitting are both used.

application.question: What is 1+i²+(−i)²?
application.explanation: Both i and −i square to −1.

transfer.question: Is an eigenspace of r automatically invariant under all G?
choices: Only if its eigenvalue is one
No; other generators may move it
transfer.explanation: Restriction decomposes the cyclic subgroup action; extending invariance needs checks for the whole group.

ureca-cyclic-eigenvalues.connection: Decompose the C₄ restriction and explain why an absent root of unity is not a contradiction.

cube-signed-permutations.hook: Why do the cube’s symmetries reduce to a permutation and three signs?
cube-signed-permutations.objects: Centre the cube at the origin. Its six face centres are $\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3$. A symmetry permutes these centres, so its matrix has one nonzero entry in each row and column, equal to $+1$ or $-1$. Conversely, every such signed permutation preserves the inequalities $|x_i|\le1$ defining the solid cube.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What directions are the cube face normals?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Faces correspond to six signed coordinate normals.

examples.title: Count coordinate choices
steps: A cube symmetry permutes the three pairs of opposite faces, determining a permutation of coordinate axes.
Each positive normal may go to either sign, giving 3!·2³=48 distinct orthogonal matrices.

examples.title: Separate orientation
steps: The determinant is sign(σ)ε₁ε₂ε₃. For each σ, four sign choices give +1.
Thus there are 24 rotations and 24 orientation-reversing symmetries.

nonexample.title: Orthogonal is not always cube-preserving
nonexample.explanation: A rotation by 45 degrees about the z-axis preserves lengths but moves a face normal away from all six cube face directions.

proofSteps: A cube-preserving orthogonal map sends faces and their outward unit normals to faces and normals.
Therefore each eⱼ maps to ±eσ(j), proving that every symmetry is a signed permutation.
