Conversely every such map preserves the coordinate inequalities |xᵢ|≤1. Counting signs and permutations proves the exhaustive list.

boundaryCheck.question: Does every element of O(3) preserve this cube?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The cube is a special finite subset/solid, not the whole metric space.

application.question: How many orientation-preserving cube symmetries exist?
application.explanation: Half of the eight sign choices for each axis permutation give determinant +1.

transfer.question: Why is −I₃ outside SO(3)?
choices: It does not preserve the cube
transfer.explanation: Its three negative eigenvalues multiply to −1.

cube-signed-permutations.connection: Recover the signed data from a matrix and explain why every such matrix preserves the cube.

cube-generator-words.hook: How can just two quarter-turns generate every cube rotation?
cube-generator-words.objects: A is a positive quarter turn about the x-axis; $B$ is a positive quarter turn about the z-axis. Vectors are columns. In a product AB, $B$ acts first. If the controls apply A, then $B$, then J, the displayed product must be JBA. Different words can represent the same group element; a breadth-first search produces a shortest word in a specified generator alphabet.

prerequisiteCheck.question: In ABv, what acts first?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The rightmost operator acts first.

examples.title: Reach all face directions
steps: The quarter-turns A about x and B about z move e₃ among ±e₁,±e₂,±e₃.
This gives an orbit of six face directions. B fixes e₃ and has four distinct powers.

examples.title: The order of two moves matters
steps: A sends e₁ to e₁; B sends e₁ to e₂.
ABe₁=Ae₂=e₃, while BAe₁=Be₁=e₂. Thus AB≠BA.

nonexample.title: Chronology versus written word
nonexample.explanation: AB applies B first to column vectors. A recorded chronological move list must reverse this order when displayed as an operator product.

proofSteps: The generated subgroup lies in the 24 rotations because both generators do.
Its face-direction orbit has six elements and its stabilizer contains the four powers of B.
Orbit–stabilizer gives at least 24 elements, so it is the entire rotation group. Adjoining central inversion gives all 48 symmetries.

boundaryCheck.question: Does seeing relations A⁴=B⁴=I prove these generate all rotations?
choices: No; a size or reachability argument is needed
boundaryCheck.explanation: Relations alone do not establish that every target motion is reached.

application.question: What are ABe₁ and BAe₁?
application.explanation: Use the displayed columns of A and B in the stated order.

transfer.question: Why does the orbit/stabilizer argument prove equality rather than just containment?
choices: Every subgroup has equal size to G
The subgroup has at least 24 elements and lies in a 24-element group
transfer.explanation: Both lower and upper size bounds are required.

cube-generator-words.connection: Verify AB≠BA on a specific vector and explain why listed relations need not be a complete presentation.

cube-four-actions.hook: Can the same symmetry be visible on vertices but invisible on diagonals?
cube-four-actions.objects: For vertices, apply $Q$ to the point. For an edge, apply $Q$ to its unordered endpoint pair. For a face, apply $Q$ to its outward unit normal. For a body diagonal, apply $Q$ to the line through an opposite vertex pair; vectors $v$ and $-v$ represent the same diagonal. Each construction respects composition, so each gives a group homomorphism.

prerequisiteCheck.question: How many unoriented body diagonals does a cube have?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Each joins an opposite pair of the eight vertices.

examples.title: Four sets of objects
steps: The cube acts on eight vertices, twelve edges, six faces and four unoriented body-diagonal lines.
Permutation matrices on these sets have different sizes; they represent different actions of the same group.

examples.title: The inversion witness
steps: −I sends every vertex to its opposite and exchanges opposite faces and edges.
Each body-diagonal line equals its own negative, so inversion fixes all four diagonal objects.

nonexample.title: A diagonal line is not an oriented endpoint
nonexample.explanation: Treating a diagonal as one selected vertex changes the action and destroys the claimed {I,−I} kernel.

proofSteps: Fixing all vertices fixes a spanning set, so the vertex kernel is trivial; faces similarly fix coordinate normals.
An edge-fixed motion fixes vertices through their incident-edge intersections.
If an orthogonal cube map fixes all four diagonal lines, it acts on each by a sign; their nonzero mutual dot products force all signs equal. Hence Q=±I.

boundaryCheck.question: Which object type makes inversion invisible?
boundaryCheck.explanation: A line Rv equals R(−v).

application.question: What is the full diagonal-action kernel?
application.explanation: The orthogonality argument excludes every other motion.

transfer.question: Why can a faithful group have a nonfaithful action?
choices: Faithfulness belongs to a chosen action, not just G
A nonfaithful action is not an action
transfer.explanation: Changing the observed objects changes which motions are detectable.

cube-four-actions.connection: Explain why −I is invisible on unoriented diagonals but not on vertices.

cube-orbit-stabilizer.hook: How many motions remain after one cube object has been chosen?
cube-orbit-stabilizer.objects: Both the rotational and full cube groups act transitively on each of the four object sets. In the rotational group, the stabilizer orders are 3 for a vertex, 2 for an edge, 4 for a face, and 6 for an unoriented diagonal. In the full group these become 6, 4, 8, and 12 respectively. A diagonal stabilizer may exchange its two endpoints.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does Gₓ consist of?
choices: Motions preserving the chosen object x
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Stabilizer is a subgroup of motions; orbit is a set of objects.

examples.title: Fix one face under rotations
steps: The 24 rotations move a chosen face among all six faces.
Its stabilizer has size 24/6=4: rotations by multiples of 90 degrees about its normal axis.

examples.title: Fix a diagonal line
steps: The rotation orbit has four diagonal lines, giving stabilizer size 24/4=6.
In the full 48-element group the same orbit gives stabilizer size twelve; inversion is now included.

nonexample.title: Setwise preservation does not fix every point
nonexample.explanation: The face stabilizer can rotate its four vertices. It fixes the face as an object, not pointwise.

proofSteps: For x with stabilizer H, gH→gx is a well-defined bijection onto the orbit.
Every left H-coset has |H| elements; finite counting gives |G|=|Gx||H|.
The cube actions are transitive, so inserting 8,12,6,4 for orbit sizes yields the stated stabilizer orders.

boundaryCheck.question: Can one divide by all six faces without proving transitivity?
choices: No; use the actual orbit size
boundaryCheck.explanation: Orbit–stabilizer uses destinations actually reachable from x.

application.question: What is an edge stabilizer size in the rotation group?
application.explanation: Twenty-four rotations divided by twelve edges gives two.

transfer.question: Why does adjoining inversion double every listed stabilizer?
choices: Orbit sizes stay the same while group size doubles
transfer.explanation: Each action remains transitive on the same object set.

cube-orbit-stabilizer.connection: Identify which stabilizer motions exchange the endpoints of an edge or diagonal.

cube-diagonals-s4.hook: Why do spatial rotations secretly form the permutation group on four objects?
cube-diagonals-s4.objects: Use representatives $d_{1}=(1,1,1)$, $d_{2}=(1,1,-1)$, $d_{3}=(1,-1,1)$, $d_{4}=(-1,1,1)$. Our generators induce $A=(1\,3\,4\,2)$ and $B=(1\,4\,2\,3)$, with the same rightmost-first composition convention as the matrices. This correspondence translates spatial composition into permutation multiplication.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What do the four permuted labels represent?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The action is on four unoriented diagonals.

examples.title: Find the faithful rotation action
steps: The kernel on diagonal lines in the full group is {I,−I}.
Among rotations only I remains, since det(−I)=−1. Thus rotations inject into S₄.

examples.title: A counting isomorphism
steps: There are 24 cube rotations and 4!=24 diagonal permutations.
An injective homomorphism between these two finite sets is surjective and therefore an isomorphism.

nonexample.title: Full cube symmetry is not S₄
nonexample.explanation: The full group has 48 elements and a two-element diagonal kernel. It is its quotient by {±I}, not the full group, that is S₄.

proofSteps: The diagonal action defines a homomorphism.
Restricting its kernel to the determinant-one subgroup gives trivial kernel.
Use the equal finite orders to prove surjectivity; apply first isomorphism to the full action for G/{±I}≅S₄.

boundaryCheck.question: Does equal order alone prove two groups are isomorphic?
choices: No; here a faithful homomorphism supplies the missing structure
boundaryCheck.explanation: The injection and equal finite cardinalities together prove bijective homomorphism.

application.question: What is the order of the diagonal image of the full group?
application.explanation: First isomorphism gives 48/2=24.

transfer.question: Why is the restricted rotation kernel trivial?
choices: −I has determinant −1 and cannot be a rotation
transfer.explanation: Intersect the known full kernel with SO(3).

cube-diagonals-s4.connection: Explain why a spatial quarter-turn has determinant +1 but an odd permutation on the diagonals.

cube-direct-product.hook: Can every reversing cube motion be written uniquely as inversion followed by rotation?
cube-direct-product.objects: If det $Q=+1$, take $\varepsilon =0$ and $R=Q$. If det $Q=-1$, take $\varepsilon =1$ and $R=-Q$. Central inversion commutes with every linear map. Its only overlap with the rotation group is the identity. These facts make the decomposition a direct product, stronger than merely splitting the set into two equal halves.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Why is J central?
choices: A scalar matrix commutes with every matrix
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Scalar multiplication commutes with every linear operator.

examples.title: Factor a reflection
steps: Let Q=diag(1,1,−1). Its determinant is −1.
With J=−I, JQ=diag(−1,−1,1) is a half-turn. Thus Q=J(JQ).

examples.title: Factor a rotation
steps: If det Q=+1, its inversion coordinate is zero and Q itself is the rotation factor.
The two cases give a unique choice ε∈{0,1} and R=JᵋQ.

nonexample.title: Odd dimension matters
nonexample.explanation: In dimension three det(−I)=−1. In even dimension inversion is orientation-preserving, so this particular complementary-factor argument does not transfer unchanged.

proofSteps: J is central and has order two. Its subgroup meets the rotation subgroup only in I.
Every determinant-negative Q becomes a rotation after multiplication by J, proving all motions are reached.
The map (R,ε)→JᵋR preserves products and is injective by the trivial intersection; combine rotations≅S₄ to get G≅S₄×C₂.

boundaryCheck.question: Which property makes this a direct rather than merely semidirect product?
choices: The inversion factor commutes with the rotations
Both factors have the same size
boundaryCheck.explanation: Centrality makes the conjugation action trivial.

application.question: What is J·diag(1,1,−1)?
application.explanation: Multiply each diagonal entry by −1.

transfer.question: What separates the two factors uniquely?
choices: The determinant selects ε; then JᵋQ is R
transfer.explanation: The determinant detects whether inversion must be included.

cube-direct-product.connection: Recover both coordinates of a full cube symmetry and explain why they are independent.

representations-square-modes.hook: Which patterns persist when the square turns or reflects?
representations-square-modes.objects: Label the square vertices cyclically and let its symmetries permute coordinates in $\mathbb R^4$. The pieces are $T=\operatorname{span}(1,1,1,1)$, $L=\operatorname{span}(1,-1,1,-1)$ and $U=\{(a,b,-a,-b):a,b\in\mathbb R\}$. The constant pattern is fixed, the alternating pattern can change sign, and opposite-vertex contrasts move within a plane. Stability of the whole subspace is the point.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Does invariant mean fixed pointwise?
choices: No; a pattern may move within its subspace
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Invariance is setwise closure under every group operator.

examples.title: Three persistent spaces
steps: Label square vertices 0,1,2,3 cyclically. The constant pattern (1,1,1,1) spans T.
The alternating pattern (1,−1,1,−1) spans L; U consists of (a,b,−a,−b). Their dimensions are 1,1,2.

examples.title: Turn a two-dimensional mode
steps: Use u=(1,0,−1,0), v=(0,1,0,−1). A quarter-turn sends u→v and v→−u.
The matrix on U is a 90-degree rotation. It has no real eigenline, proving U is irreducible over R.

nonexample.title: Cyclic eigenlines need not survive reflections
nonexample.explanation: Over C the quarter-turn splits U into two eigenlines. A square reflection exchanges them, so this does not make the full D₄ representation reducible.

proofSteps: Check the quarter-turn and reflection generators preserve T,L,U by permuting coordinates.
The spaces are pairwise orthogonal and dimensions sum to four; therefore R⁴=T⊕L⊕U.
On U the quarter-turn has no real eigenvalue, so no nonzero proper real subspace is invariant under the full group.

boundaryCheck.question: Must a rotation eigenline be invariant under the dihedral group?
choices: No; reflections must also be checked
boundaryCheck.explanation: The full group has an extra generator that can exchange eigenlines.

application.question: What are dim T,dim L,dim U?
application.explanation: The three descriptions give these dimensions, totaling four.

transfer.question: Why is U irreducible over R?
choices: Its quarter-turn has no real eigenline
transfer.explanation: A proper nonzero subspace of a real plane would be a line invariant under the quarter-turn.

representations-square-modes.connection: Recover the original vector from its three components and explain why a moving pattern can span an invariant space.

actions-regular-conjugation.hook: Why do two natural actions of the same group reveal completely different symmetries?
actions-regular-conjugation.objects: The left regular action is faithful, free, and transitive: any group element can be moved to any other in exactly one way. In the conjugation action, orbits are conjugacy classes, the stabilizer of $x$ is its centralizer $C_G(x)$, and the kernel is the center Z(G). For cube rotations, conjugation carries a rotation axis to the transformed axis while preserving the rotation angle.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is the underlying set in both actions?
choices: The coset space G/Z(G) in both
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The action formulas differ while the point set remains G.

examples.title: Regular action of S₃
steps: Under left multiplication, any x can be sent to y by yx⁻¹.
Only e fixes x, so the action is both transitive and free.

examples.title: Conjugation action of S₃
steps: The identity is fixed by every conjugation, while transpositions form a three-element orbit.
The kernel is Z(S₃)={e}, so the action is faithful but is neither transitive nor free.

nonexample.title: Faithful does not mean free
nonexample.explanation: The conjugation action of S₃ is faithful although the identity point has full stabilizer.

proofSteps: gx=x gives g=e in the regular action.
gxg⁻¹=x gives g∈C_G(x) in the conjugation action.
Fixing every x by conjugation means g∈Z(G); orbit–stabilizer gives each conjugacy class size.

boundaryCheck.question: Does trivial action kernel imply every point stabilizer is trivial?
boundaryCheck.explanation: The kernel is the intersection of stabilizers; individual stabilizers can be larger.

application.question: What is the conjugation stabilizer of e?
application.explanation: Every g satisfies geg⁻¹=e.

transfer.question: When is the conjugation action faithful?
transfer.explanation: Its kernel is exactly the center.

actions-regular-conjugation.connection: Execute every instruction in the prompt using visible controls.

actions-cube-burnside.hook: Can a motion with no fixed face still preserve a face coloring?
actions-cube-burnside.objects: Color the six faces independently from $k$ labeled colors, allowing repetition and allowing some colors to be unused. A coloring is fixed by a symmetry exactly when it is constant on each cycle of that symmetry’s face permutation. For rotations, the face cycle types and counts are $1^{6}$:1, $1^{2}2^{2}$:3, $1^{2}4$:6, $2^{3}$:6, and $3^{2}$:8. Including orientation reversal gives a different equivalence relation.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is one coloring here?
choices: A color assignment to all six faces
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The configuration set has k⁶ labelled face colorings.

examples.title: Two-color face count
steps: Rotations on six faces have total cycle-count polynomial k⁶+3k⁴+12k³+8k².
At k=2 the average is (64+48+96+32)/24=10 orbits.

examples.title: Reflection equivalence can merge orbits
steps: For three colors, the rotation-only face count is 57.
The full symmetry count is 56, so allowing orientation-reversing motions identifies one pair of rotational classes.

nonexample.title: Specify the acted-on objects
nonexample.explanation: These formulas color the six faces. Substituting them for the eight-vertex coloring formula changes the problem.

proofSteps: A coloring fixed by g must be constant on each cycle of its face permutation, giving kᶜ⁽ᵍ⁾ choices.
Double-count pairs (g,coloring) fixed by g; each coloring orbit contributes |G| pairs.
Average the enumerated face cycle counts. Finite enumeration verifies the example polynomial; Burnside proves why the averaging works.

boundaryCheck.question: Must every available color be used?
choices: No, unless an inventory is explicitly imposed
boundaryCheck.explanation: The k choices on each cycle allow unused colors.

application.question: How many rotational two-color face orbits are there?
application.explanation: Apply the displayed Burnside polynomial at two.

transfer.question: Why can a face-moving motion fix a coloring?
choices: It changes the labels but not the group
All faces in each permutation cycle can share a color
transfer.explanation: Fixed configurations are not the same as fixed individual positions.

actions-cube-burnside.connection: Recover 57 versus 56 three-color face-coloring orbits from the displayed group action.

actions-cycle-lenses.hook: Does an observed motion keep the original group element’s order?
actions-cycle-lenses.objects: A face quarter turn has vertex cycle type $4^{2}$, edge type $4^{3}$, face type $1^{2}4$, and diagonal type 4. Its two fixed faces are obvious only in the face view, yet every view detects order four. Central inversion has order two on vertices, edges, and faces but acts identically on the four diagonal lines. An action can hide part or all of an element’s order.

prerequisiteCheck.question: How is a permutation order calculated?
choices: Least common multiple of its cycle lengths
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: All disjoint cycles must return simultaneously.

examples.title: An invisible inversion
steps: Inversion has order two in the full cube group.
On diagonal lines its induced permutation is identity, of order one.

examples.title: A faithful vertex lens
steps: The action on vertices has trivial kernel.
Therefore a cube motion and its vertex permutation have the same order, even if their displayed cycle shapes differ from the face action.

nonexample.title: Different actions can hide different returns
nonexample.explanation: A permutation order lower than the matrix order can be correct when the action has a kernel. It need not signal a calculation error.

proofSteps: For finite-order g, restrict the action homomorphism to ⟨g⟩.
Its kernel is ⟨g⟩∩ker φ; first isomorphism identifies the image cyclic group.
Thus ord(φ(g))=ord(g)/|⟨g⟩∩ker φ|. The permutation order is also the lcm of its cycle lengths.

boundaryCheck.question: Is order preserved by every action?
choices: No; only a faithful action guarantees it for every element
Only if the action is transitive
boundaryCheck.explanation: A nontrivial kernel can shorten observed orders.

application.question: What order does inversion have on diagonal lines?
application.explanation: Every unoriented diagonal line is preserved, so the permutation is identity.

transfer.question: If g has order six and its cyclic kernel intersection has size two, what is the image order?
transfer.explanation: The cyclic quotient has order six divided by two.

actions-cycle-lenses.connection: Explain exactly when observed permutation order is smaller than group-element order.

linear-bruhat.hook: What remains visible when elimination is restricted to triangular moves?
linear-bruhat.objects: Work in $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ over a field. Left multiplication performs row operations; right multiplication performs column operations. Allowing only upper triangular operations leaves a unique relative position, indexed by a permutation. These relative positions are the double cosets of $B$. This is the matrix version of comparing two complete flags.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is B?
choices: All triangular matrices including singular ones
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: B is a subgroup of GLₙ.

examples.title: The two cells in dimension two
steps: For an invertible matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], c=0 means the matrix is already upper triangular, in B.
If c≠0, triangular row and column operations place it in the cell of the swap matrix s.

examples.title: A swap is not triangular
steps: The matrix [[0,1],[1,0]] lies in BsB rather than B.
Its image of the standard line differs from the standard line, distinguishing the two relative-flag positions.

nonexample.title: A Bruhat cell is not a single matrix
nonexample.explanation: The permutation labels an entire double coset BwB. Many matrices share a relative-flag position.

proofSteps: For GL₂ the zero/nonzero lower-left distinction gives a complete two-cell proof by restricted elimination.
For general n, upper-triangular operations identify pivot positions; relative-flag intersection ranks determine the unique permutation.
This is the general proof roadmap. Ordinary unrestricted row reduction loses the flag invariants and cannot establish uniqueness by itself.

boundaryCheck.question: Are the Bruhat cells ordinary left cosets?
choices: No, they are double cosets BwB
boundaryCheck.explanation: Both left and right B moves are allowed.

application.question: Which cell contains [[1,2],[0,3]] over Q?
application.explanation: The matrix is invertible upper triangular.

transfer.question: What certifies uniqueness of the permutation?
transfer.explanation: These ranks are preserved by triangular transformations and encode the pivot permutation.

linear-bruhat.connection: Decide the 2×2 cell and exhibit valid triangular factors, not just its cardinality.

linear-projective.hook: Why must scalar symmetries be removed before special linear groups become simple?
linear-projective.objects: For $n\ge2$, the center of $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ consists of nonzero scalar matrices; in $\operatorname{SL}_n(F)$ they also satisfy $\lambda^n=1$. The action on one-dimensional subspaces factors through the projective quotient. Transvections generate the special linear group, and outside two small exceptions they are commutators.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is removed in PSLₙ?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The scalar λI remains in SL precisely when λⁿ=1.

examples.title: Compute PSL₂(F₃)
steps: GL₂(F₃) has 48 elements. Divide by q−1=2 to get |SL₂|=24.
The scalar center has gcd(2,2)=2 elements, giving |PSL₂|=12. This is one of the simplicity exceptions.

examples.title: Compute PSL₂(F₅)
steps: Divide by four and then two to get |PSL₂(F₅)|=60; the simplicity theorem applies.

nonexample.title: SL and PSL are different
nonexample.explanation: SL₂(F₅) contains the nontrivial central scalar −I. It is PSL₂(F₅), its quotient by that center, that is simple.

proofSteps: The determinant quotient divides the GL order by q−1.
Scalar matrices in SL obey λⁿ=1; the cyclic F_q× gives gcd(n,q−1) such scalars.
Simplicity is an imported structural theorem for n≥2 except (n,|F|)=(2,2),(2,3). Its projective action/perfectness argument is a roadmap, not a full proof here.

boundaryCheck.question: Which small fields are exceptional for PSL₂ simplicity?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Both exceptions must remain explicit.

application.question: What is |PSL₂(F₅)|?

transfer.question: Why cannot one transfer PSL simplicity directly to SL?
choices: The scalar kernel can be a proper nontrivial normal subgroup
transfer.explanation: Quotienting removes central symmetries; the original group may retain them.

linear-projective.connection: Compute the quotient order and state exactly which earlier theorems support simplicity.

actions-primitive.hook: When does an action hide a nontrivial grouping of its points?
actions-primitive.objects: Assume $X$ is a transitive $G$-set with $|X|\ge2$ and fix $x\in X$. Blocks containing $x$ correspond to subgroups between $G_x$ and $G$: a subgroup $H$ gives $Hx$. The trivial blocks are singletons and $X$. An action is primitive when no other blocks exist. Double transitivity means transitivity on ordered pairs of distinct points.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does transitive mean?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Every point can be reached from any chosen point.

examples.title: A block in a square
steps: For rotations C₄ on {0,1,2,3}, the pair {0,2} moves either to itself or the disjoint pair {1,3}.
This is a nontrivial block, so the transitive action is imprimitive.

examples.title: A primitive action
steps: S₃ on three letters is doubly transitive.
A block containing two distinct letters must contain the third under the stabilizer of one letter, so only singleton and whole-set blocks remain.

nonexample.title: Transitivity is part of this equivalence
nonexample.explanation: The maximal-stabilizer criterion is stated for transitive actions of degree at least two. A arbitrary disconnected action does not fit its proof.

proofSteps: For a block Δ containing x, let H be its setwise stabilizer. The point stabilizer Gₓ lies in H.
Transitivity and the block condition prove Δ=Hx. Conversely Gₓ≤H≤G gives a block Hx.
These constructions are inverse. Thus nontrivial blocks correspond to intermediate subgroups, and primitivity means Gₓ is proper maximal.

boundaryCheck.question: Which assumptions support the maximal-stabilizer criterion?
choices: Transitive action with at least two points
boundaryCheck.explanation: The block/subgroup correspondence uses transitivity.

application.question: Is {0,2} a block for the four-cycle action?
choices: No, because two points are moved
Only if every rotation fixes it
application.explanation: Each translate is itself or the disjoint opposite pair.

transfer.question: Why does double transitivity force primitivity?
choices: A point stabilizer can move a second block point to every other point
transfer.explanation: Any block with two points then expands to the whole set.

actions-primitive.connection: Prove the block/intermediate-subgroup correspondence with the boundary cases specified.

group-complements.hook: When does a normal piece have an independent subgroup partner?
group-complements.objects: For a finite group, a Hall subgroup has order coprime to its index. Schur–Zassenhaus says that a normal Hall subgroup has a complement, so the group is a semidirect product. Existence of a complement and conjugacy of complements are separate assertions; the latter has an elementary treatment when the normal subgroup or quotient is solvable.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What makes a subgroup Hall?
choices: Its order is coprime to its index
It is always a Sylow subgroup for one prime
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Hall can collect several primes; coprimality is the key property.

examples.title: A coprime split
steps: In S₃, A₃ is normal of order three and index two.
The transposition subgroup C₂ meets it trivially and together they generate S₃=A₃⋊C₂.

examples.title: A noncoprime obstruction
steps: In C₄, the order-two subgroup is normal but has no complement.
Every order-two subgroup is that same subgroup, so no disjoint partner of order two exists.

nonexample.title: Complement is not centrality
nonexample.explanation: A complement need not be normal. The split in S₃ is semidirect, because conjugation by a transposition inverts A₃.

proofSteps: For finite G and normal N with gcd(|N|,[G:N])=1, Schur–Zassenhaus supplies a complement H.
The existence theorem is imported; the coprime averaging/induction description is a proof roadmap.
Given H, unique expressions nh and the conjugation action prove G≅N⋊H. No unjustified direct-product conclusion is made.

boundaryCheck.question: What does Schur–Zassenhaus existence require here?
choices: A finite group and normal Hall subgroup
boundaryCheck.explanation: C₄ shows why coprime index matters.

application.question: What complements A₃ in S₃?
choices: A subgroup generated by a transposition
application.explanation: Orders three and two multiply to six and the intersection is trivial.

transfer.question: Why does the C₄ example not contradict the theorem?
choices: The order and index are both two
transfer.explanation: It fails the Hall coprimality hypothesis.

group-complements.connection: Show explicitly why the order-two subgroup of C₄ has no complement.

group-extensions.hook: What records a failure to choose compatible quotient representatives?
group-extensions.objects: A section is initially only a set map. Conjugation by $t(a)$ gives $\varphi(a)\in\operatorname{Aut}(N)$. Associativity imposes compatibility between $\varphi$ and $f$. If $N=A$ is abelian, the action is a genuine homomorphism and the defect is an additive $2$-cocycle. Replacing the section changes the cocycle by a coboundary.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is a section t of π?
choices: A map with πt=id on the quotient
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A set-theoretic section chooses representatives; compatibility is an extra property.

examples.title: A nonsplit C₄ extension
steps: Write C₄ additively and quotient by {0,2} to get C₂. Choose section t(0)=0,t(1)=1.
Then t(1)+t(1)−t(0)=2, the nonzero kernel element. No homomorphic section exists because every order-two lift lies in the kernel.

examples.title: A split extension
steps: For C₂×C₂ projected to the second factor, choose t(b)=(0,b).
The defect t(a)+t(b)−t(a+b) is always zero, so this section is a homomorphism.

nonexample.title: Abelian formula cannot type-check an arbitrary kernel
nonexample.explanation: The additive cocycle identity assumes an abelian kernel A and a fixed quotient action. Nonabelian kernels need a full factor pair.

proofSteps: Fix an action of H on abelian A. A normalized section gives a defect f(a,b) in A.
Associating t(a)t(b)t(c) in the two ways produces the 2-cocycle equation.
Changing section by c:H→A changes f by δc; a zero cohomology class means a corrected section is a homomorphism, giving a split extension.

boundaryCheck.question: When is the additive cocycle formula used?
choices: For an abelian kernel with specified action
boundaryCheck.explanation: The additive algebra and H-action must be defined on A.

application.question: What is the section defect at (1,1) in C₄→C₂?
application.explanation: Two representatives of one add to two, whereas the representative of zero is zero.

transfer.question: What does vanishing of the extension class say?
choices: Every chosen section already is a homomorphism
Some corrected section is a homomorphism
transfer.explanation: A coboundary can be removed by changing representatives.

group-extensions.connection: Compute the carry cocycle and explain why changing a section need not change the extension class.

group-solvable.hook: Can repeated removal of noncommutativity reduce a group to identity?
group-solvable.objects: Solvability is equivalent to admitting a finite subnormal series with abelian factors. It passes to subgroups and quotients, and if both a normal subgroup and its quotient are solvable, so is the whole group. For finite groups it is equivalent to having only prime-order composition factors, or elementary abelian chief factors.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is G′?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: It measures the obstruction to an abelian quotient.

examples.title: The derived series of S₃
steps: S₃′=A₃, since commutators include a three-cycle and the sign map kills them.
A₃ is abelian, so its derived subgroup is identity. Thus S₃ is solvable.

examples.title: A nilpotent distinction
steps: S₃ is solvable, but its Sylow two-subgroups are not normal.
Therefore it is not nilpotent; solvability is the weaker condition.

nonexample.title: Abelian quotient alone is not enough
nonexample.explanation: Having one abelian quotient does not prove solvability; the normal kernel must itself be solvable.

proofSteps: An abelian factor forces the derived subgroup into the next subnormal term.
Iterating along a finite abelian-factor series makes the derived series terminate. Conversely a terminating derived series has abelian factors.
Hall existence and conjugacy for finite solvable groups is imported; the minimal-normal-subgroup induction is a roadmap, not a complete proof here.

boundaryCheck.question: Does solvable mean abelian?
boundaryCheck.explanation: S₃ supplies a nonabelian solvable example.

application.question: What is the second derived subgroup of S₃?
application.explanation: The first is cyclic A₃, whose commutator subgroup is trivial.

transfer.question: When does an extension of solvable groups stay solvable?
choices: When both the normal kernel and quotient are solvable
When only the quotient is solvable
When only the kernel is abelian
transfer.explanation: The derived series first enters the kernel and then terminates inside it.

group-solvable.connection: Prove closure under extensions and distinguish solvable from nilpotent.

group-nilpotent.hook: Why is central structure stronger than merely abelian layers?
group-nilpotent.objects: A group is nilpotent exactly when its lower central series reaches $1$, or its upper central series reaches $G$, in finitely many steps. For finite groups this is also equivalent to every Sylow subgroup being normal, to being the direct product of the Sylow subgroups, and to every proper subgroup being properly contained in its normalizer.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What does an upper central step use?
choices: The center of the quotient by the previous term
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Zᵢ₊₁ is the inverse image of Z(G/Zᵢ).

examples.title: Central layers of Q₈
steps: Z(Q₈)={±1}. Its quotient is C₂×C₂ and is abelian.
The upper central series reaches Q₈ in two steps, so Q₈ is nilpotent but not abelian.

examples.title: Solvable without nilpotence
steps: S₃ has derived series S₃≥A₃≥1.
Its center is trivial, so its upper central series does not grow; it is not nilpotent.

nonexample.title: The finite Sylow equivalence has limits
nonexample.explanation: Nilpotent iff product of Sylow subgroups is the finite-group criterion here; do not apply it to an arbitrary infinite group.

proofSteps: A nontrivial finite p-group has nontrivial center; repeat in central quotients to obtain nilpotence.
For finite nilpotent groups, the normalizer condition forces Sylow subgroups normal. Distinct normal coprime Sylows commute and give the internal direct product.
For finite p-groups, maximal subgroups have index p; their intersection contains commutators and pth powers, giving an elementary abelian Frattini quotient.

boundaryCheck.question: Is every solvable finite group nilpotent?
choices: Only if its order has two primes
boundaryCheck.explanation: S₃ is solvable but has nonnormal Sylow two-subgroups.

application.question: What is the nilpotence class of Q₈?
application.explanation: It is nonabelian but its quotient by its center is abelian.

transfer.question: Why do normal Sylows of distinct primes commute?
choices: All Sylow elements are central individually
Their commutators lie in both subgroups, whose intersection is trivial
transfer.explanation: Normality and coprime orders provide both ingredients.

group-nilpotent.connection: Distinguish derived length from nilpotency class and use the Frattini quotient to test generators.

characters-integrality.hook: Why do complex traces constrain integer representation degrees?
characters-integrality.objects: Algebraic integers form a ring, and a rational algebraic integer is an ordinary integer. Since a finite-order complex matrix has roots of unity as eigenvalues, every character value is an algebraic integer. For an irreducible character, the scalar by which a conjugacy-class sum acts is also an algebraic integer.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What makes a polynomial equation certify integrality?
choices: It is monic with integer coefficients
It has any nonzero leading coefficient
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: A rational algebraic number need not be integral.

examples.title: A root of unity is integral
steps: A finite-order eigenvalue ζ satisfies ζᵐ−1=0, a monic integer equation.
Character values are sums of such eigenvalues and hence algebraic integers.

examples.title: Check S₃ degrees
steps: The irreducible degrees are 1,1,2, all dividing six.
For a three-cycle and the standard character, |class|χ(g)/χ(1)=2·(−1)/2=−1, an algebraic integer.

nonexample.title: The theorem is for complex irreducibles
nonexample.explanation: The divisibility assertion must not be transferred without qualification to arbitrary real or modular representation degrees.

proofSteps: Class sums multiply with integer structure constants, so their scalar actions on complex irreducibles satisfy monic integer polynomials.
Row orthogonality writes |G|/χ(1) as a sum of these scalars multiplied by conjugate character values.
The algebraic-integer closure and rational-integral lemma imply this rational quotient is an integer. The class-sum integrality lemma is an imported proof dependency.

boundaryCheck.question: Which characters satisfy the degree-divisibility theorem stated here?
choices: Irreducible complex characters of a finite group
boundaryCheck.explanation: Finite complex ordinary character theory supplies the orthogonality proof.

application.question: For standard S₃ at a three-cycle, what is |class|χ(g)/χ(1)?
application.explanation: The class has two elements, character value −1, degree two.

transfer.question: Why is a rational algebraic integer an ordinary integer?
choices: The rational-root theorem forces its denominator to be one
Its absolute value is at most one
transfer.explanation: Apply the rational-root divisibility argument to a monic integer polynomial.

characters-integrality.connection: Explain why |G|/χ(1) is both rational and an algebraic integer.

characters-burnside.hook: How can the size of one conjugacy class rule out simplicity?
characters-burnside.objects: Burnside proves that every finite group of order $p^aq^b$ is solvable. The key character-theoretic obstruction says that a nonabelian finite simple group has no conjugacy class of size a nontrivial prime power. Prime-power here describes the size of the class, not the order of its representative. In the nonabelian simple case, $z$ is not central in $G$, so the class size is greater than one. Having excluded all nonabelian simple groups of two-prime order, induction on group order makes both a proper normal subgroup and its quotient solvable; their extension is solvable.

prerequisiteCheck.question: How is |gᴳ| obtained?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Conjugation orbit–stabilizer gives the class size.

examples.title: A small class in S₃
steps: The three transpositions form a conjugacy class of prime-power size three.
S₃ has the proper normal subgroup A₃, consistent with the prime-power class theorem.

examples.title: Two-prime order
steps: A group of order 72=2³·3² is solvable by Burnside’s theorem.
It need not be abelian: S₃×C₁₂ is a nonabelian example of that order.

nonexample.title: Solvable is not a classification
nonexample.explanation: Burnside does not identify a unique group or imply commutativity; it constrains the derived series.

proofSteps: Import the character-theoretic lemma that a nonabelian finite simple group has no nontrivial prime-power conjugacy class.

For a hypothetical simple group of order pᵃqᵇ, choose nonidentity z in the center of a Sylow q-subgroup. Its centralizer contains that Sylow, so its class size is a p-power; simplicity makes it nontrivial.
The lemma rules out simplicity. Induction on proper normal subgroups and quotients, with solvable-extension closure, proves the theorem. Prime-power cases use the center theorem.

boundaryCheck.question: Does the prime-power class obstruction include a singleton central class?
choices: No; the stated obstruction requires size greater than one
boundaryCheck.explanation: Every identity class is singleton, even in simple groups.

application.question: What does order 72 guarantee?
application.explanation: It has only the two prime divisors two and three.

transfer.question: Why can a Sylow-central z have a p-power class size?
choices: Its centralizer contains the full q-Sylow subgroup
z is central in the entire group necessarily
transfer.explanation: The q-part cancels from the centralizer index.

characters-burnside.connection: No necklace controls appear; a reader can follow why a Sylow-central element produces a prime-power class size.

actions-frobenius.hook: Why is closure of fixed-point-free motions a surprising theorem?
actions-frobenius.objects: For a finite faithful permutation group satisfying this condition, the identity together with the fixed-point-free elements is the Frobenius kernel. It is a regular normal subgroup. A point stabilizer is a complement, so the group is a semidirect product. The closure assertion is the surprising part: it does not follow just by inspecting fixed points of a product.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is a derangement of X?
choices: An element in the action kernel
An element fixing exactly one point
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Fixed-point-free refers to the entire point set.

examples.title: Affine motions on F₅
steps: The group x→ax+b has 4·5=20 elements. A nonidentity translation x→x+b has no fixed point.
For a≠1 the fixed-point equation (1−a)x=b has one solution.

examples.title: Kernel and complement
steps: Translations form a normal C₅ acting regularly on the five field elements.
Maps x→ax fix zero and form C₄; together the group is C₅⋊C₄.

nonexample.title: Counting does not prove closure
nonexample.explanation: A set of derangements in a general transitive action need not become a subgroup after adding identity. The at-most-one-fixed-point premise matters.

proofSteps: For a finite faithful transitive action of degree greater than one, assume every nonidentity element fixes at most one point.
Different point stabilizers intersect trivially; counting identifies the size of the proposed kernel.
Frobenius’s theorem, imported via induced characters, supplies the missing closure and normality. Its regular action then gives the semidirect product with a point stabilizer.

boundaryCheck.question: What condition is required for every nonidentity element?
boundaryCheck.explanation: It is a global condition on the action, not just the selected generators.

application.question: Where does x→2x+1 fix a point in F₅?
application.explanation: (1−2)x=1 gives −x=1, hence x=4.

transfer.question: What step is supplied by Frobenius’s theorem rather than counting?
choices: Closure and normality of the proposed kernel
transfer.explanation: A cardinality calculation alone cannot establish subgroup multiplication.

actions-frobenius.connection: Verify the fixed-point condition and identify the kernel and complement in AGL₁(𝔽₅).

linear-quotient.hook: Why does collapsing the kernel preserve exactly the outputs of a linear map?
linear-quotient.objects: Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map over a field. The quotient has vector addition and scalar multiplication inherited from $V$. If two representatives differ by a kernel vector, their images agree, so the displayed map is well-defined. Every image vector has a representative, and only the zero coset maps to zero.

prerequisiteCheck.question: What is one element of V/ker T?
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: The quotient identifies inputs having the same output.

examples.title: Collapse a diagonal line
steps: Let T:Q²→Q, T(x,y)=x+y. Its kernel is ⟨(1,−1)⟩.
Every coset has one sum value; the induced map Q²/ker T→Q is a linear bijection.

examples.title: Keep the actual image
steps: Let S:Q²→Q², S(x,y)=(x+y,0).
Its image is the first coordinate line, not all Q². The quotient has dimension one.

nonexample.title: Codomain is not automatically image
nonexample.explanation: The first isomorphism theorem identifies V/ker T with im T. It reaches the whole codomain only if T is surjective.

proofSteps: If v−u lies in ker T, then T(v)=T(u), proving representative independence.
The induced map is linear, onto im T, and injective because equal outputs give a kernel difference.
For finite-dimensional V, extend a kernel basis; images of the added basis vectors form an image basis, proving rank–nullity.

boundaryCheck.question: Which target is always isomorphic to V/ker T?
boundaryCheck.explanation: Surjectivity onto the codomain is a separate premise.

application.question: For T(x,y)=x+y, what is ker T?
application.explanation: Solve x+y=0.

transfer.question: For a 4-dimensional domain and 1-dimensional kernel, what is dim im T?
transfer.explanation: Finite-dimensional rank–nullity gives 4−1.

linear-quotient.connection: Build a basis of V/ker T and identify its image under the induced isomorphism.

quadratic-quotient.hook: How can one quadratic relation produce a field, a product, or a nilpotent?
quadratic-quotient.objects: Every residue class has a unique representative $u+v\alpha$, because the modulus is monic of degree two. The quotient therefore has $p^2$ elements. Addition works coefficient by coefficient. Multiplication expands first, then uses the defining relation. The same construction gives fields, products of fields, or rings with nilpotents depending on factorisation.

prerequisiteCheck.question: Why are there p² classes in a monic quadratic quotient over Fₚ?
choices: Two independent coefficients each have p choices
prerequisiteCheck.explanation: Unique degree-below-two remainders give the count.

examples.title: A field case
steps: Over F₂, X²+X+1 has no root and is irreducible.
Its quotient is F₄; the nonzero class α has inverse α+1.

examples.title: A repeated-root case
steps: Over F₂, X²+1=(X+1)². In its quotient ε=α+1 is nonzero but ε²=0.
The quotient still has four elements, but is not a field. The split distinct-root polynomial X²+X instead yields F₂×F₂.

nonexample.title: Cardinality cannot determine structure
nonexample.explanation: All three quadratic quotients have four elements. A nonzero nilpotent, a pair of zero divisors, or absence of both distinguishes their rings.

proofSteps: Monic division gives unique representatives a+bα and relation α²=−bα−c.
For an irreducible modulus, Bézout gives an inverse to every nonzero lower-degree representative.
A reducible modulus yields nonzero factor classes with product zero. Repeated factors give nilpotents; coprime distinct factors give a product by CRT.

boundaryCheck.question: When is the quotient a field?
choices: Exactly when the quadratic is irreducible
boundaryCheck.explanation: Irreducibility makes the modulus ideal maximal.

application.question: In F₂[X]/((X+1)²), what is (α+1)²?
application.explanation: The defining relation is precisely (α+1)²=0.

transfer.question: What distinguishes distinct-root splitting from a repeated root?
choices: The first yields a product; the second has a nonzero nilpotent
transfer.explanation: Both have dimension two, but their multiplication and nilpotents differ.

quadratic-quotient.connection: Diagnose all three ring types from factorization of the modulus and verify the diagnosis arithmetically.
